docs.title: CBX-250 (TCR-mimetic CG1/HLA-A*02:01 bispecific T-cell engager, CROSSCHECK-001) (cbx-250)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker1lowThis is the one on-axis lever that doesn't make an 85%-blast patient wait weeks for a cell product to be manufactured, and with peripheral blasts climbing 58 to 82% in a month, wait time is the whole game. The preclinical package is genuinely strong for a phase 1 asset: sub-nanomolar killing across a range of antigen density, survival benefit in a primary-AML PDX at doses as low as 0.005 mg/kg, and no activation against normal neutrophils, CD34+ cells, or PBMCs (doi:10.1182/blood-2024-201699). The upside I'm buying: a T-cell engager that debulks refractory marrow fast and bridges to the second transplant that actually cures. I'm not pretending this is proven; it is first-in-human with zero efficacy readout, it needs the same pending A*02:01 typing as the rest of the axis, and CRS is a real class risk.First-in-human phase 1 with no efficacy or safety readout yet; the strong signal is all preclinical, one of which is an ASH abstract not a full paper; Gated on the still-pending HLA-A*02:01 typing; if the patient is A*02:01-negative the whole pick collapses; Cytokine release syndrome is the expected class toxicity and organ/cardiac fitness is undocumented; CG1 antigen density on this patient's blasts is not established conservative5lowI am ranking this last and flagging it, not endorsing it. The preclinical package (doi:10.1182/blood-2024-201699) is genuinely strong: sub-nanomolar killing across a range of antigen density, no activity against normal neutrophils, CD34+ cells, or PBMCs, and off-the-shelf delivery with no cell-manufacturing wait. What keeps it at the bottom of MY list is a specific missing safety datum, not novelty for its own sake: CROSSCHECK-001 (nct:NCT06994676) is first-in-human with no MTD established and no characterized adverse-event profile in a single treated patient. As a CD3 T-cell engager the anticipated class toxicity is cytokine release syndrome, and CRS severity scales with tumor burden, which in an 85%-blast marrow is the worst-case setting to meet an uncharacterized engager. There is no published human CRS-management experience for this specific agent to lean on. I would not advance it ahead of cytoreduction, and I would want it only after the burden is brought down and HLA-A*02:01 is confirmed. Pre-emptive statement for round 2: if this is nominated as a rank-1 or front-line pick over the transplant/cytoreduction backbone, I will dissent on evidence maturity, and I would move to a toxicity veto contingent on there being no CRS-mitigation plan (step-up dosing, tocilizumab availability, burden reduction first) documented for the high-blast setting.First-in-human with NO established MTD and NO characterized AE profile in any treated patient; the missing datum is a human safety readout, full stop; CD3-engager cytokine release syndrome scales with tumor burden, and 85% marrow blasts is the highest-risk CRS setting to debut an uncharacterized engager; No agent-specific CRS-management experience published to guide dosing, monitoring, or rescue; Gated on still-pending HLA-A*02:01 typing, so eligibility is not even established yet critic——did not pick— concensusite4lowTrial enrollment is the preferred route in R/R AML under both NCCN AML v3.2026 and ELN 2022, and CBX-250 is a recruiting phase-1 on the patient's own A*02:01 axis (CROSSCHECK-001, NCT06994676), so as an enrollment target it is guideline-consonant. Unlike the donor and autologous TCR-T handles it is off-the-shelf, so there is no cell-manufacturing wait, and as a CD3 engager it can in principle work on the active marrow rather than only as post-transplant consolidation. Prior allo-HCT is allowed once 60 days have passed, which fits her. What keeps it at rank 4 on my axis: it is first-in-human with no efficacy or safety readout, it carries no consensus category of its own, and it is gated on the same pending HLA-A*02:01 typing as the rest of that axis.First-in-human, no clinical readout yet; a novel agent with no results has no consensus category, so the only guideline support is the general 'enroll in a trial' preference, not the agent itself.; Eligibility is gated on HLA-A*02:01, still pending typing; without that result she is not a confirmed-eligible patient for this trial.; As a CD3-engaging bispecific the expected class toxicity is cytokine release, and no organ-function or fitness workup is on file to size that risk. advocate1lowThis is the closest match to what the patient actually asked for: an HLA-A*02:01-restricted immunotherapy, recruiting now, that they can travel for. Its edge over the TCR-T options is practical rather than theoretical — off-the-shelf, so no autologous or donor cell-manufacturing lead time, and prior allo-HCT is explicitly permitted once 60 days have passed, which fits a post-transplant relapse. I rank it first on the primary axis while naming the caveats plainly: it is phase 1 first-in-human with no efficacy readout, it carries the T-cell-engager CRS risk, and it sits behind the same pending HLA-A*02:01 typing as every other pick on this axis — the one records pull that unlocks all of them.Fully satisfied: the stated primary axis (HLA-A*02:01-restricted immunotherapy), curative intent, prefers_trials incl. travel, no toxicity veto, efficacy lean; In tension: phase 1 FIH, no efficacy yet, CRS risk expected for a CD3 engager; a lower evidence tier than the HA-1 TCR-T precedent; Gated on the same pending HLA-A*02:01 typing; unlike the TCR-T picks it does NOT require the HA-1/HA-2 mismatch or an HCT2 platform, which is why it can move fastest once A*02:01 is confirmed

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment risktakerconservativedissentpreference_fitRanking the one off-the-shelf agent dead last treats a missing human safety readout as the only cost while ignoring the cost of the wait; peripheral blasts went 58 to 82% in a month, so every autologous or donor product on your slate loses weeks this marrow doesn't have. Your threatened CRS veto is at least conditional on there being no mitigation plan, which I can live with, because step-up dosing plus tocilizumab defeats it and preferences.json lists no toxicity_vetoes. Concede the phase-1 has zero efficacy readout, but don't let 85% blasts harden that conditional into a real veto before the burden-reduction-first plan is even asked for. risktakercriticdissentevidence_qualityDeclining to rank CBX-250 at all makes evidence tier the sole axis and drops the time axis entirely; for a marrow climbing 58 to 82% in a month, the off-the-shelf option with no manufacturing lag earns a place on the list even below every human-readout pick. Mechanism potency isn't clinical evidence, agreed, but a sub-nanomolar engager with a clean normal-tissue profile (doi:10.1182/blood-2024-201699) is a defensible high-upside bet, not a non-entity. I'll concede the honest limit you're right about: NCT06994676 has zero efficacy or safety readout in a single treated patient. risktakeradvocateendorsepreference_fitCBX-250 at rank 1 is the call I'd make too: it is squarely on the stated HLA-A*02:01 axis (preferences.json names HLA-restricted immunotherapy as the reason for the run), recruiting, off-the-shelf, and prior-HCT is permitted at 60 days. For an 85%-blast marrow with no cell-manufacturing wait, that speed edge over the TCR-T handles is the whole argument, and you named the phase-1/no-efficacy caveat honestly. conservativerisktakervetotoxicityThis acts on the conditional I pre-stated in round 1, and the condition is met, so I am issuing the veto rather than restating a worry. CROSSCHECK-001 (nct:NCT06994676) is first-in-human with the MTD/RP2D listed as not yet established, no characterized AE profile in a single treated patient, and no agent-specific CRS step-dose or priming schema anywhere in the dossier; a CD3 engager's cytokine release scales with tumour burden, and 85% marrow blasts with peripheral blasts climbing 58 to 82% is the worst setting to debut an uncharacterized one. The veto is liftable, not absolute: document burden reduction below this threshold first, a step-up dosing schedule, and tocilizumab on-hand monitoring, and I move to dissent, but ranking it first over the cytoreduction backbone with none of that on file is the safety incompatibility I flagged I would stop. conservativeadvocatevetotoxicitySame acted-on conditional as against risktaker: you ranked CBX-250 first on the primary axis, and a first-in-human CD3 engager with no established MTD (nct:NCT06994676) and no characterized AE profile, delivered to an 85%-blast marrow where cytokine release scales with burden, is the safety incompatibility I pre-stated I would stop. I hear that off-the-shelf speed is the case for it, but speed into an uncharacterized engager at peak burden cuts the wrong way on toxicity. The veto lifts to a dissent the moment a documented CRS-mitigation plan exists for this setting: burden reduced below threshold first, step-up dosing, tocilizumab availability; none is on file, so the stop stands. conservativeconcensusitedissenttoxicityYou placed this at rank 4 behind the cytoreduction backbone rather than front-line, so this is a dissent and not the veto I am issuing against the rank-1 nominations. My point is that the 'enroll in a trial' guideline fit carries no safety datum: CROSSCHECK-001 (nct:NCT06994676) has no established MTD and no characterized AE profile, and a CD3 engager's cytokine release scales with the 85%-blast burden. Keep the CRS-in-high-burden gap explicit alongside the enrollment logic, and hold it behind burden reduction plus a documented step-dose and tocilizumab plan, which is the same threshold underneath my veto. criticrisktakerdissentevidence_qualityRanking this first inverts the evidence hierarchy: everything under it is preclinical, and the one supporting row (DOI 10.1182/blood-2024-201699) is an ASH 2024 trial-in-progress-adjacent abstract with no PMID, no per-arm n, and a DOI the dossier itself could not verify and left fail-closed. CROSSCHECK-001 (NCT06994676) has zero human efficacy or safety readout, so a sub-nanomolar EC50 and a PDX survival curve at 0.005 mg/kg tell you the molecule engages the target, not that it helps a patient. The speed argument is real and I will grant it as a tie-breaker among equally unproven off-the-shelf options, but speed is not a reason to seat it above Iomab-B, which actually has a randomized readout in this exact debulk-into-transplant problem. criticadvocatedissentevidence_qualityPreference fit is genuine here and I do not contest that the patient asked for an A*02:01-restricted trial they can travel for. But 'closest match to what the patient asked for' is a preference argument doing the work an evidence argument should do: CBX-250 is first-in-human with no efficacy or safety readout, and the only data are a fail-closed ASH 2024 abstract (DOI 10.1182/blood-2024-201699, no PMID). Off-the-shelf logistics is a fair tie-breaker, not grounds to rank it above Iomab-B (PMID 39298738) or the HA-1 precedent that at least have human readouts; the strongest honest framing is 'preference-matched fastest-to-open trial,' not 'rank 1.' criticconcensusitequalifiedevidence_qualityRank 4 is far more defensible than the rank-1 the risktaker and advocate gave it, and I credit that you seated it below the on-label and platform picks. The one thing I would tighten: the 'enroll in a trial' preference in NCCN/ELN is category-agnostic and attaches to any open trial, so it supports enrollment as an activity, not CBX-250 as an agent, which has no consensus category and no human readout (NCT06994676, ASH 2024 abstract only). The guideline language should not be allowed to launder a first-in-human asset into looking guideline-backed. criticconservativeendorseevidence_qualityThis is the right call and for the right reason: you ranked it last because the missing datum is a human safety readout, and there is none (NCT06994676 first-in-human, no MTD, no AE profile, ASH 2024 abstract only). I would add the evidence-quality mirror of your toxicity point, that the preclinical strength does not offset the absence of any clinical confirmation, and I share your view that a rank-1 nomination over the transplant backbone inverts the hierarchy. Your conditional CRS veto is well-placed given CRS scales with the 85%-blast burden. concensusiterisktakerdissentguideline_fitBoth NCCN AML v3.2026 and ELN 2022 do prefer trial enrollment in R/R AML, so CBX-250 is guideline-consonant as an enrollment target, and I keep it on my own list for that. But that preference attaches to the act of enrolling, not to this agent, which is first-in-human with no results and carries no consensus category of its own. Ranking it above the curative backbone that ELN actually names for post-transplant relapse, a second allo-HCT after cytoreduction, treats 'eligible for a phase 1' as if it were the endorsed intervention. concensusiteadvocatedissentguideline_fitThe advocate's preference-fit case for CBX-250 is coherent on its own terms, and I agree that enrolling on an A*02:01 trial is the guideline-preferred route in R/R AML under NCCN AML v3.2026 and ELN 2022. Where I split: that preference endorses trial participation, not this specific first-in-human agent, which has no results and no consensus category (NCT06994676). Placing it at rank 1 over the curative backbone lets 'closest to what the patient asked for' outrank 'what the guideline actually endorses for this relapse setting.' advocatecriticdissentpreference_fitLeaving CBX-250 off the ranked list entirely answers an evidence-maturity question, not the patient's: free_text names HLA-A*02:01-restricted immunotherapy as the explicit reason for the run, and this is the one on-axis option that is off-the-shelf, recruiting now (NCT06994676), and permits prior allo-HCT after 60 days. I grant the phase-1-no-efficacy reality and that mechanism elegance is not a survival readout. But the workup that unlocks it, HLA-A*02:01 typing, is the same fast records pull the whole axis needs, so it deserves a place in the ranking rather than exclusion. advocateconservativedissentpreference_fitRanking CBX-250 last and threatening a CRS veto de-prioritizes the exact axis the patient came for, and toxicity_vetoes is empty, so there is no stated veto to lean on. I fully concede your load-bearing condition: a CRS-mitigation plan (step-up dosing, tocilizumab on hand, cytoreduction to lower the 85%-blast burden first) has to be documented before this moves, and the phase-1 no-efficacy status is real. But 'no characterized CRS profile yet' is an argument to make the mitigation plan a gate, not to bury an off-the-shelf, recruiting on-axis trial (NCT06994676) beneath cytoreduction options the patient did not prioritize. advocateconcensusitequalifiedpreference_fitYou correctly credit CBX-250 with the NCCN/ELN 'enroll in a trial' preference, but ranking it fourth behind gemtuzumab undersells the patient's own framing: prefers_trials is true, travel is acceptable, and this is the on-axis A*02:01 trial that is off-the-shelf and recruiting (NCT06994676). Your own logic that enrollment is the preferred R/R route argues for lifting it above an on-label cytoreductive bridge that is not the reason for this run. I would keep gemtuzumab as the available fallback and let the recruiting on-axis trial sit higher on preference grounds, with the pending HLA-A*02:01 typing as the honest gate. advocaterisktakerendorsepreference_fitRank-1 CBX-250 lands on the patient's stated axis: HLA-A*02:01-restricted immunotherapy, curative intent, trials acceptable including travel, no toxicity or modality veto to trip. Your off-the-shelf-speed rationale for the 85%-blast marrow tracks the trial row (recruiting, prior allo-HCT permitted after 60 days, NCT06994676), and you name the phase-1 CRS caveat honestly rather than hiding it. One preference-lens note: the HA-1 TCR-T at your rank 3 is the literal reason the case was submitted, so I would keep it visibly close behind, not below two non-axis picks.

docs.title: Second allogeneic HCT (HCT2) for relapse after first allo-HCT (second-allo-hct)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker——did not pick— conservative1moderateA second transplant is the one curative move on this slate with a real registry behind it rather than a first-in-human hope. The Christopeit/Schmid EBMT series (pmid:23918951) is 179 second transplants; the matched-sibling subgroup that fits this patient ran ~37% 2-year OS, and her ~6-year remission after HCT1 sits on the favorable side of that curve. The toxicity here is not a mystery. NRM, GVHD, and infection are the known hazards, and every transplant unit has a worked-out management algorithm for each. What I want settled before signing off is fitness: no cardiac or organ-function numbers are documented, and 85% marrow blasts with an extramedullary thigh lesion argue for cytoreduction first rather than transplanting into florid disease. Rank 1 because it carries the curative intent on the best-characterized safety footing in the dossier, not because it is gentle.Fitness and organ-function data are absent; NRM in a post-HCT1 patient turns on cardiac/hepatic/renal reserve that has not been measured; Transplanting into 85% blasts is a poor bet; this needs cytoreduction to a lower burden first; GVHD risk on a second graft, compounded if a donor change is pursued; Registry OS (~37% at 2 years, sibling subgroup) is honest but not high; roughly half who reach CR relapse again critic2moderateThe evidence here is a retrospective EBMT registry (PMID 23918951, ROBINS-I Serious), not a trial, but it is large (n=179) and directly on-point: ~37% 2-year OS in the related-donor subgroup that matches this matched-sibling patient. The long first remission (~6 years) sits on the favorable side of the registry's own survival drivers. I rank it second rather than first only because a registry cohort cannot adjust away confounding-by-indication the way a randomized comparison would, and the 85%-blast active-disease burden at HCT2 pulls hard against that 37% figure.ROBINS-I confounding: who gets an HCT2 is selected on fitness and disease control, which inflates the apparent survival; the 37% is a subgroup estimate, and this patient's active high-burden disease is the adverse tail of it, not the middle; no per-term NRM/toxicity breakdown in the source abstract concensusite1moderateELN 2022 (Dohner, Blood 2022;140:1345) puts a second allo-HCT at the center of curative-intent management for AML that relapses after transplant, conditioned on getting the marrow back into remission first. Her ~6-year first remission is the favorable variable: in the EBMT related-donor subgroup that maps to roughly 37% 2-year OS after HCT2 (Christopeit 2013), better than the cohort overall. NCCN AML v3.2026 keeps second transplant among the category 2A options for post-transplant relapse in fit patients, and ECOG 1 with no vetoed modality keeps her inside that population. It is the platform the rest of the plan, including any HLA-restricted consolidation, has to be built on.85% marrow blasts plus a thigh myeloid sarcoma mean HCT2 cannot be delivered up front; the guideline recommendation is explicitly conditioned on cytoreduction first, which is the unsolved step here.; No cardiac or organ-function labs are on file, so the fitness assumptions ELN/NCCN attach to a second transplant are unverified.; TP53-aberrant complex-karyotype disease escaped graft-versus-leukemia once already; a durable HCT2 is far from assured even with a good first remission. advocate——did not pick—

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment risktakerconcensusitequalifiedevidence_qualityHCT2 as the curative backbone is fine, but leaning on a 37% 2-year OS from the EBMT related-donor subgroup (pmid:23918951) overstates the footing for a patient who sits in that registry's adverse tail: 85% blasts, MECOM, KMT2A amplification. The favorable ~6-year first remission helps, but this is a retrospective registry, not a reason to slow-walk the faster on-axis levers while the transplant is still weeks of cytoreduction away. conservativeconcensusitequalifiedtoxicityWe both rank HCT2 first, so my caveat is specific to how it is delivered: the ELN/NCCN endorsement you cite is explicitly conditioned on fitness, and non-relapse mortality in a second allograft turns on cardiac, hepatic, and renal reserve that has not been measured in this patient. The Christopeit registry (pmid:23918951) gives ~37% 2-year OS in the related-donor subgroup but no per-term NRM breakdown, and transplanting into 85% blasts sits in the adverse tail of that curve, not the middle. Guideline-consistent, but the fitness gate and cytoreduction-first step stay open before this is deliverable. criticconcensusitequalifiedevidence_qualityI agree HCT2 belongs near the top, but the ~37% 2-year OS you lean on comes from a retrospective EBMT registry (PMID 23918951, ROBINS-I Serious), and who gets a second transplant is selected on fitness and disease control, so that number is confounding-by-indication-inflated, not a clean expectation. The ELN 2022 and NCCN 2A framing is expert consensus resting on this same registry tier, not RCT-grade evidence, and it is explicit that the recommendation is conditioned on cytoreduction first, which is the unsolved step in an 85%-blast marrow. The favorable ~6-year first remission helps, but this patient's active high-burden disease is the adverse tail of that 37%, not its middle. concensusiteconservativeendorseguideline_fitI ranked this first for the same reason, so this is a concession, not a critique. ELN 2022 centers a second allo-HCT in curative-intent management of post-transplant relapse, NCCN AML v3.2026 keeps it as a category 2A option for fit patients, and the ~6-year first remission puts her on the favorable side of the EBMT related-donor curve (pmid:23918951). The one place we fully agree that matters: the guideline recommendation is conditioned on cytoreduction first, so transplanting into 85% blasts is off-protocol until the marrow is brought down.

docs.title: Iomab-B (131I-apamistamab anti-CD45 radioimmunotherapy conditioning) to second allo-HCT (apamistamab-iomab-b)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker2moderateFor a marrow this hot, the boldest move that still has randomized evidence behind it is targeted radioimmunotherapy that carries active disease straight into a transplant rather than waiting for a remission that FLAG-IDA/venetoclax already failed to produce. SIERRA hit a durable CR of 17.1% versus 0% for conventional care (pmid:39298738), and it did it in exactly the age-appropriate active-R/R-AML population, with grade 3+ toxicity essentially matched to control. The upside is the only thing on this list with a real shot at cure: get to HCT2, then layer HLA-restricted consolidation on top. The honest caveat is that SIERRA enrolled patients heading to a first transplant, so second-HCT eligibility has to be confirmed, and OS was flat because half the control arm crossed over.SIERRA enrolled first-transplant patients; prior allo-HCT eligibility for the go-forward conditioning study (NCT07157514) must be verified; OS was not improved (HR 0.99) in the trial, driven by heavy crossover; Second transplant on an 85%-blast marrow with adverse cytogenetics carries substantial non-relapse mortality; organ function undocumented; Extramedullary thigh sarcoma may need directed radiotherapy that CD45 RIT will not fully cover conservative2moderateThis is the highest-tier evidence in the whole dossier and it earns a safety-first ranking on that alone. SIERRA (pmid:39298738) is a randomized phase 3: durable CR 17.1% vs 0% (p<0.0001), EFS HR 0.23. The number that matters most to me is the toxicity comparison, and it is reassuring: grade >=3 treatment-related AEs were 59.7% on apamistamab versus 59.2% on conventional care, so the targeted conditioning did not add net high-grade toxicity for the cytoreduction it bought. It gives a defensible route to carry an 85%-blast marrow into HCT2 without simply repeating the FLAG-IDA chemistry that already failed. Two caveats keep this out of rank 1: SIERRA enrolled patients heading to a FIRST transplant, so prior-HCT eligibility is unverified, and marrow-directed radioimmunotherapy may not touch the extramedullary thigh sarcoma.Prior-allo-HCT eligibility unverified; SIERRA was a first-transplant population, so this is an extrapolation; OS was flat (HR 0.99), plausibly from ~52% control crossover; the durable-CR benefit did not read through to survival; Marrow-directed RIT likely does not address the extramedullary thigh disease; Adds a radiation-conditioning hit on top of HCT2 in a patient whose organ reserve is undocumented critic1moderateSIERRA is the one randomized phase 3 in this whole set (PMID 39298738, tier 1b, RoB2 Some), and it hit its registered primary endpoint: durable CR 17.1% vs 0%, p<0.0001, which is exactly the problem this 85%-blast marrow poses, getting active disease into a transplant. What keeps it off a clean endorsement is that ITT OS was flat (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.7-1.41, p=0.96) once 52% of the control arm crossed over, so the durable-CR win is a surrogate, not a survival claim. SIERRA also enrolled patients heading to a FIRST transplant, and this patient needs an HCT2, so eligibility is an extrapolation the phase 3 does not cover.RoB2 deviations-from-intervention / measurement: open-label conditioning and a surrogate (durable CR at >=180 days) rather than OS; generalizability: enrolled first-transplant candidates, so the HCT2 setting is off-protocol and unverified; the OS null under 52% crossover means the effect on the endpoint patients care about is unproven concensusite——did not pick— advocate3moderateThe HA-1/HA-2 cells at rank 2 need a transplant under them, so honoring that side of the primary axis means getting the patient safely to HCT2 with an 85%-blast marrow. SIERRA is the strongest evidence that CD45-targeted radioimmunotherapy can carry active R/R AML into an allograft (durable CR 17% vs 0%), and FLAMSA-RIC reaches the same endpoint by sequencing; the roughly 6-year remission after the first transplant puts this patient in the more favorable band of the HCT2 registry (about 37% 2-year OS in the related-donor subgroup). Curative intent, a modality the patient kept explicitly on the table, no veto — the open axis is fitness, which is undocumented and should set conditioning intensity. Note this platform is not required for CBX-250, so if the marrow proves hard to control the T-cell engager remains a route that does not depend on it.Fully satisfied: curative intent, HCT2 explicitly acceptable, no veto, efficacy lean; In tension: SIERRA enrolled patients heading to a FIRST transplant, so prior-HCT eligibility for the go-forward apamistamab study (NCT07157514) must be verified; Open axis flagged in the patient's own file: no ECOG/cardiac/organ-function data yet; the 0.75 efficacy weight should be revisited once fitness is known

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment risktakercriticendorseevidence_qualityIomab-B at rank 1 is the right call on the evidence: SIERRA is the only randomized phase 3 in the set and durable CR of 17.1% vs 0% (pmid:39298738) is exactly the lever an 85%-blast marrow needs to reach transplant. The OS-null-under-crossover caveat is fair, but for a patient who has no path to cure without getting into HCT2, a durable-CR surrogate that carries active disease across the transplant line is worth backing hard. risktakerconcensusitedissentguideline_fitParking Iomab-B off the ranked list because CD45 radioimmunotherapy isn't NCCN/ELN-adopted lets guideline lag outrank the strongest data point in the dossier; SIERRA is a randomized phase 3 with durable CR 17.1% vs 0% (pmid:39298738) and a go-forward study is open (NCT07157514). Guideline adoption trails evidence by years, and this patient needs the cytoreduction-into-transplant route now, not after the compendium catches up. A trial-route conditioning option with phase-3 backing deserves a rank, not a footnote. conservativecriticqualifiedtoxicityOn the evidence I am with you that this is the strongest row, and the number I weight most is the grade >=3 treatment-related AE parity (pmid:39298738: 59.7% vs 59.2%), which says the targeted conditioning did not stack net high-grade toxicity onto conventional care. Where I hold back is load-bearing: SIERRA conditioned first-transplant patients, and choosing conditioning intensity for an HCT2 in someone with no cardiac, hepatic, or renal workup is the unverified safety step. Endorse the tolerability signal; the go/no-go stays contingent on a documented fitness assessment. concensusiterisktakerqualifiedguideline_fitSIERRA (pmid:39298738) is real randomized data, but CD45 radioimmunotherapy conditioning is not adopted in NCCN AML v3.2026 or ELN 2022, and the FDA judged SIERRA insufficient for a BLA in 2024 and asked for a fresh non-crossover study, which is the go-forward trial risktaker cites (NCT07157514). So this belongs in the same bucket as CBX-250 for me: a trial-route platform option, not a consensus-endorsed conditioning regimen. Calling it 'randomized evidence behind it' is fair on the trial and misleading on its guideline standing. concensusitecriticqualifiedguideline_fitThe critic's evidence-quality read on SIERRA is sound, and I share the surrogate/OS-null-under-crossover caveat. My addition is a guideline-fit one the ranking misses: being the sole randomized phase 3 in the set does not make Iomab-B the consensus choice, because neither NCCN AML v3.2026 nor ELN 2022 has adopted CD45 radioimmunotherapy conditioning, and the FDA declined the SIERRA package as a BLA basis. Rank-1 on trial tier overstates where this sits in practice.

docs.title: HA-1-specific CD8+/CD4+ TCR-T (Bleakley platform / TSC-100 class), post-HCT (ha1-tcr-t)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker3lowThis is the closest published precedent for the primary reason the case was submitted, and it delivered 4 of 9 CRs with no dose-limiting toxicities in exactly the post-transplant relapse setting (pmid:38683966). The mechanism is the graft-versus-leukemia effect aimed at a recipient-restricted antigen, so it can reach leukemia while largely sparing the tissues that drive GVHD; one patient stayed in remission past two years. My upside case is durable, HCT2-consolidating cellular immunity that turns a second transplant into a cure rather than a bridge. It is gated on A*02:01 plus a recipient HA-1-positive / donor HA-1-negative mismatch that neither the patient nor the sibling has been genotyped for, and n=9 is a thin efficacy base.Eligibility gated on A*02:01 AND a recipient-positive/donor-negative HA-1 mismatch, none genotyped yet in either the patient or the sibling donor; n=9 feasibility cohort, not powered for efficacy; Requires a fresh allo-HCT platform and recipient-origin relapse confirmed by sorted-CD34 STR chimerism before it is even applicable; Manufacturing lead time is a liability given the pace of this relapse conservative——did not pick— critic5lowI am ranking the marquee cellular option last on purpose, and the reason is evidence maturity, not biology. The closest published human data are n=9, single-arm phase 1 (PMID 38683966, ROBINS-I Serious), reported as 4/9 CR with 0 DLTs, which is a feasibility and safety readout, not an efficacy estimate you can size a decision on, and I could not retrieve the per-term AE table for it. Eligibility is doubly gated on pending HLA-A*02:01 typing plus a recipient HA-1(H)-positive / donor HA-1-negative genotype in both patient and sibling, none of which is resolved. The related TCR-T trials (TSC-100/101 NCT05473910, BSB-1001 NCT06704152) are all phase 1 with no efficacy readouts, so the whole axis is early-phase behind a biomarker gate.ROBINS-I Serious on an n=9 feasibility cohort: no efficacy powering, no comparator, per-term safety table unretrievable; double eligibility contingency (HLA-A*02:01 + HA-1 recipient-positive/donor-negative genotyping of both parties) all unresolved; CR proportion from 9 patients is not a stable effect estimate; wide uncertainty regardless of point value concensusite2lowBoth NCCN AML v3.2026 and ELN 2022 name clinical-trial enrollment as the preferred route in relapsed/refractory AML, and this handle is the stated reason for the run: HA-1-directed donor TCR-T (TSC-100, NCT05473910; Fred Hutch platform, pmid 38683966). The phase 1 signal is early but real, with 4 of 9 recurrent post-HCT patients reaching or holding CR and no dose-limiting toxicity. It slots onto an HCT2 as consolidation, which is where the guideline-endorsed adoptive-cell approach for post-transplant relapse actually lives. I rank it second rather than first because eligibility is undetermined, not established.Eligibility is gated on HLA-A*02:01 plus a recipient HA-1(H)-positive / donor HA-1-negative mismatch, and neither the patient nor the sibling donor has been genotyped; she sits in an undetermined enrolling population, not a confirmed-eligible one.; The guideline support is for 'enroll in a trial,' not for TCR-T as such; this is a phase-1 investigational product with no consensus category behind it.; It is post-transplant consolidation, so it does nothing for the 85%-blast marrow that has to be controlled first. advocate2lowThis is the handle the case was originally submitted for, and it fits the patient's terms: curative intent, a trial they will travel for, and a graft-versus-leukemia mechanism that spares the tissues that drive GVHD. Bleakley's phase 1 got 4 of 9 recurrent post-HCT patients into CR with no dose-limiting toxicity, and TSC-100/101 runs the same mechanism on the back of a fresh matched transplant — a deeper published precedent than CBX-250, which is why the two sit close at the top. The catch is a heavier eligibility gate: HLA-A*02:01, a recipient HA-1(H)-positive / donor-negative mismatch genotyped in both the patient and the sibling, and recipient-origin relapse confirmed by sorted-CD34 STR chimerism. It ranks just behind CBX-250 only because that gate is longer and it needs the HCT2 platform under it, not because the mechanism is weaker.Fully satisfied: primary axis, curative intent, prefers_trials incl. travel, no veto, efficacy lean; In tension: three-part eligibility gate — A*02:01 typing, HA-1/HA-2 genotyping of patient AND sibling, and sorted-CD34 STR chimerism for recipient origin — all unresolved; Sequencing: delivered on the back of HCT2 (rank 3), so it inherits that platform's timeline

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment risktakeradvocatequalifiedotherRanking HA-1 TCR-T second is defensible on the 4/9 CR precedent (pmid:38683966), but it inherits the HCT2 timeline plus a three-part gate (A*02:01, recipient-positive/donor-negative HA-1, sorted-CD34 chimerism), none genotyped in patient or sibling. For this pace of relapse I'd flag it more sharply as the slow lever: real cure story, but it can't touch the marrow that's climbing now. criticrisktakerqualifiedevidence_qualityThe 4/9 CR you cite (PMID 38683966, ROBINS-I Serious) is a feasibility and safety cohort of nine, not an efficacy estimate a decision can lean on, and I could not retrieve its per-term AE table to even confirm the safety half. A CR proportion off nine patients has an interval wide enough to contain both a real effect and near-nothing, so 'durable HCT2-consolidating immunity' is a hope, not a result. Ranking it third above the xenograft-only cCAR is defensible on maturity grounds; presenting the 4/9 as if it sizes the upside is not. advocatecriticqualifiedpreference_fitRanking the HA-1 TCR-T last on n=9 maturity is defensible on your axis, but it is the literal handle the case was submitted for, so from the patient's lens it should read as 'gated, not disfavored.' The 4/9 CR with 0 DLTs (pmid:38683966) is thin but sits on exactly the post-HCT relapse setting the run targets, and the gate is genotyping the patient and sibling, not a toxicity or access wall. I would keep it in-frame as a live pathway pending HA-1/HA-2 typing rather than let the maturity rank imply it is off the table.

docs.title: CD123-CD33 compound CAR-T (dual-antigen, iCell cCAR, NCT04156256) (cd33-cd123-ccar)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker4lowThis patient carries both CD33 and CD123 and is visibly evolving clonally at relapse, so a dual-antigen construct is the antigen-escape hedge the single-target agents don't give you. Preclinically the compound CAR beat single-antigen targeting for survival across four AML xenograft models and killed each antigen-positive population (pmid:29515236). The upside is deep cytoreduction that covers two targets at once ahead of transplant. Weaknesses are real: xenograft-only data, no post-allo-HCT experience, CAR-T-grade CRS, and an unclear registry/eligibility status.Preclinical evidence only; no clinical efficacy or safety readout in humans; CAR-T after a prior transplant raises its own eligibility, CRS, and myelosuppression concerns; Recruitment/registry status listed as unknown; access may not be real; Manufacturing lead time competes with a fast-moving relapse conservative——did not pick— critic——did not pick— concensusite——did not pick— advocate6lowGiven the clonal evolution documented between 2019 and 2026, single-antigen cytoreduction invites escape, and the patient carries both CD33 and CD123. A compound CD33/CD123 CAR-T covers both antigens and is the escape hedge the profile flags — trial-acceptable and consistent with the curative goal. The honesty here is real: it is early-phase with xenograft-only support, no post-allo-HCT data, and CRS plus prior-transplant eligibility are open. On-label gemtuzumab is the lower-ceiling but immediately available CD33 option if a trial slot does not materialize.Fully satisfied: no veto, trial-acceptable, curative-intent framing; In tension: earliest-phase evidence of any pick; xenograft-only, no post-HCT data, CRS and prior-transplant eligibility unresolved; Quantitative CD33/CD123 density (requested) would gate the ADC/CAR decision it depends on

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment conservativerisktakerdissenttoxicityA dual CD33/CD123 construct stacks two toxicities I cannot plan against here: CAR-T-grade cytokine release plus on-target myeloablation of normal CD33- and CD123-positive progenitors, and the supporting data (pmid:29515236) are xenograft-only with no post-allo-HCT human experience. In a re-transplant candidate whose cardiac and organ-function reserve is undocumented, there is no clinical toxicity table to build a management algorithm from. Survival curves in four mouse models do not tell me how to manage marrow aplasia or CRS in this patient, so it does not clear the bar for a ranked slot.

docs.title: Rezatapopt (PC14586, Y220C-selective p53 reactivator) + venetoclax, myeloid trial NCT06616636 (rezatapopt)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker5lowIf the pending NGS lands on TP53 Y220C, this is a variant-matched targeted shot with a clean mechanistic story: rezatapopt refolds the Y220C mutant and, paired with venetoclax, restores real apoptotic killing in Y220C AML (pmid:40608889). The solid-tumor readout shows a 30% response in Y220C/KRAS-wild-type disease (pmid:41740031), which is a meaningful signal for a p53-reactivator. I'm ranking it low because the contingency is double: the TP53 aberration has to be confirmed, then confirmed as Y220C specifically, and neither is resolved. Single-agent activity in myeloid disease looks weak, so it would need the venetoclax partner.Double contingency: TP53 status unresolved (2019 mutant vs 2026 negative on a limited assay), and Y220C not established; All clinical response data are in solid tumors; the myeloid trial has no results; Needs a venetoclax partner for apoptosis, and the patient just progressed on a venetoclax-containing regimen; Not cytoreductive fast enough alone for an 85%-blast marrow conservative——did not pick— critic——did not pick— concensusite——did not pick— advocate——did not pick—

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment criticrisktakerqualifiedevidence_qualityThe 30% figure you quote is not in the source: PYNNACLE (PMID 41740031, NEJM) reports ORR 20% in solid tumors, all responders KRAS-wild-type, and zero myeloid patients. Ranking it sixth-to-last is the right instinct, but the number attached to the rationale drifts from the paper and the myeloid trial NCT06616636 has no results at all, so this is cross-tumor extrapolation behind a double biomarker gate (confirm TP53 aberration, then confirm Y220C), not a 30%-response bet. concensusiterisktakerdissentguideline_fitRezatapopt sits outside guideline-endorsed use on every axis I track: no NCCN or ELN listing, all response data in solid tumors (pmid:41740031), and the myeloid trial (NCT06616636) has posted nothing. docs.title: Pivekimab sunirine (IMGN632, CD123 ADC) monotherapy (pivekimab-sunirine)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker6lowAs a CD123-directed debulking option this has actual single-agent clinical activity in R/R AML (ORR 21%, CI 8-40; CR 17%, CI 6-36 at the RP2D; pmid:38423051) and picomolar preclinical potency with a wide window over normal progenitors (pmid:29661755). The upside is a lower-drama, off-the-shelf way to knock the marrow down toward a transplant if the cellular routes stall on typing. I keep it toward the bottom because the response depth is modest and the veno-occlusive-disease signal is exactly the wrong toxicity to carry into a planned second transplant.VOD signal is a serious liability peri-transplant given the HCT2 plan; Modest single-agent depth (ORR ~21%); unlikely to be curative on its own; Benefit-predictive quantitative CD123 antigen density still pending; One treatment-related death in the escalation cohort conservative——did not pick— critic——did not pick— concensusite——did not pick— advocate4lowTo reach a transplant or a cellular consolidation you first have to bring an 85%-blast marrow down, and re-running the FLAG-IDA scaffold the disease already failed is not the way. Pivekimab is a CD123 ADC with single-agent activity in R/R AML (ORR 21%) against the patient's confirmed CD123-positive blasts, without stacking onto a backbone that has already lost. It clears the preference filter — no veto, trial-acceptable — with two honest caveats: quantitative CD123 antigen density is still pending and would sharpen the choice, and the veno-occlusive signal matters with a transplant ahead. Tagraxofusp is a reasonable alternative but carries capillary-leak risk that argues for fitness data before committing.Fully satisfied: efficacy-leaning bridge, no veto, trial route available; In tension: quantitative CD123 density (requested) not yet back; VOD signal is relevant with HCT2 planned; Role is cytoreduction, not cure on its own — it earns its rank as a bridge to ranks 1-3, and it would also buy time to the CBX-250 slot

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment conservativerisktakerqualifiedtoxicityYou ranked this last and named the veno-occlusive-disease signal yourself, so this is a sequencing caveat, not a fight: VOD was a dose-limiting toxicity (2 of 68) with a 1% treatment-related death against a 21% ORR (pmid:38423051), which is the wrong hepatic risk to carry into a planned HCT2. Gemtuzumab fills the same CD33/CD123-adjacent bridging role with 20-plus years of VOD-surveillance and fractionated-dosing algorithm behind it. Hold the ADC behind the on-label handle until organ-function data land. conservativeadvocatequalifiedtoxicityThe bridging logic is sound and you flagged the VOD signal, so my caveat is only about sequencing under a transplant plan: reversible VOD was a dose-limiting toxicity (2 of 68) with a 1% treatment-related death at a 21% ORR (pmid:38423051), and that hepatic risk lands squarely in the peri-HCT2 window. Gemtuzumab covers the same cytoreductive-bridge role with a mature VOD-surveillance and fractionated-dosing playbook. Given a second transplant ahead, I would run the on-label CD33 handle before this ADC until fitness and organ-function data are in. criticadvocatequalifiedevidence_qualityThe ORR 21% is real single-arm activity (PMID 38423051, ROBINS-I Serious) but it comes off the n=29 RP2D expansion, a single-arm surrogate with no comparator, and the response depth is modest for a bridge you are asking to debulk an 85%-blast marrow. docs.title: Gemtuzumab ozogamicin (Mylotarg, CD33 ADC) (gemtuzumab-ozogamicin)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker——did not pick— conservative3moderateWhen I weight toxicity this heavily, an FDA-approved agent with more than twenty years of post-marketing safety and a fully worked-out AE-management playbook beats a novel mechanism I cannot yet characterize. CD33 is confirmed on the blasts, and the Sievers pooled phase 2 (pmid:11432892) gives a clean per-grade toxicity picture: G>=3 hyperbilirubinemia 23%, transaminase elevation 17%, no cardiotoxicity, low mucositis (4%). The class risk is hepatic veno-occlusive disease, and that is exactly the risk that has an established mitigation pathway (fractionated dosing, VOD surveillance, defibrotide on hand) rather than an open question. I am honest that single-agent depth in first relapse was only ~30% and this patient is further along than that population, so I position it as a predictable, manageable cytoreduction lever ahead of HCT2, not as a curative move on its own. Quantitative CD33 density is still pending and should gate the commitment.Hepatic VOD is the black-box class risk and it lands squarely in the peri-transplant window; fractionated dosing and VOD surveillance are mandatory, not optional; Single-agent remission was ~30% in a LESS pretreated first-relapse cohort; expect lower after FLAG-IDA/venetoclax failure; Benefit is CD33-density-dependent and quantitative flow has not been done; Does not address the extramedullary thigh sarcoma critic3moderateThis is the only on-label, primary-indication option in the set for the patient's confirmed CD33 positivity, which is why it clears the others on regulatory footing. But the depth is honest and modest: pooled single-arm phase 2 (PMID 11432892, ROBINS-I Serious), ~30% CR+CRp, and the population was CD33+ first relapse with no antecedent hematologic disorder, meaning less pretreated than this FLAG-IDA/venetoclax-refractory patient with extramedullary disease. CR+CRp is a surrogate with no randomized comparator, and the calicheamicin VOD signal is not trivial with an HCT2 planned. I would want quantitative CD33 antigen density before leaning on it, since single-arm ADC response tracks density.ROBINS-I: pooled single-arm, no comparator; CR+CRp is a surrogate; population mismatch: first-relapse, treatment-naive-marrow patients, not this refractory/post-transplant/extramedullary state, so the ~30% likely overstates the achievable rate here; hepatic/VOD class risk peri-HCT2; benefit-predictive CD33 density still only qualitative concensusite3lowGemtuzumab is the one on-label, guideline-listed drug in play: NCCN AML v3.2026 carries single-agent gemtuzumab (category 2A) for CD33-positive relapsed AML, and her blasts are CD33+ by flow. I read it as a cytoreductive bridge toward HCT2, not as definitive therapy. The honest ceiling is modest, about 30% overall remission in first relapse (Sievers 2001, pmid 11432892), and she is well past first relapse with extramedullary disease. Quantitative CD33 density is still pending, and that is the readout that tells us whether ADC-level expression is even there.The single-agent remission figure comes from a first-relapse population less pretreated than this patient; carrying it over to post-FLAG-IDA/venetoclax failure with a myeloid sarcoma overstates likely benefit.; Calicheamicin hepatotoxicity and VOD are the class risk and matter directly with an HCT2 planned soon after (Sievers reported grade 3+ hyperbilirubinemia in 23%).; Qualitative CD33 positivity is not antigen density; committing before the quantitative flow is target selection done backwards. advocate——did not pick—

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment conservativecriticqualifiedtoxicityWe agree this is the on-label floor and I rank it similarly, so my caveat is narrow: the calicheamicin VOD you name is the black-box class risk, and it lands in the peri-HCT2 window this patient is heading toward. The per-grade picture is otherwise reassuring and worth stating (pmid:11432892: G>=3 hyperbilirubinemia 23%, transaminase 17%, no cardiotoxicity), which is exactly why the VOD mitigation cannot stay implicit. Fractionated dosing, VOD surveillance, and defibrotide availability are mandatory conditions on this pick, not optional add-ons. criticconservativequalifiedevidence_qualityThe 20-year post-marketing safety record is a fair basis for a toxicity-first ranking, but on efficacy the ~30% remission comes from a pooled single-arm phase 2 in CD33+ FIRST relapse with no antecedent haematologic disorder (PMID 11432892, ROBINS-I Serious), a less pretreated population than this FLAG-IDA/venetoclax-refractory patient with extramedullary disease. CR+CRp is a surrogate with no comparator, and single-arm ADC response tracks antigen density that here is still only qualitative. So it is a predictable cytoreduction lever, but expect below 30% and gate it on quantitative CD33 flow before committing. concensusitecriticqualifiedguideline_fitThe critic dings gemtuzumab as a single-arm surrogate (pmid:11432892) and ranks it below two registry backbones, which reads the raw evidence tier correctly but skips a layer. NCCN AML v3.2026 lists single-agent gemtuzumab as category 2A for CD33-positive R/R AML: the panel saw the same modest single-arm data the critic is reading and still reached uniform consensus to recommend it, which is what a 2A designation encodes. It is the only on-label, guideline-listed drug on the whole slate, and that standing is worth more than its RoB label alone suggests.

docs.title: Donor lymphocyte infusion (DLI) from the sibling donor (donor-lymphocyte-infusion)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker——did not pick— conservative4moderateDLI has decades of registry experience and a single, well-understood toxicity in GVHD, which every transplant program manages with an established steroid-and-escalation algorithm. That maturity is why it earns a slot on a safety-first slate. The Schmid EBMT registry (pmid:17909197) is clear-eyed about who benefits: relapse >5 months after HCT (this patient ~6 years) favors it, and DLI beat no-DLI (2-year OS 21% vs 9%, P=0.04). But the same data show the benefit concentrates in patients treated in remission or with favorable karyotype (~56% 2-year OS), while active high-burden disease like this drops to ~15%. That is the honest read: DLI alone into 85% blasts and adverse cytogenetics is low-yield. I rank it here as a well-characterized adjunct to be given AFTER cytoreduction, not as a standalone.GVHD is the defining toxicity; manageable but real, and additive to any HCT2 GVHD risk; Low yield as a standalone in active high-burden disease (~15% 2-year OS in the active-disease subgroup); needs cytoreduction first; Adverse cytogenetics (MECOM, KMT2A amplification) put this patient in the worse-prognosis DLI subgroup; Requires confirmed recipient-derived relapse on CD34-sorted STR chimerism before proceeding critic4lowThe DLI registry does carry an adjusted signal (PMID 17909197, ROBINS-I Serious): 2-year OS 21% vs 9%, p=0.04 after multivariate adjustment, and this patient's very late relapse (~6 years) is on the favorable side of the timing driver. The catch is that the benefit concentrates in a subgroup he is not in: DLI given in remission or with favorable karyotype reached ~56% 2-year OS, while DLI in active/high-burden disease sat at ~15%, which is where an 85%-blast marrow with adverse cytogenetics lands him. This is a confounding-by-indication-prone comparison, so I read it as an argument for cytoreduction before any DLI, not for DLI alone.ROBINS-I confounding-by-indication: DLI recipients were selected for lower burden and better performance; the favorable estimate is a subgroup this patient does not belong to; his active-disease subgroup is ~15% 2-year OS; unadjusted vs adjusted subgroup contrasts from a registry, not a randomized signal concensusite5lowSibling DLI sits squarely inside ELN 2022's framing of post-transplant relapse: immunosuppression taper plus cytoreduction plus adoptive cellular therapy is the combination they credit with occasional durable remissions. Her late relapse (>5 months, here ~6 years) is exactly the feature that predicts DLI benefit in the EBMT series (Schmid 2007, pmid 17909197; 21% vs 9% 2-year OS with vs without DLI). The catch is burden: given in active high-burden disease, that same series shows ~15% 2-year OS, so DLI has to follow cytoreduction, not lead it. I treat it as an adjunct to the transplant platform, not a standalone.At 85% blasts she is in the active-disease/high-burden DLI group where the registry outcome is worst; DLI alone is not defensible here.; GVHD is the characteristic toxicity and would complicate a subsequent HCT2.; The registry benefit is a minority effect and selection-confounded; it calibrates expectations rather than promising much. advocate——did not pick—

docs.title: WT1 HLA-A02:01 TCR-T (WT1-TCRc4 / FH-WT1-E50); A24:02 WT1-siTCR as the fallback lever (wt1-tcrc4)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker——did not pick— conservative——did not pick— critic——did not pick— concensusite——did not pick— advocate5lowIf the HA-1/HA-2 pair does not mismatch but the patient is A*02:01-positive, WT1 keeps the HLA-restricted axis alive rather than foreclosing it — a second lever on the same primary reason for the run. The Chapuis WT1-TCRc4 work held 12 high-risk AML patients relapse-free post-transplant, and FH-WT1-E50 carries the current version, best positioned as post-cytoreduction or post-HCT2 consolidation rather than for florid relapse. If A*02:01 comes back negative, A*24:02 opens the WT1-siTCR lever, which is why both alleles should be typed in parallel before anyone forecloses this pathway. Same preference fit as the top picks, with a prophylaxis/MRD evidence base and a disease-state mismatch at the current blast burden.Fully satisfied: same HLA-restricted, curative-intent, trial-acceptable profile the run was built around; In tension: prophylaxis/MRD evidence, not active-relapse salvage; gated on A*02:01 (or A*24:02), still pending; Kept explicitly so an A*02:01-positive but HA-non-mismatched result does not close the immunotherapy axis the patient prioritized

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment criticadvocatequalifiedevidence_qualityThe '100% relapse-free' read from Chapuis (PMID 31235963, n=12) is a prophylaxis cohort infused post-HCT to prevent relapse, against a historical/concurrent comparator, so the survival contrast is confounded and does not transfer to an 85%-blast active relapse. You flag the disease-state mismatch in your own concern line, which I credit, but the effect it implies is relapse-prevention in a selected low-burden setting, not salvage. Keeping it as an allele-contingent lever is reasonable; the n=12 prophylaxis number should not be read as active-disease efficacy. concensusiteadvocatequalifiedguideline_fitKeeping WT1 TCR-T alive as a fallback allele-lever is reasonable trial hygiene, and I do not object to typing A*02:01 and A*24:02 in parallel. The guideline caveat: the Chapuis evidence (pmid:31235963) is post-transplant prophylaxis/MRD, not active-relapse salvage, so even as a trial option it is being proposed outside the disease state where it has data, on top of no NCCN/ELN listing. That is a further stretch than the HA-1 handle, which at least has a relapse-setting readout.

docs.title: What this page is
docs.text:
Libby is an experimental tool that reads a person's cancer details and the published research, then lays out the treatment options worth talking through with the oncology team. This page is the plain-language version of that work. A separate, more technical page holds the same options written for clinicians.

One thing to know up front. This is not a simple case, and the honest answer to "what should I do" is "run a short set of tests first, because those results decide which doors are actually open." So this page leads with the tests, then walks through the treatments in the order they would most likely be used.

docs.title: What we know about your cancer
docs.text:
You have acute myeloid leukemia, or AML, that grew out of an earlier bone-marrow condition (MDS). It has come back and is not responding to your most recent chemotherapy (the FLAG-IDA plus venetoclax combination).

Right now the leukemia is active. Your bone marrow is roughly 85% "blasts," which are the immature leukemia cells, so it has largely crowded out normal blood production. There is also a lump of leukemia in your right thigh. Doctors call that a myeloid sarcoma, which is just a solid collection of leukemia cells sitting outside the marrow.

The leukemia came back about six years after your first donor stem-cell transplant, which used a matched sibling as the donor. The way it returned suggests the leukemia found a way around the donor's immune cells rather than the transplant simply wearing off. That distinction matters, and it shapes a lot of what follows.

A few more pieces. The chromosome changes in the leukemia are complex and high-risk. The leukemia cells carry two surface markers, CD33 and CD123, that some treatments can lock onto. And a handful of results that the whole plan hinges on are not back yet: your tissue type (HLA), a pair of markers called HA-1 and HA-2 in both you and your sibling donor, and a gene called TP53 whose status is genuinely unsettled and is being confirmed rather than assumed.

docs.title: What you told us matters most
docs.text:
You said your goal is a cure, and you are willing to accept harder, riskier treatment for a real shot at controlling the disease. You noted that this willingness should be looked at again once your fitness and heart tests are done, since those are still outstanding.

You did not rule out any type of treatment. A second transplant and immune-cell therapies are all acceptable to you. You are open to clinical trials, including traveling for one.

And the main reason you asked for this review: you want to know whether the immune therapies, the ones that depend on your tissue type, are actually possible for you. That question sits at the center of everything below.

docs.title: The first step everyone agreed on
docs.text:
Before any treatment, there is one step that is not a drug and that everyone lands on first: a short set of tests. They are the tests that unlock the options. None of them is toxic. They run on records that already exist, on blood and marrow samples you are already giving for disease checks, and on one sample from your sibling donor. Most results come back within one to three weeks.

Here is what they settle and why each one matters.

  • Your tissue type (HLA typing). HLA is a set of markers on your cells that the immune system uses to tell "you" from "not you." One specific type, called HLA-A*02:01, is the master switch for most of the immune therapies you came here to ask about. High-resolution typing was done around your first transplant, so the first move is to pull that result from the old records (often same-day). If it cannot be found, the test is repeated in about a week.

  • The HA-1 and HA-2 markers, in you and your sibling donor. Even a fully matched sibling can differ from you at these smaller markers. That difference is what one of the most promising immune therapies depends on, so both you and your donor need to be tested. This is a specialized test, usually run through a trial's central lab rather than an ordinary lab, and it takes one to two weeks.

  • Resolving your TP53 result. A TP53 mutation was found back in 2019. A more recent test reported it as negative, but that test can miss low-level changes and certain kinds of gene loss, so it cannot be trusted to say the mutation is gone. The team is deliberately not calling this either way. Instead they are confirming it by reading the newer, more sensitive test alongside a protein stain, a chromosome test for the relevant region, and the original 2019 report. Whether a particular TP53 option is on the table depends on how this lands.

  • Whether the relapse is coming from your own cells. After a donor transplant, a relapse can, rarely, come from the donor's cells instead of yours. A test called chimerism, run on the leukemia cells specifically, confirms which it is. This is load-bearing for two reasons: the immune therapies are designed to aim donor cells at your cells, and if the leukemia turned out to be donor-derived, the whole plan would change.

While these results come in, your transplant team can hold parallel conversations with the trial programs so nothing waits longer than it has to.

docs.title: The options
docs.text:
The plan that comes out of all this is a sequence, not a single drug. Think of it as three moves in order.

First, bring the leukemia in the marrow down. A second transplant cannot be done while the marrow is 85% leukemia, so the disease has to be reduced first. Second, a second donor stem-cell transplant, which is the only option here with a real chance at cure. Third, if the tissue-typing tests allow it, add immune therapy on top to keep the leukemia from coming back.

A word on how a transplant fights leukemia, because most of the newer options rest on it. A donor transplant is not only a fresh set of blood cells. The donor's immune cells can recognize the leukemia as foreign and attack it. Doctors call that graft-versus-leukemia, sometimes shortened to GVL. The catch is that those same donor cells can also attack your healthy tissues, which is called graft-versus-host disease, or GVHD. Much of the newest work is about aiming the anti-leukemia effect more precisely so it hits the cancer while sparing the rest of you.

The options below are in the order they were ranked. Some are steps toward the transplant, some are the transplant itself, and some are the immune therapies that only become possible depending on your test results.

docs.title: Option 1 - A second donor stem-cell transplant
docs.text:
This is the backbone of the whole plan and the one option with a genuine cure fraction. In a large registry of second transplants, among patients most like you (a matched relative as donor), about 37 out of 100 were still alive two years later, compared with about 25 out of 100 across everyone. Your long first remission, roughly six years, sits on the favorable side of those odds.

The risks are real and serious. A second transplant carries a substantial chance of life-threatening complications from the transplant itself, plus GVHD and infection. It also cannot be done at 85% marrow blasts, so it depends on the earlier options reducing the leukemia first. And the conditioning intensity, the treatment given right before the new cells go in, cannot be chosen safely until your heart and organ-function tests are done. Those tests have not happened yet.

This matches what you told us: curative intent, no treatment type ruled out. The open question is honest. This leukemia already slipped past donor immune cells once, and its genetics are the kind that can escape a second time, so even a good first remission does not guarantee a lasting result. It stays the top option because nothing else here offers a real cure, but only once the marrow is reduced and your fitness is checked.

docs.title: Option 2 - Targeted-radiation conditioning to make the transplant possible
docs.text:
One of the hardest problems in your case is that your marrow is packed with leukemia right now, which normally makes a transplant impossible. This option is a way around that. It is an antibody that carries radiation and homes in on blood and marrow cells (it targets a marker called CD45), delivering the radiation where the leukemia lives while sparing the rest of the body. It is the conditioning step, done right before transplant, and it can carry an active, high-blast marrow into the transplant.

This is the best-tested option on the page. In a randomized trial, where half the patients got this and half got usual care, about 17 out of 100 had a lasting remission with this approach compared with essentially none on usual care. Just as important, it did not pile on extra severe side effects: serious side effects were about equally common on both sides, near 60 out of 100, which is what these patients already face.

Two honest caveats. Overall survival in that trial did not clearly separate between the two groups, largely because many people in the comparison group crossed over and received this treatment too, which muddies the survival picture. And the trial enrolled people heading to their first transplant, so whether it is offered for a second transplant has to be checked, and the follow-on study is not open for enrollment yet. There is also a chance the marrow-aimed radiation does not reach the thigh lump, which may need its own directed radiation.

docs.title: Option 3 - A CD33-targeted drug to reduce the leukemia (gemtuzumab)
docs.text:
This is the one option a treating team can simply prescribe today, without a trial. It is an antibody aimed at CD33, one of the markers confirmed on your leukemia, and it carries a cell-killing payload to those cells. In an older study, about 30 out of 100 patients went into remission. But those patients were less heavily treated than you are, so the real number for you is likely lower. This is a way to reduce the disease before transplant, not a cure on its own.

The main risk is liver toxicity, including a condition where small veins in the liver get blocked. That same liver risk can complicate the transplant this drug is meant to bridge you toward, so the timing between the two has to be handled carefully.

One honest point about how well it might work. The test confirmed CD33 is present on your leukemia, but not how much of it there is, and these drugs tend to work better when there is a lot of the marker. A test that measures the amount should guide whether this is worth using, rather than assuming it will help.

docs.title: Option 4 - Extra donor immune cells (donor lymphocyte infusion)
docs.text:
This is a straightforward way to boost the graft-versus-leukemia effect: give you more of your sibling donor's immune cells. Because your donor is available, it is readily doable. Overall, adding these cells was linked to about 21 out of 100 patients alive at two years, versus about 9 out of 100 without. But in patients with active, high-burden disease like your marrow right now, the figure was closer to 15 out of 100.

So the honest read is that this works best after the leukemia has been reduced and alongside the transplant, not as a stand-alone treatment poured into a full marrow. Given into active disease, it mostly drives GVHD without much benefit. The main risk is GVHD, which could also complicate a later transplant. Your long first remission is exactly the feature that predicts these cells could help, but the timing has to be right.

docs.title: Option 5 - A CD123-targeted drug to reduce the leukemia (pivekimab)
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. It is another way to reduce the disease before transplant, aimed at the CD123 marker, and its appeal is that it does not reuse the chemotherapy your leukemia already shrugged off. About 21 out of 100 patients responded and about 17 out of 100 reached remission.

The tradeoff is the liver. This drug carries the strongest level of warning for the same liver-vein blockage mentioned earlier, and that is exactly the kind of harm that could jeopardize the transplant it is meant to bridge you toward. For that reason, the on-label CD33 drug in Option 3 is often preferred for the same reduce-the-disease job, at least until your organ-function tests are back. As with the CD33 drug, a test of how much CD123 is present should guide whether it is worth the risk.

docs.title: Option 6 - HA-1/HA-2 immune-cell therapy (the reason for this review)
docs.text:
This option is only available if the tissue-typing tests come back the right way: HLA-A*02:01 positive, and a specific HA-1/HA-2 difference confirmed between you and your sibling donor. If either result does not line up, this option is off the table. And because this page only ranks options tied to your specific targetable features, a result that closes this door does not open a different one on this page. Standard care for the leukemia still exists, but that is a separate conversation with your treating team, not something this page tries to rank.

Here is what it is, when it is possible. This is one of the immune therapies you came to ask about, and it has the highest ceiling of anything on the page. Doctors take your donor's immune cells and engineer them to target HA-1 or HA-2, which are minor markers found mainly on blood-lineage cells. Because those markers sit mostly on blood cells and not on other tissues, the therapy aims the anti-leukemia attack at the leukemia while largely sparing the organs that GVHD would otherwise hit. It is graft-versus-leukemia, pointed more precisely.

The evidence is early and promising in equal measure. In a small first-in-human study of nine patients whose leukemia had returned after a transplant, four of the nine went into or held remission, one for more than two years, with no dose-limiting side effects. That is a real signal, but it is a small, early study, and the detailed side-effect breakdown could not be retrieved from the published paper, so "no dose-limiting toxicities in nine patients" is most of what is known about safety. This therapy is given after the second transplant, so it does nothing for your marrow right now. It is the layer meant to keep the leukemia from coming back, and it hangs entirely on whether the HA-1/HA-2 test shows the right difference, which is close to a coin flip until the pair is actually tested.

docs.title: Option 7 - A chemo-based way to deliver the transplant (FLAMSA-RIC)
docs.text:
This is the chemotherapy-based alternative to Option 2 for the same job: getting a marrow full of leukemia into a transplant. It combines sequential chemotherapy with a reduced-intensity transplant and a planned dose of donor immune cells afterward. In a study built for exactly the hard, high-risk situation you are in, about 88 out of 100 patients reached remission and about 42 out of 100 were alive at two years, and the high-risk subgroup did as well as lower-risk patients.

This is not really a separate treatment so much as a different route to the same transplant. Which route your center uses, this chemo-based one or the targeted-radiation one in Option 2, is a decision for the transplant team, guided partly by your heart and organ tests. The main risk is GVHD, including from the planned donor-cell dose.

docs.title: Option 8 - A two-target immune-cell therapy (dual CD33/CD123 CAR-T)
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here is the tradeoff to weigh. The idea behind it is smart: your leukemia has already changed over time, so betting on a single target risks the leukemia dodging it. This therapy hits two markers at once, CD33 and CD123, both confirmed on your cells, to close off that escape route.

The problem is that there is no human data at all. Everything known about it comes from laboratory and animal studies, so nobody can tell you how well it works in people or how to manage its side effects, which are expected to include an inflammatory reaction and destruction of healthy blood-forming cells. On top of that, the trial sites are overseas, which raises real practical and coverage questions before it could even be considered. If a slot never materializes, the CD33-targeted drug in Option 3 is the available fallback for that target.

docs.title: Option 9 - WT1 immune-cell therapy (a backup immune path)
docs.text:
This option is only available if your HLA-A*02:01 test comes back positive. It exists as a backup: if you are A*02:01 positive but the HA-1/HA-2 difference in Option 6 does not line up, this keeps an immune-therapy path open. If the tissue-typing does not support it, this option is off the table too, and, as before, a closed door here does not open a different ranked option on this page. That would be a conversation with your treating team about standard care.

When it is possible, this therapy uses engineered immune cells aimed at a protein called WT1 on the leukemia. In a small study of 12 patients, it was used to prevent relapse after a transplant, and all of them stayed relapse-free at about 44 months. That sounds striking, but read it carefully: those patients were already in remission and the therapy was preventing a return, not clearing a marrow that is 85% leukemia. The comparison group was not randomized, so the number is softer than it first appears. This fits best as a way to keep the leukemia from coming back after disease control, not as a treatment for active disease.

docs.title: Option 10 - An off-the-shelf immune drug on the same tissue-type axis (CBX-250)
docs.text:
This option is only available if your HLA-A*02:01 test comes back positive. Like the two immune therapies above, it rides on that same tissue-type result. If the typing comes back negative, this option is off the table, and a closed door here does not open a different ranked option on this page.

Here is what makes it different from the other immune options, and why it earns its own spot. The HA-1/HA-2 therapy in Option 6 and the WT1 therapy in Option 9 both need cells grown to order, either from your donor or engineered from scratch, which takes time. This one is an antibody-style drug that is made ahead of time and kept on the shelf. It works by grabbing a marker on your leukemia cells and, at the same time, grabbing your own T cells and pulling them onto the leukemia to kill it. Because there is no cell-manufacturing wait, it could move faster than the others once the tissue typing confirms, and your marrow is moving fast, so speed genuinely counts here.

Now the honest part, and it is a lot. This is the earliest option of the whole immune group. It is a first-in-human study, which means it is the first time the drug is being tried in people at all, and there are no results yet, no efficacy data, no established safe dose. Everything encouraging about it so far comes from laboratory and animal work. The specific risk to plan for is an immune-overactivation reaction called cytokine release syndrome, where the immune cells the drug switches on flood the body with signals and can make you very sick. That risk is worse when there is a lot of leukemia to react against, and your marrow is roughly 85% leukemia right now, so this is the highest-risk setting to try a drug like this for the first time. Before it could be used, the team would need a concrete plan to manage that reaction: bring the leukemia down first, start at a low dose and step it up, and keep the medicine that calms the reaction on hand. None of that plan is in place yet.

So the fair way to hold this: it is the fastest-moving option on the exact tissue-type axis you came here for, and it is also the least proven, gated behind a safety plan and the same pending typing as the rest of the group. It does not outrank the more-established transplant path; it sits alongside the other immune options as one more thing to weigh, not a replacement for the backbone.

docs.title: Option 11 - A TP53-targeted pill (rezatapopt)
docs.text:
This option is only available if your TP53 result is confirmed aberrant and the specific change is confirmed to be a particular variant called Y220C. That is a double condition, and your TP53 status is exactly the result that is still being sorted out, so this is doubly uncertain. If TP53 turns out not to be Y220C, this option is closed, and it does not open a different ranked option here.

When it is possible, it is a pill that reshapes that specific mutant protein back toward its normal working form. It is easier to tolerate than the transplant options, mostly low-grade nausea and some anemia. But the honest limits are large. Every response reported so far has been in solid tumors, not leukemia, at about 20 out of 100, and there is no leukemia data yet. It also works best paired with another drug, venetoclax, that your leukemia has already become resistant to. This sits off to the side of the main immune-therapy plan, worth sorting out in parallel rather than counting on.

docs.title: Questions to ask your oncologist
docs.text:
• Which of my tissue-typing and gene tests can be pulled from my first-transplant records today, and which need to be redone? When will we have all of them back?
  • If the HLA and HA-1/HA-2 results do not line up for the immune therapies, what does my plan look like then?
  • What would it take to get my marrow leukemia low enough to make a second transplant possible, and how will we know we are there?
  • Between the targeted-radiation conditioning and the chemo-based conditioning, which does this center offer, and which is safer for my heart and organs?
  • What heart and organ-function tests do I need before a transplant, and could the results change whether transplant is an option at all?
  • If we use a CD33- or CD123-targeted drug to reduce the leukemia first, how will you time it so the liver risk does not threaten the transplant?
  • If I am HLA-A*02:01 positive, how would you weigh the faster off-the-shelf immune drug (CBX-250) against the transplant path, and what is the plan to prevent and treat a cytokine-release reaction given how much leukemia is in my marrow?
  • Does the lump in my thigh need its own radiation, separate from the transplant plan?
  • Is my TP53 result settled yet, and does it change anything we do right now while we wait?

Reading the columns

These are candidate ideas that are earlier than clinical development, or not yet developed at all. Stage is how far the candidate has progressed (conceptual through IND-enabling). Evidence strength is the qualitative weight of the preclinical support. Counter-productive MoA is the mechanism-level risk that the candidate's own pathway could blunt its therapeutic goal. None of these options is enrollable today; they are a horizon scan, not the ranked clinical recommendations on the Recommendations table.

Reading the columns

Toxicity burden is patient-level G3+ AE severity (Low / Moderate / High) summarized from trial publications. Counter-productive MoA is the mechanism-level risk that the intervention's own pathway could blunt the therapeutic goal — distinct from patient AEs. The board's endorse / dissent / veto state appears as pills under each intervention; full per-persona rationale lives on the board page.
