docs.title: Lirafugratinib (RLY-4008) (lirafugratinib)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker1lowIf the pending CGP returns an FGFR2 fusion, this is the biggest upside on the board: ORR 46.5% (95% CI 37.1-56.1), DCR 96.5%, mPFS 11.3 mo in the FGFRi-naive ReFocus cohort of 114, and the FGFR2-selective design largely dodges the FGFR1-driven hyperphosphatemia that dogs pemigatinib. I know the weakness and I am naming it: the evidence is an ASCO GI 2026 abstract with no PMID, the drug is pre-approval (PDUFA Sept 2026), and everything rides on a fusion nobody has tested yet. In a treatment-naive-to-FGFR patient with ~10-15% pretest odds of the axis being live, that is a bet I take, because the response and durability numbers beat the on-label agents. Access before approval means a trial slot or expanded access, so line that up in parallel with the genomic panel.Whole thing is dead on arrival if FGFR2 fusion is negative on CGP; Abstract-only data, no peer-reviewed full text and no PMID; grade 3+ PPE 32.8% is a real quality-of-life hit; Not yet FDA-approved, so real-world access depends on a trial or expanded-access route conservative——did not pick— critic4lowThe FGFR2-selective class is the most interesting new signal in this refresh, and I want to name both its strength and its two weak points. ReFocus reported ORR 46.5% (95% CI 37.1-56.1) in n=114 FGFRi-naive CCA with an FGFR2-selective design that largely spares FGFR1-driven hyperphosphatemia, which is a real tolerability argument. But this is abstract-only (ASCO GI 2026, no PubMed record, ROBINS-I:Moderate on an unread full paper), and it is single-arm ORR like the rest of the class, so I discount it below the two approved FGFR agents that have peer-reviewed pivotal data. One point that keeps getting garbled: lirafugratinib's own basket NCT07359820 EXCLUDES cholangiocarcinoma, so nobody should cite that trial as an enrollment route here. The 46.5% comes from the separate ReFocus CCA cohort, not the basket. NDA is under FDA priority review with a Sept 2026 PDUFA, so its status is still pending.Abstract-only readout; the full paper is unread, so I cannot verify the RoB profile beyond the ROBINS-I:Moderate placeholder and cannot audit response ascertainment or censoring.; Single-arm ORR with no comparator; not yet approved (PDUFA pending), so this is investigational, not an on-label option.; The often-cited basket NCT07359820 does not enroll CCA; conflating it with the ReFocus cohort is an evidence-provenance error to flag, and FGFR2 status is untested here regardless. concensusite——did not pick— advocate2moderateFGFR2 fusion is the axis most likely to test positive at 10 to 15% of intrahepatic disease, and among the FGFR options this is the one whose design fits a balanced efficacy/toxicity preference best. Because it is FGFR2-selective it largely spares the FGFR1-driven hyperphosphatemia that dogs pemigatinib and futibatinib, where hyperphosphatemia runs 30 to 55%; the ReFocus cohort instead reports ORR 46.5% (95% CI 37.1-56.1), median PFS 11.3 months, and a 96.5% disease-control rate, with the main grade 3+ events being hand-foot skin reaction and stomatitis. That is a cleaner tolerability trade at a response rate matching or beating the approved agents, which is exactly what a 0.5 weight should favor. It is oral and, since the user wants trials surfaced first, it is enrollable now through ReFocus with an NDA under FDA priority review. The honest caveat is that this is abstract-stage data with no PMID yet, so if the patient needs an established on-label option today, pemigatinib or futibatinib is the ranked-3 fallback on the same axis.Fully satisfied: oral, best tolerability profile on the FGFR axis for a balanced weight, and enrollable now which serves the trials-first preference.; In tension with evidence maturity: ReFocus is a single-arm phase 1/2 cohort reported in abstract with no peer-reviewed PMID yet, so certainty is lower than for the approved FGFR agents.; FGFR2 status is untested; a negative fusion read closes this axis entirely.

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment risktakeradvocateendorsepreference_fitThis is the one other position that puts the FGFR2-selective magnitude bet where it belongs, rank 2 behind the gate, on ORR 46.5% and mPFS 11.3 mo (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476). We are aligned; my only caution is that the abstract-only status and Sept 2026 PDUFA mean access runs through the ReFocus slot or expanded access, so line that up alongside the panel rather than assuming an on-label prescription. conservativerisktakerdissentevidence_qualitySeating lirafugratinib at rank 1 puts an ASCO GI 2026 abstract with no PubMed record and no registration-scale safety follow-up above pemigatinib, which has carried an FDA label since 2020. You name the abstract weakness yourself, so I will name the safety one you skip past: grade 3+ palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia ran 32.8% (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476), and hand-foot at that grade is a dose-limiting, quality-of-life event, not a footnote. The FGFR2-selective design does spare FGFR1-driven hyperphosphatemia, which I credit, but sparing one on-target toxicity while carrying a 32.8% grade 3 skin toxicity with no mature long-tail data is not a cleaner safety bet than the approved agent. The specific missing datum is durable tolerability at approval scale; until the PDUFA read and a peer-reviewed safety table land, I do not rank it above pemigatinib. conservativeadvocatedissenttoxicityYou rank lirafugratinib second and call it the best-tolerated option on the FGFR axis for a balanced weight. That claim rests on the hyperphosphatemia comparison alone and skips the toxicity that actually differentiates it: grade 3+ palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia at 32.8% plus grade 3+ stomatitis at 12.1% (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476). Trading away FGFR1-driven hyperphosphatemia for a one-in-three grade 3 hand-foot rate is a lateral move on tolerability, not an improvement, and grade 3 hand-foot is the kind of dose-interrupting, function-limiting event a patient feels every day. Pemigatinib's on-target hyperphosphatemia was 55% any grade with no grade 3-4 (pmid:32203698), which is a milder grade distribution at the same axis. Under a 0.5 weight I would not call the abstract-stage selective agent the tolerability winner over the approved one; the grade-3 arithmetic points the other way. criticadvocatedissentevidence_qualityYou rank abstract-only data at 2 and call it 'enrollable now,' and I think that overstates what we can stand on. ReFocus reads ORR 46.5% (95% CI 37.1-56.1) in n=114, single-arm, but it is an ASCO GI 2026 abstract with no PubMed record and a ROBINS-I:Moderate placeholder on a paper none of us has read (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476). Against two FGFR2 agents with peer-reviewed pivotals (futibatinib ORR 42%, pmid:36652354; pemigatinib 35.5%, pmid:32203698), a moderate confidence at rank 2 is more than the evidence maturity supports. Credit on provenance: you cited NCT04526106, the ReFocus cohort, correctly, not the non-CCA basket NCT07359820 that some conflate. I would drop this to a trial-enrollment option behind the approved agents until the full paper lets us audit response ascertainment and censoring. criticrisktakerdissentevidence_qualitySeating an abstract at rank 1 is exactly the trade I push back on. The 46.5% ORR (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476) is a single-arm number with no comparator, no PMID, and no full text to check how responses were adjudicated, and the drug is pre-approval (PDUFA pending). You concede all of that and rank it first anyway on magnitude. My objection is not the tolerability argument for FGFR2-selective design, which is real, it is putting an unaudited abstract above futibatinib's NEJM pivotal (ORR 42%, mOS 21.7 mo, pmid:36652354). One thing you got right that others muddle: the enrollment route is the ReFocus cohort (NCT04526106), not the basket NCT07359820, which excludes CCA outright. Rank the peer-reviewed agent first; keep the selective drug as the upside bet it currently is. concensusiterisktakerdissentguideline_fitRanking lirafugratinib first over approved futibatinib and pemigatinib inverts the guideline order: it is under FDA priority review with a 27 Sep 2026 PDUFA, so it is not approved and not listed in NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v2.2025, while futibatinib and pemigatinib are both category 2A there. On a confirmed FGFR2 fusion the guideline-consonant use of the ReFocus data (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476) is trial enrollment, not a standard rec displacing the two approved agents. Burying ivosidenib at rank 6 also passes over the only NCCN category-1 anchor in this whole set. concensusiteadvocatedissentguideline_fitThe prefers_trials preference makes lirafugratinib a legitimate enrollment option once FGFR2 confirms, and to your credit you named futibatinib as the on-label fallback. But ranking the pre-approval agent at 2, above approved futibatinib, still reads as a standard rec over a NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v2.2025 category-2A agent, and lirafugratinib is neither approved (PDUFA 27 Sep 2026) nor NCCN-listed. The guideline-consonant framing is a trial slot sitting alongside the approved FGFR pair, not ahead of it in the treatment order. advocateconcensusitedissentpreference_fitYou put lirafugratinib in a 'trial-enrollment lane, not the ranked set' because it is not yet approved or NCCN-listed, and for a guideline-anchored read that is consistent. But the patient set prefers_trials=true, and the ReFocus cohort (NCT04526106, doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476) is a recruiting on-axis route with ORR 46.5% and the lowest hyperphosphatemia burden on the FGFR lane. Under the one preference on file, an enrollable next-gen agent is exactly what should be surfaced first, not fenced off from the ranked menu. advocatecriticqualifiedpreference_fitYour evidence discount is fair and the provenance flag is worth keeping: the ReFocus readout is abstract-only, and NCT07359820 does exclude CCA so nobody should cite it as the route (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476, nct:NCT04526106). Where I pull back is calling it 'investigational, not an on-label option' as the reason it sits below the approved agents. For a patient who set prefers_trials=true, pre-approval status is not a demotion; the recruiting ReFocus cohort is a live door, and the preference asks me to put it in front of them alongside the on-label picks, not beneath them by default. advocaterisktakerendorsepreference_fitSeating the FGFR2-selective agent at the head of the therapeutic picks and lining up trial or expanded-access enrollment in parallel with the panel is exactly what prefers_trials=true asks for, so from the patient's lens I am with you (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476, nct:NCT04526106). Leaving T-DXd off over the ILD signal with no organ-function labs supplied also reads as user-protective under a balanced 0.5 weight, not just a risk call. My one caution is that you name the abstract-only maturity plainly to the patient, which you did, so this holds.

docs.title: Futibatinib (futibatinib)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker2lowThe FGFR2 play I would actually reach for first if I want published, on-label evidence rather than an abstract: FOENIX-CCA2 gave ORR 42% (95% CI 32-52), mDoR 9.7 mo, mOS 21.7 mo in NEJM, with only 2% discontinuing for toxicity. Its covalent irreversible chemistry holds up against several FGFR2 kinase-domain resistance mutations that sink the reversible inhibitors, so it doubles as a sequencing option after pemigatinib. Same hard gate as every FGFR pick here: the fusion is untested. I rank it just under lirafugratinib only because the raw response and PFS numbers are a notch lower, not because the evidence is weaker; the evidence is stronger.Requires a confirmed FGFR2 fusion the patient has not been tested for; Hyperphosphatemia grade 3+ in 30%, higher than the selective next-gen agents; Intrahepatic subsite drove the trial; the patient's subsite is unspecified at intake conservative——did not pick— critic3moderateThe FGFR2-fusion axis is the closest thing to replication in this dossier, and that is what earns it rank 3 rather than any single ORR. FOENIX-CCA2 (ORR 42%, 95% CI 32-52, median OS 21.7 mo, 2% discontinuing for toxicity) and FIGHT-202 converge on the same effect direction in centrally confirmed fusions, and the new FGFR2-selective agents point the same way. The hard ceiling is that the registered endpoint is ORR, a surrogate, with no randomized comparator and no OS control. I put futibatinib at the head of the FGFR lane because its activity against some post-pemigatinib kinase-domain resistance mutations is documented in the trial rather than extrapolated, which is a sequencing fact I can stand on.Single-arm design with a surrogate ORR primary endpoint; no comparator, so the response rate carries the usual single-arm inflation.; FGFR2 fusion is untested (ngs_pending) and eligibility was built on intrahepatic CCA while subsite is unspecified at intake.; Open-label response ascertainment; independent central review reduces the bias but does not remove it. concensusite2moderateOn a confirmed FGFR2 fusion, futibatinib is NCCN BTC v2.2025 category 2A for subsequent-line disease, and the 2024 ESMO interim update backs the FGFR-inhibitor class after one prior line at ESMO-MCBS v1.1 score 3. FOENIX-CCA2 gave ORR 42% (95% CI 32-52), median OS 21.7 months, and only 2% stopped for toxicity. I edge it ahead of pemigatinib because it holds activity against some FGFR2 kinase-domain mutations that defeat the reversible inhibitors, which matters for sequencing. FGFR2 fusions sit at 10-15% in intrahepatic CCA, the highest-yield molecular axis to test in this disease.FGFR2 fusion is untested (ngs_pending); the indication was built in intrahepatic CCA and subsite is blank at intake, so a non-intrahepatic primary weakens the fit.; Category 2A here reflects single-arm phase 2 with a surrogate ORR endpoint, not a randomized survival comparison. The MCBS 3 is scored on the FGFR-inhibitor class, not on futibatinib over pemigatinib.; On-target hyperphosphatemia hits grade 3 in 30% and needs the phosphate management the guideline assumes is on hand. advocate3moderateThis is the established, on-label safety net for the same FGFR2 axis, and I rank it right behind the selective agent so the patient is never stuck choosing between the best-tolerated option and a proven one. FOENIX-CCA2 showed ORR 42% (95% CI 32-52), median PFS 9.0 months, median OS 21.7 months, and only 2% discontinued for toxicity, which is a strong durability record. The irreversible binding also holds against several kinase-domain mutations that defeat pemigatinib, so it buys a second FGFR move if the patient progresses. The cost is the on-target hyperphosphatemia, grade 3+ in 30%, which needs active phosphate management but is manageable and not a stated veto. Oral, once daily. Between the two approved FGFR agents I put futibatinib ahead of pemigatinib on the slightly higher response rate and the lower discontinuation rate.Fully satisfied: FDA-approved on-label oral option, no veto to clear, balanced tolerability that a 0.5 weight accepts.; Hyperphosphatemia is near-universal on target and grade 3+ in 30%, so it needs phosphate monitoring even though no toxicity veto was set.; Approval and trial eligibility were built on intrahepatic CCA, so a non-intrahepatic subsite weakens the match, and the fusion is untested.

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment conservativeconcensusitedissenttoxicityYou seat futibatinib above pemigatinib on a kinase-domain resistance sequencing edge, which is a real point in the second-line setting but is not where a treatment-naive patient starts. In the first-line FGFR2 slot the toxicity gap runs the other way: grade 3 hyperphosphatemia hit 30% on futibatinib (pmid:36652354) against no grade 3-4 events on pemigatinib, where the on-target effect was 55% any grade (pmid:32203698). At a comparable response rate I take the lower-grade burden and the longer post-approval record, so within the lane I reverse your order. The resistance-mutation coverage is a genuine reason to switch to futibatinib after pemigatinib progression, and I would document that as the sequencing plan rather than as the reason to lead with the higher grade-3 agent.

docs.title: Dabrafenib + trametinib (dabrafenib-trametinib)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker5lowA confirmed BRAF V600E opens a 47% ORR (95% CI 31-62) with mPFS 9.0 mo from the ROAR biliary cohort, plus a tumor-agnostic label, so a positive call is immediately actionable off the same CGP. BRAF V600E sits at only 1-5% of biliary cancer, but the response rate rivals the FGFR agents and the doublet is well-characterized with pyrexia as the main nuisance rather than an organ threat. I rank it here rather than higher because the prevalence is low and the pick lives or dies on the NGS result. If it comes back positive, I would not hesitate.BRAF V600E prevalence 1-5%; likely negative; Non-V600E class 2/3 BRAF alterations do not qualify and could be miscalled as actionable; Pyrexia in ~19% needs active management though it is rarely dangerous conservative——did not pick— critic——did not pick— concensusite5moderateA confirmed BRAF V600E gives a doublet that NCCN BTC v2.2025 (category 2A, subsequent-line) and the tumor-agnostic FDA label both endorse, with the ROAR biliary cohort at ORR 47% (95% CI 31-62) and median PFS 9.0 months. The cross-society and cross-label convergence is real, but I hold it at rank 5 because V600E turns up in only about 1-5% of BTC and the cohort is small (n=43) and single-arm. The gate is a true V600E on NGS or PCR; a VE1 IHC screen alone, or a class 2/3 BRAF alteration, does not qualify. Pyrexia is the signature combination effect and comes with a standard dose-hold and antipyretic playbook the consensus assumes is in place.BRAF V600E is untested (ngs_pending); only a confirmed V600E on NGS/PCR meets the gate, IHC alone and class 2/3 alterations do not.; Category 2A here rests on a small single-arm basket cohort (n=43).; Pyrexia drove the treatment-related serious AEs at 21% and needs the monitoring the guideline presumes, unconfirmed against absent baseline data. advocate——did not pick—

docs.title: Ivosidenib (ivosidenib)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker6moderateThe one randomized phase 3 signal in the whole set: ClarIDHy gave a PFS HR of 0.37 (95% CI 0.25-0.54, p<0.0001) versus placebo with a low risk-of-bias grade, and IDH1 R132 shows up in 15-20% of intrahepatic CCA, so the pretest odds are respectable. My honest hesitation is the effect size, not the evidence quality: ORR was 2%, median PFS 2.7 mo, and the OS read got blunted by crossover to a crossover-adjusted HR 0.46. For a persona that weights magnitude, a hazard ratio this clean but an absolute benefit this thin lands it at the bottom of my ranked picks rather than off the list.Absolute PFS gain is small (2.7 vs 1.4 mo) despite the strong HR; ORR only 2%; disease stabilization rather than tumor shrinkage is the realistic goal; Gated on a confirmed IDH1 R132 mutation, untested here conservative3moderateThis is the cleanest safety dataset in the whole dossier, and that is why I rank it here despite a modest efficacy signal. ClarIDHy is the only randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 on the board (RoB2 low), and the grade 3+ AE profile tracked placebo closely: ascites was the most common grade 3+ event in both arms at 7%, and there were no treatment-related deaths. The one class effect to watch is QT prolongation, which showed up as a single grade 3 event and has a standard ECG-monitoring answer. Yes, the median PFS gain is only 2.7 versus 1.4 months and the ORR is 2%, with the OS read blunted by 70% crossover (HR 0.37 for PFS, p<0.0001; crossover-adjusted OS HR 0.46). But for a patient where do-no-harm is the priority, a well-tolerated oral agent with randomized evidence and a benign toxicity ledger is a defensible confirmed-positive choice. IDH1 mutations run roughly 15-20% in intrahepatic disease.Absolute PFS benefit is small and the ORR is 2%; this buys disease control and tolerability, not deep responses.; IDH1 R132 is untested; IDH2 and non-R132 IDH1 variants do not qualify, so the DNA panel must cover the exact hotspot.; QT prolongation is a known class effect and warrants baseline and on-treatment ECGs. critic2moderateThis is the only intervention in the whole option set backed by a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3. ClarIDHy is RoB2:Low and hit its registered PFS primary endpoint (HR 0.37, 95% CI 0.25-0.54, p<0.0001). On evidence quality alone it clears everything else here, which is all single-arm. I want to be precise about what it buys, though: ORR was 2%, so the benefit is delayed progression rather than tumor shrinkage, and the survival story is unresolved. The intention-to-treat OS HR was 0.69 (p=0.060) and did not cross alpha; the 0.46 that gets cited is an RPSFT crossover adjustment after 70% of placebo patients crossed over, which is a sensitivity model, not the trial result. Rank 2 because it is gated on an IDH1 R132 call we have not made.ITT OS was not significant at the pre-specified alpha (HR 0.69, p=0.060); the 0.46 crossover-adjusted figure is modeling, not a clean survival endpoint.; IDH1 R132 is untested (ngs_pending); the entire pick collapses if the hotspot is wild-type, and a limited fusion-only panel could miss the codon.; RoB2: PFS in a symptomatic disease is the residual domain, mitigated but not erased by independent review. concensusite1moderateIf the IDH1 hotspot reads positive, ivosidenib is the strongest guideline anchor in this whole option set: NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v2.2025 now lists it category 1 for subsequent-line IDH1-mutant disease, and the 2024 ESMO interim BTC update recommends it after at least one prior line (ESMO-MCBS v1.1 score 2). It is also the only randomized phase 3 among the candidate axes, ClarIDHy, with a PFS HR of 0.37 (95% CI 0.25-0.54). I rank it first on that category-1 status, not on shrinkage, since ORR was only 2% and the realistic aim is delayed progression. IDH1 R132 runs 15-20% in intrahepatic CCA, so it is also one of the likelier positives the panel returns.IDH1 R132 is untested (ngs_pending); a negative NGS read voids the pick.; The category-1 listing sits on a phase 3 whose ITT overall survival did not separate (HR 0.69, p=0.060); the 0.46 is RPSFT crossover-adjusted modeling. NCCN graded it category 1 on the PFS win with crossover-adjusted OS support, which is worth naming rather than glossing.; Guidelines assume measurable progression and an ECOG-fit patient; intake gave no organ-function labs and ECOG 1 is an assumption, so QT-monitoring feasibility is unconfirmed. advocate4moderateIDH1 R132 is the second most likely axis to land at 15 to 20% of intrahepatic disease, and this is the only randomized phase 3 in the whole dossier, ClarIDHy, with a PFS hazard ratio of 0.37 (p<0.0001). For a patient who values evidence quality, that randomized read is worth a lot. It is also the gentlest option here: grade 3+ events tracked placebo, ascites was the most common at 7%, and there were no treatment-related deaths, so on the tolerability side of a balanced weight it is easy to defend. What holds it at rank 4 rather than higher is the modest single-agent payoff, median PFS 2.7 versus 1.4 months and ORR only 2%, so the realistic goal is holding disease steady rather than shrinking it. Oral, once daily. If the patient wants more than stabilization, the preclinical work pointing to an immune-mediated mechanism and synergy with CTLA-4 blockade is the reason to ask about an ivosidenib-plus-checkpoint trial, which also serves the trials-first preference.Fully satisfied: cleanest safety profile in the set, oral, on-label, and the only randomized evidence, which suits a patient weighting evidence and tolerability evenly.; Absolute single-agent benefit is small (median PFS 2.7 vs 1.4 months; ORR 2%) despite the strong hazard ratio, so expectations need framing.; IDH1 hotspot is untested, and the OS read was blunted by 70% placebo-to-ivosidenib crossover.

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment risktakerconservativequalifiedpreference_fitRanking ivosidenib at 3 on the strength of its clean safety ledger while banishing lirafugratinib entirely undersells the trade a balanced 0.5 weight actually allows: ivosidenib's ORR is 2% (pmid:32416072) against the ReFocus cohort's 46.5% (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476). If FGFR2 confirms, the selective agent's 32.8% grade 3+ PPE is a real but manageable cost for a tenfold-better response, not a reason to keep it off the ranked list. risktakercriticdissentevidence_qualityElevating ivosidenib to rank 2 purely because it is the lone RCT, then dropping lirafugratinib to rank 4 as abstract-only, weights design tier over what the patient gets: ClarIDHy's own ORR is 2% and the ITT OS missed alpha (HR 0.69, p=0.060, pmid:32416072). The FGFR2-selective 46.5% ORR (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476) is single-arm and pre-approval, which I concede, but a randomized read on a 2% response is a clean answer to the wrong question if the FGFR2 axis lights up. risktakerconcensusitedissentguideline_fitThe NCCN category-1 badge is doing all the lifting for rank 1, but it sits on a PFS win of 2.7 vs 1.4 months and a 2% ORR (pmid:32416072), which is the thinnest actionable signal on the board. If futibatinib's FGFR2 axis reads positive, its 42% ORR and 21.7-month OS (pmid:36652354) is the pick I would put in front of the patient first, and guideline lettering should not bury a tenfold response difference under an IDH1 call that is no more likely to be positive. criticconservativequalifiedevidence_qualityWe land in the same place and I want to sharpen one word. You sell ivosidenib on 'randomized evidence,' and ClarIDHy is the only RCT here (RoB2:Low), so that is fair. But the randomized endpoint that actually cleared alpha is PFS (HR 0.37, p<0.0001). The survival read did not: ITT OS was HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.44-1.1, p=0.060 (pmid:32416072). The 0.46 you cite is an RPSFT crossover adjustment after 70% of placebo patients crossed, which is a sensitivity model, not the trial's OS result. For a do-no-harm pick that is fine, the tolerability case carries it, but the phrase 'randomized evidence' should attach to delayed progression, not to a survival benefit the trial never demonstrated at conventional alpha. criticconcensusitequalifiedevidence_qualityYou already named the ITT OS caveat in your own concern list, so credit where it is due, most personas glossed it. My qualifier is on what the category-1 label actually rests on. NCCN v2.2025 graded ivosidenib category 1 off the PFS primary (HR 0.37) with crossover-adjusted OS support, not off a survival endpoint that separated. So when you seat it at rank 1 on 'the strongest guideline anchor,' the anchor is a PFS win plus modeling, which is thinner than a category-1 badge reads to a casual eye. That is a fair rank-1 given the RCT pedigree, but the anchor is the PFS endpoint, and I would not let the category number stand in for a survival claim that ITT OS (p=0.060, pmid:32416072) does not support. concensusiterisktakerdissentguideline_fitThe 2% ORR and 2.7-vs-1.4-month PFS (pmid:32416072) are exactly why ivosidenib sits at rank 6 here, but NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v2.2025 read that same ClarIDHy result, crossover-blunted OS and all, and still graded it category 1 for IDH1-mutant subsequent-line disease. That grade reflects a randomized win no other axis in this dossier can match. Effect size is your lens and I take the point, but category 1 is not a badge to file at the bottom of the list. concensusitecriticqualifiedguideline_fitWe land on the same rank-2 placement and I agree the ITT OS missed alpha (HR 0.69, p=0.060, pmid:32416072), so the precision is fair. Worth adding to the record: the NCCN panel had that non-significant ITT OS and the RPSFT-adjusted 0.46 in front of it and still made ivosidenib category 1 in Biliary Tract Cancers v2.2025 on the PFS win, so the category-1 grade is the panel's calibration of the same evidence you are reading, not a number that skipped the caveat. That is a reason to name it category 1 explicitly rather than treat the listing as softer than the data. advocateconcensusiteendorsepreference_fitKeeping comprehensive genomic profiling as the rank-1 gating workup even while ivosidenib takes the top therapeutic slot is the right call for this patient, since every axis is ngs_pending and nothing else can be acted on until the panel reads. The IDH1 pick itself sits fine against a balanced 0.5 weight: oral, near-placebo grade 3+, and an open registration trial (NCT02989857) that serves prefers_trials. My only ask is that the CGP gate stay explicitly ahead of it in what the patient sees, not just in your notes.

docs.title: Pemigatinib (only if an FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement is confirmed) (pemigatinib)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker——did not pick— conservative2moderateOf the FGFR options this is the one with the longest track record: FDA approval since 2020, so roughly five years of post-marketing safety follow-up on top of the FIGHT-202 pivotal. The toxicity is on-target and predictable. Hyperphosphatemia ran 55% any grade with no grade 3-4 in the trial, and it has a well-worn management algorithm of low-phosphate diet, phosphate binders, and dose holds. The nail, skin, and dysgeusia effects are mostly low grade, and serous retinal detachment at 4% has an established ophthalmologic monitoring pathway. Grade 3+ AEs sat at 64% in the 146-patient safety population, which I do not minimize, but the events are ones oncologists already know how to run. ORR was 35.5% (95% CI 26.5-45.4). FGFR2 fusion is also the highest-yield axis at roughly 10-15% in intrahepatic disease, so this is the confirmed-positive I most expect to see.Fusion is untested (ngs_pending) and subsite is unspecified; eligibility was built on intrahepatic CCA, so a non-intrahepatic subsite weakens the match.; Serous retinal detachment (4%, one grade 3) requires baseline and periodic ophthalmologic exams before and during treatment.; Single-arm phase 2 pivotal; the efficacy read has no randomized comparator even though the safety base is now mature. critic——did not pick— concensusite3moderatePemigatinib is the other guideline-endorsed FGFR2 option, NCCN BTC v2.2025 category 2A and ESMO-recommended within the same FGFR-inhibitor class (MCBS v1.1 score 3), and it was the first FGFR inhibitor approved in CCA with a companion diagnostic behind it. FIGHT-202 gave ORR 35.5% (95% CI 26.5-45.4). I place it just below futibatinib because the sequencing edge on kinase-domain resistance runs the other way, so once the fusion is confirmed this is a within-lane call. Two independent single-arm trials converging on the same fusion axis is what gives the consensus its footing here.FGFR2 fusion is untested (ngs_pending); subsite unspecified at intake against an intrahepatic-built indication.; Single-arm phase 2 behind an accelerated approval; the reported OS of 21.1 months is immature at 40 events.; Serous retinal detachment (4%) needs the scheduled ophthalmologic monitoring the guideline presumes, unconfirmed here. advocate——did not pick—

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment concensusiteconservativequalifiedguideline_fitNo quarrel with the CGP gate or with favoring the longer-approved FGFR agent on safety-follow-up depth, and both pemigatinib and futibatinib are NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v2.2025 category 2A. The one thing I would flag: ivosidenib is now category 1 in that same version for IDH1-mutant disease, the sole category-1 listing in the set, so among the biomarker-conditional therapies it has a firmer consensus footing than the rank-3 slot behind pemigatinib and ivosidenib implies. Not a safety objection, just a guideline-weight one. advocateconservativequalifiedpreference_fitDefaulting to pemigatinib on depth of post-approval safety follow-up is defensible, and the concern about immature registration-scale tolerability for the selective agents is real, I grant that. But you set aside lirafugratinib partly on 'no US access,' and the ReFocus cohort is actively recruiting (NCT04526106), which for a prefers_trials=true patient is an open door rather than a closed one (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.476). At a balanced 0.5 weight, its FGFR2-selective profile sparing FGFR1-driven hyperphosphatemia is a live tolerability argument the patient's preference asks us to at least surface next to pemigatinib, not omit.

docs.title: Zanidatamab (only if HER2 is confirmed by IHC 2+/3+ with reflex ISH) (zanidatamab)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker——did not pick— conservative5moderateFor the HER2 axis I put the antibody ahead of the ADC on safety grounds. Zanidatamab's toxicity is manageable and mostly familiar: diarrhea 40% any grade with 5% grade 3, infusion-related reactions 35%, and a HER2-class decreased-ejection-fraction signal at 3% grade 3 that inherits the cardiac-monitoring algorithm built over decades of trastuzumab use. HERIZON-BTC-01 gave a confirmed ORR of 41.3% (95% CI 30.4-52.8) with a median DoR of 12.9 months. I deliberately rank this over trastuzumab deruxtecan, whose 10.5% adjudicated interstitial lung disease rate and three treatment-related ILD deaths in DESTINY-PanTumor02 are the kind of uncharacterized long-tail toxicity I flag, even with no toxicity veto set in preferences. The gate is HER2 IHC with reflex ISH, not an NGS amplification call, and HER2 skews toward extrahepatic and gallbladder disease, so subsite uncertainty is the main soft spot.HER2 status is untested and the correct gate is IHC with reflex ISH, not an NGS-only amplification signal.; Decreased ejection fraction (3% grade 3) requires baseline and periodic cardiac function monitoring.; HER2 is more common in extrahepatic/gallbladder disease, and subsite is unspecified at intake, weakening the prior. critic5moderateHER2 is the other on-indication axis with a pivotal single-arm readout rather than a basket subgroup. HERIZON-BTC-01 cohort 1 reported confirmed ORR 41.3% (95% CI 30.4-52.8, n=80) with median DoR 12.9 mo, ROBINS-I:Moderate, driving accelerated approval. I rank it fifth, below the FGFR lane, for two reasons: it is single-arm ORR with no comparator, and the gating test is HER2 IHC 4B5 with reflex ISH, not the NGS panel, so a copy-number amplification call alone will not qualify the patient or pick the right agent. I am deliberately keeping the HER2 early-phase crowd (T-DXd basket subgroup, the bispecifics, ADCs, CAR-NK, neratinib) off my ranked list: those are basket subgroup signals or phase-1 dose-finding with no CCA efficacy readout, and I will not rank a subgroup or a first-in-human safety run ahead of a pivotal cohort.Single-arm phase 2b, confirmed-ORR endpoint, accelerated approval; no randomized survival comparison exists.; Gating test is HER2 IHC/ISH (4B5), not the DNA panel; an NGS amplification signal alone does not establish protein expression or select the agent, and HER2 is untested here.; Cardiac signal (decreased ejection fraction) warrants monitoring; more relevant to extrahepatic/gallbladder subsite, which is unspecified at intake. concensusite4moderateZanidatamab is the guideline-endorsed HER2 lead here: NCCN BTC v2.2025 category 2A for HER2-positive (IHC 3+) subsequent-line disease off HERIZON-BTC-01 (confirmed ORR 41.3%, 95% CI 30.4-52.8, median DoR 12.9 months). It is the only dedicated biliary HER2 trial behind a guideline listing, which is why I rank it over T-DXd (basket route) and over the wave of investigational HER2 agents now on the trial list, none of which any society endorses. The gate is HER2 IHC with reflex ISH on the trial's own scoring, not a breast or gastric cutoff and not an NGS copy-number call standing in for the protein read. HER2 skews toward extrahepatic and gallbladder disease, so a positive depends on a subsite intake never gave.HER2 is untested and needs IHC plus reflex ISH, not NGS amplification alone, to meet the guideline gate.; The category 2A rests on single-arm phase 2b accelerated-approval data with no randomized comparator.; HER2 prevalence hinges on a subsite intake left blank, and no baseline cardiac function was supplied for the 3% grade-3 ejection-fraction signal. advocate5moderateIf HER2 tests positive this is the option I would put in front of the patient first, and I rank it above T-DXd deliberately on the user's behalf. HERIZON-BTC-01 gave a confirmed ORR 41.3% (95% CI 30.4-52.8) with median DoR 12.9 months, and the safety read is favorable: the main concern is a 3% grade 3 ejection-fraction drop that baseline and serial cardiac monitoring handles. Trastuzumab deruxtecan carries adjudicated interstitial lung disease at 10.5% with three treatment-related deaths in DESTINY-PanTumor02, and while no toxicity veto was stated, a balanced 0.5 weight should not reach for the ILD-risk ADC when a comparably effective antibody with a milder profile is available on the same axis. HER2 skews toward extrahepatic and gallbladder disease and the subsite is unknown here, which is the real uncertainty. The gate is HER2 IHC with reflex ISH, not the DNA copy-number call alone, so the rank-1 workup has to include the protein readout. If the patient specifically wants a trial, several HER2-positive BTC cohorts are recruiting, which serves the trials-first preference.Fully satisfied: on-label, and the milder cardiac profile beats the T-DXd ILD signal on the user's behalf under a balanced weight, even with no explicit veto set.; Gated on HER2 IHC plus reflex ISH, not NGS alone; HER2 prevalence depends on a subsite that is unspecified at intake.; Decreased ejection fraction is a HER2-directed class effect and no baseline cardiac function was supplied, so monitoring is required.

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment conservativeadvocateendorsetoxicityPlacing zanidatamab above T-DXd on the patient's behalf is the right safety call and I back it fully, even though no toxicity veto was set in preferences. The reasoning holds on its own terms: an adjudicated 10.5% ILD rate with three treatment-related deaths on T-DXd (pmid:37870536) against a 3% grade-3 ejection-fraction signal on zanidatamab that inherits the cardiac-monitoring algorithm built over decades of trastuzumab use (pmid:37423227). One thing to tighten in the framing: the gate is HER2 IHC with reflex ISH, not the NGS amplification call, so the rank-1 workup has to carry the protein readout or this pick cannot be selected correctly. And with no baseline cardiac function supplied at intake, the echo monitoring you cite is a plan to schedule, not one already confirmed feasible. concensusiteadvocateendorseguideline_fitThis one is squarely guideline-consonant: zanidatamab is NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v2.2025 category 2A for HER2-positive subsequent-line disease off the dedicated HERIZON-BTC-01 cohort (pmid:37423227), and putting it ahead of basket-route T-DXd matches how the guideline treats the biliary-specific trial. The IHC-plus-reflex-ISH gate you name is the right one, not an NGS amplification call. Agreement here, not qualification.

docs.title: Pembrolizumab (FDA-approved, on-label; if MSI-H/dMMR or TMB-high confirmed) (pembrolizumab)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker——did not pick— conservative——did not pick— critic——did not pick— concensusite——did not pick— advocate6lowThis is the low-prevalence, high-payoff pick I keep on the ranked list because when it lands it is durable in a way nothing else here is. MSI-H/dMMR runs only 1 to 3% in biliary cancer, but KEYNOTE-158 showed ORR 34.3% with median OS 23.5 months in the MSI-H basket, and the TMB-high subgroup reached ORR 29% with responses still ongoing past two years. The same rank-1 panel returns both the MSI call and the TMB number, and MMR IHC is a cheap orthogonal check that catches cases a low-purity NGS score can miss, so there is no extra burden to chase it. Grade 3+ treatment-related events sat at 14.6%, lower than most targeted options here, which fits a balanced weight. The reason it is sixth and not higher is prevalence alone; on effect-per-positive-test it earns its place, and the durability is the argument to run the MMR IHC alongside the DNA panel rather than waiting.Fully satisfied: lowest grade 3+ rate among the targeted options, on-label, and resolved by the same rank-1 workup at no added cost.; Prevalence is the constraint at 1-3% MSI-H, so the test is most often negative; no CCA-specific subgroup ORR was published in KEYNOTE-158.; Immune-mediated toxicity is the characteristic checkpoint risk; no veto was set, but it warrants counseling.

docs.title: What this page is
docs.text:
This is the patient and caregiver version of a longer report Libby put together about treatment options for metastatic cholangiocarcinoma, a cancer of the bile ducts. The case Libby was handed had almost nothing in it: the diagnosis, and little else. No genetic testing of the tumor had been done yet.

That one fact shapes everything below. Cholangiocarcinoma can carry any of several specific genetic changes, and for most of those changes there is a drug built to go after it. But you cannot know which of those drugs might help until you know what the tumor is actually made of. So the page is organized around one honest reality: there is a single test that comes before any of the drug choices, and it is the test that tells you which door is open. The drug choices only come into focus once that test is back.

A couple of things to know going in. Libby only looks at treatments aimed at a specific genetic feature of the tumor. The ordinary chemotherapy that most people with this cancer start on is real and important, but it is not what this page covers, and your oncologist owns that conversation. And because no test results were available, a lot of what would normally personalize a plan (your other health conditions, what you care about most, what you have already tried) was filled in with neutral placeholders. Treat everything here as a starting point for a conversation, not a plan.

docs.title: What we know about your cancer
docs.text:
Not much was provided, and it is worth being upfront about that.

The cancer started in the bile ducts (cholangiocarcinoma) and has spread beyond where it began (metastatic, stage IV). Whether it started inside the liver or in the ducts outside the liver was not recorded, and that detail matters, because some of the genetic changes are more common in one location than the other.

No genetic testing of the tumor had been done. Performance status was assumed to be relatively good (up and about, able to care for yourself), age was assumed to be in the 60s, and no prior treatments were on record. These are placeholders, not facts about you. If any of them is wrong, the plan should be revisited.

docs.title: What you told us matters most
docs.text: No preferences were recorded for this case, so Libby used a balanced setting: how well a treatment works and how hard its side effects hit were weighed equally, with nothing ruled in or out ahead of time. One thing was noted, that being open to clinical trials counts as a plus. If you have strong feelings, say a real fear of a particular side effect, or a preference for pills over infusions, those would shift the order of what follows, and they are worth telling your oncologist directly.

docs.title: The first step everyone agreed on
docs.text:
Before any drug below is on the table, the tumor needs to be genetically tested. This is called comprehensive genomic profiling, and it is the clear first move. Think of it as the test that tells us which door is open, because right now every door is closed until we look.

Here is why it sits first. The test reads several genetic features at once, and roughly four in ten people with this cancer turn out to have at least one feature that a targeted drug can act on. The test itself does not treat the cancer. What it does is tell you which, if any, of the options further down this page are even reachable.

It is also about as low-risk as a test gets. Usually it can be run on a tumor sample that was already taken and stored, so no new procedure is needed; when stored tissue is not enough, a blood draw can sometimes stand in. Results generally come back in one to three weeks. There is no toxicity to weigh against, which is part of why it was an easy call.

One practical note worth raising with your team: a few features need their own specific tests rather than the standard panel. A marker called HER2 is best checked by staining the tumor tissue directly, and a feature called mismatch-repair deficiency is fastest to confirm with a tissue stain too. And catching an FGFR2 fusion reliably takes a test that reads RNA, not DNA alone. So the right order is the full genetic panel, run with an RNA arm, plus those couple of tissue stains, all together.

docs.title: The options
docs.text: Everything in this section depends on the test above coming back positive for the matching feature. None of these is something you start tomorrow; each one waits on a specific result. They are listed in the order Libby ranked them, which reflects a mix of how strong the evidence is and how likely the feature is to show up in this cancer. Two things hold true throughout: most of these options ride on a test result that is not yet in hand, and some of the newer drugs are still early or trial-stage. I will flag which is which as we go.

docs.title: Option 1 — Ivosidenib (only if the tumor has an IDH1 R132 change)
docs.text:
This option is only available if the test comes back positive for a genetic change called IDH1 R132. If it comes back negative, this option is off the table, and Libby's recommendations on this page are limited to treatments aimed at a specific genetic feature, so a negative result here does not by itself leave you with nothing; it just means this particular door is closed and you move on to the others. (More on what happens if every door is closed at the end of this section.)

Ivosidenib is a once-a-day pill. Of all the options on this page, it rests on the strongest kind of evidence: a trial where people were randomly assigned to the drug or a placebo, which is the most reliable way to know a drug is doing something. In that trial, the drug roughly doubled the time before the cancer grew, from about 1.4 months to about 2.7 months on average, and that difference was statistically convincing.

Honesty matters here. The tumors very rarely shrank on this drug, only about 2 in 100 had measurable shrinkage. The realistic goal is to hold the cancer steady for a while, not to make it smaller. On whether it helps people live longer, the published numbers point toward a benefit, but the cleanest version of that analysis did not quite clear the bar for certainty, and the more favorable number leans on a statistical adjustment made after most placebo patients later crossed over to the drug. So I can't give you a precise survival improvement here without overstating what the trial actually showed.

Side effects were mild overall, close to placebo. The one thing that needs watching is an effect on heart rhythm, checked with an ECG before and during treatment. This change shows up in maybe 15 to 20 percent of intrahepatic (inside-the-liver) cholangiocarcinomas, so it is one of the more likely features to turn up.

docs.title: Option 2 — Futibatinib (only if the tumor has an FGFR2 fusion)
docs.text:
This option is only available if the test comes back positive for an FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement. If it comes back negative, this option is off the table.

Futibatinib is a daily pill, and the FGFR2 fusion it targets is the single most common targetable change in this cancer, roughly 1 in 8 of the inside-the-liver cases. In its trial, about 42 percent of tumors shrank, and people lived a little under two years on average. Very few had to stop the drug because of side effects. What gives this option extra weight is that a second, separate drug in the same family showed a similar result, which is the closest thing on this page to one trial confirming another. This drug also tends to keep working against some of the resistance the cancer develops to the gentler relative below it, which matters if you need to switch later.

The tradeoff is a side effect called high blood phosphate. It is a built-in consequence of how the drug works, and it reaches a more serious level in roughly 30 percent of people, so it needs active management with diet and medication. The gentler relative of this drug is the next option, and the choice between the two comes down to this: futibatinib has the slightly stronger response data and may still work after the gentler one stops, while the gentler one is easier on the body. That is a genuine conversation to have, not a settled answer.

The fine print: the evidence is from a single-group study, everyone got the drug with no comparison group, and the response numbers are a stand-in for the harder question of how much longer people live. The trial was also built around inside-the-liver cases, so if the cancer started outside the liver the fit is weaker.

docs.title: Option 3 — Pemigatinib (also only if the tumor has an FGFR2 fusion)
docs.text:
This option is only available if the test comes back positive for an FGFR2 fusion. It targets the exact same feature as the option above, so the two are alternatives within the same lane rather than separate paths.

Pemigatinib is a pill taken on a schedule of two weeks on, one week off. About 36 percent of tumors shrank in its trial, in line with futibatinib. It was the first drug of its kind approved for this cancer, so it has the longest real-world track record. Its version of the high-phosphate side effect tends to stay milder, common but rarely at the serious level, which is the whole argument for choosing it over futibatinib when going gentler matters more. It does carry one effect worth knowing about: a fluid buildup behind the retina that needs scheduled eye checks.

Same fine print as above: single-group study, response numbers standing in for survival, and the reported survival figure is too early to lean on.

docs.title: Option 4 — Lirafugratinib (also only if the tumor has an FGFR2 fusion)
docs.text:
This option is only available if the test comes back positive for an FGFR2 fusion. It targets the same feature as the two options above. This option carries caveats. Here is the tradeoff to weigh.

Lirafugratinib is a newer pill designed to hit FGFR2 more selectively. In an early study, its response numbers were the strongest in this lane, about 47 percent of tumors shrank, and because of its more selective design it largely skips the high-phosphate side effect that the two approved drugs cause. On paper that reads like the best of both worlds: higher response and an easier phosphate profile.

The caveats are what keep it here rather than at the front of the lane, and they are worth stating plainly. First, this drug is not yet approved. The only ways to get it in the US right now are through a clinical trial slot or an early-access route while its approval decision is pending. Second, the response figure comes from a conference presentation, not a fully published, peer-reviewed paper, so the underlying details cannot be checked as thoroughly as the numbers for the two approved drugs above. Third, the gentler phosphate profile is not a free win: this drug brings its own tough side effect, a severe hand-and-foot skin reaction that reaches a serious, function-limiting level in about 1 in 3 people. So swapping one drug's side effect for another's is closer to a lateral move than a clear upgrade. If you are drawn to trials, this is a real and higher-response door worth asking about, with those three caveats fully on the table.

docs.title: Option 5 — Zanidatamab (only if the tumor is HER2-positive)
docs.text:
This option is only available if the test comes back positive for HER2. If HER2 is negative, this option is off the table. Worth noting: HER2 has to be confirmed by staining the tumor tissue, not by the DNA panel alone, and it tends to show up more in cancers that started outside the liver.

Zanidatamab is an infusion given every two weeks. The reason it leads the HER2 options is that its trial was done specifically in bile-duct cancer, rather than borrowing results from a grab-bag of different cancers. In that trial, about 41 percent of tumors shrank, and responses lasted a meaningful stretch, around a year on average for those who responded.

The main thing to watch is the heart's pumping strength, monitored with periodic echocardiograms; a more serious drop happened in about 3 percent of people. Some people also had infusion reactions or diarrhea. The evidence is again from a single-group study, so it carries that limitation. There is a second HER2-targeting drug that was considered but held below this one because of a lung-inflammation risk; that one is described further down.

docs.title: Option 6 — Dabrafenib plus trametinib (only if the tumor has a BRAF V600E change)
docs.text:
This option is only available if the test comes back positive for a specific BRAF change called V600E. If that exact change is not present, this option is off the table. The "exact" part matters: a quick screening stain hinting at BRAF is not enough, and other BRAF changes do not qualify, so it has to be confirmed precisely.

This is a pair of pills taken together. In its trial, about 47 percent of tumors shrank, a strong result, and the cancer was held in check for around 9 months on average. A confirmed V600E change gives two separate routes to access these drugs, so getting the drug is usually not the hard part.

The reason this sits below the gentler pill options, despite the strong response, is the side-effect load. Recurring fever is a characteristic effect of this combination, and serious side effects of some kind happened in roughly 40 percent of people. None of the trial deaths were tied to the drugs, and there is a well-worn playbook for managing the fever, but it is a heavier regimen day to day. This change is uncommon in this cancer, somewhere in the 1 to 5 percent range, and the trial group was small.

docs.title: A HER2 option that was considered but held back — trastuzumab deruxtecan
docs.text:
There is a second HER2-targeting drug, trastuzumab deruxtecan, that was looked at and carries serious caveats, which is why it sits below zanidatamab rather than beside it. It is on the page because Libby shows what was weighed and where it pulled back, not only what it kept. Like zanidatamab, it only applies if HER2 comes back positive.

In the group whose tumors most strongly expressed HER2, its response numbers were competitive with zanidatamab. The concern is a specific lung inflammation that showed up in about 1 in 10 people in its trial, with three treatment-related deaths, and there was no baseline lung assessment on file to judge that risk against. With zanidatamab covering the HER2 situation on bile-duct-specific data and a lighter safety profile, this drug was held in reserve. It could come back into the conversation, but only with a confirmed HER2 result, a baseline lung check, and a written monitoring plan in place first. One more note on the biomarker: the approval here is for tumors that express HER2 at the strongest level. If the tumor is only "HER2-low," that is a weaker signal that this drug will help, and using it there would be experimental rather than standard, so a low result should not be read as the same green light as a strong one.

docs.title: Option 7 — Pembrolizumab (only if the tumor is MSI-high / mismatch-repair deficient or has high TMB)
docs.text:
This option is only available if the test comes back positive for one of two related immune-system markers: mismatch-repair deficiency (also called MSI-high) or a high tumor mutational burden (TMB). If neither shows up, this option is off the table. These markers are uncommon in this cancer, roughly 1 to 3 percent, but they change the picture completely when present.

Pembrolizumab is an immunotherapy infusion given every three weeks. It works by helping the immune system recognize the cancer, and when it works, the benefit can be unusually durable. In the relevant studies, about 29 to 34 percent of tumors shrank depending on which marker qualified the patient, and people lived close to two years on average.

Two honest limits. First, these numbers come from studies spanning many cancer types with no bile-duct-specific group, so the size of the benefit here is inferred rather than measured. Second, immunotherapy can push the immune system into attacking healthy organs; serious immune-related side effects happened in about 15 percent of people, and there was one treatment-related death in the study. These effects have an established management approach, but they are real and need close monitoring. One more note: the high-TMB marker is a less well-proven predictor in this cancer than mismatch-repair deficiency, so a positive there is a softer signal than an MSI-high result.

docs.title: What if the test comes back negative for everything
docs.text:
This is the case worth naming plainly. If the genetic test finds none of these features, then none of the options on this page applies, because every one of them is keyed to a specific feature being present. Libby's recommendations here are limited to feature-targeting treatments, so a fully negative test means there is nothing further for Libby to rank.

That does not mean there is no treatment. Standard care for metastatic cholangiocarcinoma exists and is the path most people take. It is simply outside the scope of this page, and it is a conversation to have with your oncologist, who knows your full situation. I am deliberately not naming specific standard-care drugs here, because choosing among them is your treating team's call, not Libby's.

One more thing: these features are checked independently. A negative result on one does not rule out the others. A tumor could be negative for the IDH1 change but positive for an FGFR2 fusion, and the FGFR2 options would still be live.

docs.title: Questions to ask your oncologist
docs.text:
• Has my tumor had comprehensive genomic profiling yet, and if not, can we order it now using stored tissue or a blood test rather than a new biopsy?
  • Will the testing include the DNA panel, an RNA arm for FGFR2 fusions, and the separate tissue stains for HER2 and mismatch-repair, so we don't miss anything that needs its own test?
  • Did my cancer start inside the liver or outside it, and how does that change which of these genetic features is most likely?
  • If the genetic test comes back negative for all of these features, what standard treatment would you recommend, and where do clinical trials fit in?
  • For whichever targeted option my result points to, what is the plan for monitoring its main side effect (the heart-rhythm checks for ivosidenib, the phosphate management for the FGFR2 drugs, the echocardiograms for zanidatamab, the fever for the BRAF pills, or the lung monitoring for the immunotherapy)?
  • If I turn out to have an FGFR2 fusion, how would we choose among futibatinib, pemigatinib, and the trial drug lirafugratinib for me specifically, given the differences in side effects and approval status?
  • If HER2 is positive, why zanidatamab over trastuzumab deruxtecan for me, and what lung monitoring would we need if the second drug ever came up?
  • Before starting any of these, do we have the baseline tests we'd need (an ECG, an echocardiogram, lung function), and should we get them now so we're ready?

Reading the columns

Toxicity burden is patient-level G3+ AE severity (Low / Moderate / High) summarized from trial publications. Counter-productive MoA is the mechanism-level risk that the intervention's own pathway could blunt the therapeutic goal — distinct from patient AEs. The board's endorse / dissent / veto state appears as pills under each intervention; full per-persona rationale lives on the board page.

docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences mediumRNA-based fusion NGS for NTRK1/2/3 and RET (pan-TRK IHC as an optional screen)confirmatoryRNA_seqno additional tissue if paired DNA/RNA CGP is runcovered within CGP turnaround if RNA is included; 1-2 weeks standaloneLarotrectinib/entrectinib (NTRK) and selpercatinib (RET) tumor-agnostic labels; confirms RNA fusion coverage.NTRK and RET fusions are rare in biliary tract cancer (<1%) but tumor-agnostically actionable, and an RNA-based assay detects them more reliably than DNA-only calling, especially for partners with large intronic breakpoints. docs.title: Research question
docs.text: In treatment-naive metastatic high-grade chondrosarcoma with dedifferentiated features, presenting with a pathologic left acetabular fracture and dispersed bilateral pulmonary metastases, what non-standard interventions could target the dedifferentiated histology and the untested IDH1/IDH2 and wider molecular landscape, gated on a comprehensive tumour DNA plus RNA panel that has not yet been ordered? Approved and guideline-carried care for the same presentation is assessed on the Standard-of-care table, a co-equal surface on this same case page.

docs.title: Patient profile (scrubbed)
docs.text:
• Woman, age band 40-49. ECOG recorded as 2.
  • The ECOG is an assumption, not a measurement. It was recorded because a pathologic fracture of a weight-bearing joint plausibly limits ambulation and self-care. The true value may be better or worse, and it gates trial eligibility broadly.
  • Chondrosarcoma, high-grade with dedifferentiated features (user-stated; a formal pathology report has not been reviewed). Expert bone-sarcoma pathology review to confirm the WHO diagnosis and quantify the dedifferentiated component is a hardening item, not an open fork.
  • Stage IV, metastatic at diagnosis: large left acetabular mass with pathologic acetabular fracture, plus multiple small pulmonary nodules dispersed through both lungs. Multiple and dispersed rather than oligometastatic.
  • Treatment-naive. No prior therapies, no current therapy.
  • IDH1 mutation — untested (not performed). IDH2 mutation — untested.
  • Comprehensive genomic profile — untested: no NGS, no RNA fusion panel, no COL2A1 / TERT promoter / CDKN2A-B / TP53 status.
  • MSI / dMMR — untested. TMB — untested. PD-L1 — untested.
  • HEY1-NCOA2 fusion — untested; low-yield given the stated histology, which is not mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.
  • Organ function: renal panel, hepatic panel and baseline echo/LVEF all not obtained. Pain and weight-bearing status not documented.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text:
• Efficacy / toxicity weight: 0.8 (efficacy-leaning).
  • Toxicity vetoes: none recorded (empty list, inferred default).
  • Modality constraints: none recorded (empty list, inferred default).
  • Trial preference: prefers trials — yes (inferred default).
  • Free text: the one preference actually stated by the patient is that she wants to pursue all possible therapeutic options. Every other value in the file is an inferred default consistent with that stance, not something she was asked. Goals of care, travel tolerance and fitness were never discussed.

docs.title: Target validation paths
docs.text: Two orders decide most of what this case can become, and both ride the archival diagnostic block: IDH1/IDH2 sequencing, and a comprehensive tumour DNA plus RNA panel read on macrodissected dedifferentiated tissue. A confirmed IDH1 or IDH2 mutation opens an off-label conversation about ivosidenib or olutasidenib rather than a trial seat, because the active chondrosarcoma IDH studies are closed to this histology (the phase 3 ivosidenib trial NCT06127407 enrolls conventional histology only); a wild-type result closes that axis cleanly and leaves the rest of the workup standing. The same panel's TMB, MSI and CDK-pathway readouts decide whether tumour-agnostic pembrolizumab, the abemaciclib study NCT04040205 and TAPUR (NCT02693535) matching are reachable at all. If the panel comes back quiet, which chondrosarcoma genomes often do beyond IDH, the molecular half of this report is exhausted, and the conversation about standard systemic care from there belongs to the treating team, not Libby.

docs.title: IDH1/IDH2
docs.text: Order sequencing, not R132H immunohistochemistry. The R132H antibody was raised for glioma, and roughly 40 percent of IDH1-mutant cartilage tumours carry R132C instead (PMID 21598255), so a stain would read negative in the commonest mutant scenario here. The pre-test probability is high: 71 percent of dedifferentiated chondrosarcomas carried an IDH1/IDH2 mutation in a paired genomic series, against 36 percent of conventional tumours (PMID 36926116). A targeted hotspot assay answers in 3-10 days; on the comprehensive panel the same answer takes 2-3 weeks. Two sampling rules matter as much as the assay. Macrodissect the dedifferentiated component, and require the report to state which lesion was sampled, because mutant IDH1 is recurrently lost during metastatic evolution (PMID 41299743) and a call on the acetabular primary may not describe the lung nodules. Plasma ctDNA (two Streck tubes, 7-10 days) is the fallback when the block is exhausted, and the shedding data are favourable in exactly this population: digital PCR found circulating tumour DNA in all six patients with grade 3 or dedifferentiated disease (PMID 28834325). Whatever comes back, temper the expectations that travel with the word "mutation": the widely quoted ivosidenib response rate belongs to conventional-histology patients, and olutasidenib in dedifferentiated disease read out at a median PFS of 1.5 months.

docs.title: Dedifferentiated histology
docs.text: The histology on file is user-stated, and it is the fact that makes cytotoxic chemotherapy worth giving, so hardening it is essential rather than optional. Expert bone-sarcoma pathology review should report the formal WHO diagnosis and the percentage of the specimen occupied by the dedifferentiated, non-cartilaginous component; it runs 5-10 business days on the existing slides and block, no new biopsy. Ancillary subtyping earns its slot because the differential changes the chemotherapy backbone: HEY1-NCOA2 fusion testing on an RNA panel separates mesenchymal chondrosarcoma, and morphology plus the IDH genotype separates chondroblastic osteosarcoma, which would move treatment toward a MAP-type regimen. Two baseline studies stand between her and an anthracycline: a transthoracic echocardiogram with LVEF plus a 12-lead ECG with QTc (1-3 days), and an organ-function panel with creatinine clearance and urinalysis before any ifosfamide or cisplatin.

docs.title: Molecular landscape
docs.text: Everything molecular in this case runs off one block, and dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma is biphasic by definition, so the pathology block review with macrodissection instructions and a written tissue-allocation plan comes before anything is cut. A core that sampled only the low-grade cartilage returns a falsely reassuring result on every assay downstream of it. The comprehensive DNA plus RNA panel (IDH1/IDH2, TP53, CDKN2A/B, TERT promoter, NTRK1-3, RET, BRAF, TMB, MSI, fusions; 2-3 weeks) is the single order that answers the IDH question and every tumour-agnostic one at once. Around it sit the fast reads: four-antibody mismatch-repair IHC (2-5 days off four unstained slides) as the orthogonal check on the panel's MSI call, which would put tumour-agnostic pembrolizumab or dostarlimab in reach if protein loss appears, though MSI-high showed up in only 0.7 percent of sarcomas in the largest sequenced cohort (PMID 42531431); PD-L1 IHC with the clone and scoring system recorded explicitly, read on the dedifferentiated component, since positivity in this disease is confined to that subtype (9 of 22 dedifferentiated against 0 of 119 conventional, PMID 27312065); and CD3/CD8 density with tumour HLA class I expression as context for any checkpoint or cell-therapy discussion. A germline predisposition panel is a reflex, ordered only if the tumour panel returns a BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2 or TP53 variant at an allele fraction suggesting germline origin.

docs.title: Fitness, fracture and measurable disease
docs.text: The recorded ECOG of 2 is an intake assumption made from the fracture, not a score, and it decides more than any single molecular result: chemotherapy intensity, and eligibility for every protocol that caps performance status, including the ECOG 0-1 bars on the IACS-6274 study NCT05039801 and the abemaciclib study NCT04040205. Scoring it in clinic is free and same-day; record weight-bearing status, ambulatory aids and analgesic requirement alongside it. Orthopaedic oncology assessment of the periacetabular fracture, with thin-slice bone-algorithm pelvic CT and MRI of the hemipelvis, settles whether fixation precedes or accompanies systemic therapy and starts the surgical-washout clock that trial protocols read. A baseline contrast CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis with thin lung reconstructions establishes RECIST 1.1 measurability, which protocol entry generally requires, and answers whether the bilateral nodule distribution truly forecloses any local pulmonary approach.

docs.title: HLA class I and the cancer-testis antigens
docs.text: One blood draw that spends no tumour tissue: allele-level (4-digit) HLA class I typing (1-2 weeks) decides whether any HLA-restricted TCR-T or ImmTAC programme, afamitresgene autoleucel, uzatresgene autoleucel, IMA203, brenetafusp or letetresgene autoleucel, can be pursued at all. The antigen stains behind it are reflexes, not parallel orders: MAGE-A4, NY-ESO-1 and PRAME expression are worth measuring only after a documented HLA-A*02:01, because an expression result cannot be read for eligibility without the restricting allele. Hold expectations low even then; in the largest cancer-testis antigen survey of bone and soft tissue tumours, 1 of 13 chondrosarcomas stained PRAME-positive (PMID 40152485).

docs.title: Biomarkers measured, but not to decision resolution
docs.text: This case has no under-resolved results, because it has no results: nothing molecular has been measured at all, and the survey behind this report handed four items forward on exactly that basis rather than because an existing number fell short. HLA class I genotype is simply absent, and it is the one that stacks: MAGE-A4, NY-ESO-1 and PRAME are recorded as not assessable rather than negative, since two gaps sit on top of each other for each of them, an unknown restricting allele and an expression level nobody has stained for. Each of the four has a matching workup row above, and the ordering dependency is the whole story: type first, stain second, and read any expression result on the dedifferentiated component.
