docs.title: What this page is
docs.text:
Libby searched published studies, open clinical trials, and treatment guidelines for anything that could treat the specific features of your cancer. What came back is organized as two separate lists, and this page walks through both in plain language.

The first list holds the standard treatments: nine options that are already approved or carried in treatment guidelines. This is where your actual first decisions live, and chemotherapy sits at the top of it. The second list holds the experimental options: twenty-two entries covering trial seats, off-label ideas, and drugs with no route to you yet. It starts with a genetic test, not a drug.

One thing to get straight before anything else: each list is numbered from 1 within itself, so this page contains two number 1s, and they are not competing for the same slot. The first standard treatment (chemotherapy) and the first experimental entry (a genetic test) are not rivals; the plan below asks for both in the same week, because one is a treatment and the other is a test that runs alongside it. Wherever a number could confuse, this page says "standard treatment" or "experimental option" in full, or just names the thing.

docs.title: What we know about your cancer
docs.text:
You have chondrosarcoma, a bone cancer that arises from cartilage-forming cells. Yours is high grade, with what pathologists call dedifferentiated features, meaning part of the tumor has transformed into a faster-growing, more aggressive form. The main tumor sits in your left acetabulum, the socket of the hip joint, and it has broken the bone there (a pathologic fracture). Scans also show multiple small nodules scattered through both lungs, consistent with spread. They are many and dispersed rather than one or two, which is why treatments aimed at the whole body matter more for the lungs than anything local. You have not had any cancer treatment yet.

Two facts about your situation shape everything on this page. First, almost nothing has been tested. The tumor has not been checked for IDH mutations (a genetic change common in this cancer that some drugs target), and no broader genetic profiling has been done; of the fourteen tumor features this review tracked, eleven were never measured. Untested is not the same as negative. The doors those tests control are simply still unopened, which is why a test, not a drug, leads the experimental list. Second, your fitness score was assumed, not measured. Doctors use a scale called ECOG performance status, from 0 (fully active) to 4, to judge who can tolerate which treatments, and most clinical trials require a 0 or 1. Your chart says 2, but that number was written down because a broken hip plausibly limits walking and self-care, not because anyone examined you and scored it. The real number could be better or worse, and it decides which trial doors are open. Getting it actually measured is one of the highest-value things that can happen this week.

One hard number belongs here rather than buried. In published series of people with metastatic dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma, the middle survival ran about five to seven months. Half of people lived longer than that, some a good deal longer, and a middle value says nothing certain about any one person. It is on this page for a single reason: it explains why nearly every recommendation below is built around moving fast and doing things in parallel rather than one at a time.

A smaller caveat: the diagnosis itself came from what you reported, and the formal pathology report has not been reviewed here. Expert review by a bone-sarcoma pathologist is part of the recommended workup, to confirm the diagnosis and measure how much of the tumor is the aggressive component.

docs.title: What you told us matters most
docs.text:
The one preference you actually stated is that you want to pursue all possible therapeutic options. Everything else in your preferences file, the tilt toward effectiveness over gentleness, the openness to trials, the absence of any treatments you have ruled out, was filled in as a reasonable default consistent with that sentence, not something you were asked.

Here is the honest problem with that sentence: two very different plans can both claim to honor it. One reading says start with the treatments most likely to help and keep every later door open. Another reading says chase experimental options aggressively, even ones with almost no evidence in your disease, because "all possible" means all. Both readings shaped this page, and the gap between them never fully closed. Only you can say which one you meant, and telling your care team costs a conversation, not an option. It is worth having early.

Goals of care, how far you can travel, and what side effects you would refuse were never discussed. Several judgments below lean on those unasked questions, and they are flagged where they do.

docs.title: The standard treatments, ranked 1 to 9
docs.text: These are the approved and guideline-carried options, in the order this review ranked them. The top three are where the strongest recommendations in the whole case sit. Two entries at the bottom were assessed and set aside, and they are kept visible so you can see they were weighed rather than missed. One entry, ivosidenib, waits on the genetic test described after this list; nothing else here depends on any test result.

docs.title: Standard treatment 1 — doxorubicin-based chemotherapy
docs.text:
This is the strongest recommendation anywhere on this page, and the option to discuss first. Nothing else in the entire review came close to its level of support, and nothing about it was contested except the dose and which response number to quote. Conventional chondrosarcoma famously resists chemotherapy, but the dedifferentiated variant is the exception: the aggressive component behaves more like other high-grade bone sarcomas, where chemotherapy has a real role. Doxorubicin is approved for metastatic bone sarcomas, and guidelines carry it for your variant. It needs no trial seat, no test result, and no insurance fight, so it is also the treatment that can start soonest.

The honest numbers deserve care. Across published studies, somewhere between about 9 and about 20 out of every 100 people with this subtype saw their tumors shrink on first-line chemotherapy, and this review deliberately did not settle on a single figure, because the two ends come from different kinds of studies. The 9 comes from a recent series across several hospitals. The 20 (strictly, 20.5) comes from an older series of patients treated between 1988 and 2011, rests on only 44 people with your subtype, and used scans judged by each hospital's own doctors rather than an independent central read, which tends to flatter the result. Nobody can tell you which end is closer to the truth. Neither study compared chemotherapy against no chemotherapy, so the exact added benefit is not precisely known, and shrinkage is not the only way treatment can help. You are entitled to hear the whole range, with the reasons the ends disagree, rather than one number chosen for you.

Three measurements stand between you and the first cycle, and none exists yet: a heart ultrasound with an ejection fraction (doxorubicin can strain the heart), kidney and liver blood work, and a properly scored fitness rating. Then comes a genuine choice that belongs to you. One version is doxorubicin alone. The other adds a second drug, ifosfamide or cisplatin, which asks more of the body: ifosfamide can stress the kidneys and nervous system, cisplatin the kidneys and hearing. In the one forward-planned study of intensive chemotherapy in this disease, 18 of the 57 patients, all selected as fit enough to try, never made it through six of the nine planned cycles, and the patients who did best were largely those whose disease could also be operated on, so the survival tail may say more about who they were than about the drugs. The main day-to-day risks of the whole class are low blood counts and infection, on top of the heart question. Which version fits you depends on your measured fitness and on what you decide once you have heard both sets of numbers. Nobody has asked you yet.

One timing note that connects the two lists: the first experimental option below is a trial that would also take a patient who has not yet had chemotherapy. Starting chemotherapy closes that particular door, and going through chemotherapy is also what opens several other trial seats set up for the line after it. That trade is named honestly in the experimental section; it is a real decision, not a footnote.

docs.title: Standard treatment 2 — surgery to stabilize your hip
docs.text:
Fixing the fractured acetabulum is probably the rate-limiting step for everything else, which is why it sits this high. Trial protocols commonly require about four weeks of recovery after major surgery before starting (one trial on this page needs only two), so the operative date sets the calendar for trial enrollment. Radiation to that bone should come after it is fixed rather than before, because irradiating a broken, unrepaired bone can stop it from healing. And the same operation is a chance to bank fresh tumor tissue for the genetic testing described below, while you are already under anesthesia.

Be clear about which operation this is. What is on the table is repair and stabilization of the fracture, not surgical removal of the tumor. The bigger operation was examined separately, and in your subtype the published data do not show that removing the primary tumor helps people live longer, while the operations that achieve clean margins in this part of the pelvis are drastic. Repair for function is the question here; removal is not.

And there is a genuinely open question that nobody has measured: repairing the hip might get you out of pain, back on your feet, and into a better measured fitness score that opens trial doors, or the weeks of surgical recovery might cost you ground you do not get back, against a disease that moves in months. Published studies do not answer this, and your surgical fitness itself has not been assessed, so even the operation's risk is unquantified right now. Your surgical team, looking at your specific fracture, is who can weigh it. It is the first question on the list at the bottom of this page.

docs.title: Standard treatment 3 — early specialist palliative care, alongside active treatment
docs.text:
The name needs translating before anything else: palliative care here does not mean hospice and does not mean giving up. It means a specialist team focused on pain, symptoms, and support, working next to your cancer treatment from the start.

It is also, by a clear margin, the best-evidenced item on this entire page. In a randomized trial, the strongest kind of study and the only one anywhere in this review, people with metastatic lung cancer who got early palliative care alongside their cancer treatment reported better quality of life at twelve weeks, received less aggressive care at the very end of life, and lived longer on average, a median of 11.6 months against 8.9. That trial was in lung cancer, not sarcoma, and nobody has repeated it in your disease; that limit is stated here rather than hidden. The guideline built on it applies across cancer types and explicitly includes people on early-phase trials, so this referral cannot cost you an experimental option.

For you specifically it aims at the most concrete problem in your chart: the pain and mobility of a broken hip, which nobody has even quantified yet. It costs no line of therapy, needs no eligibility screen, and closes no door. Most of the drugs on the experimental list rest on far thinner evidence than this does.

docs.title: Standard treatment 4 — getting your care to a high-volume sarcoma center
docs.text:
This treats nothing by itself. It is the door. Expert pathology review, the surgeons who operate on this part of the pelvis, the genetic testing, and essentially every trial seat on the experimental list run through a center that sees a lot of bone sarcoma; one referral opens all of it at once. In nationwide French registry data, patients whose plan was reviewed by a specialist sarcoma team before their first treatment did better on several measures, including survival. The honest caveat: those registries were mostly soft-tissue sarcoma rather than bone, so the benefit is extrapolated to your situation rather than measured in it. The window the data describe is the one you are in now, before first treatment, which is why this referral should not wait.

Nobody has asked how far you can travel, and a center across town and a center five hundred miles away are very different propositions with a fractured hip. If distance is a problem, say so early.

docs.title: Standard treatment 5 — radiation to the hip, for pain
docs.text:
Radiation can ease pain from a bone tumor, and guidelines carry it for exactly this use, with short schedules that run from a single visit to about two weeks.

The limits are real, though. The pain-relief numbers come from bone metastases of other cancers, not from chondrosarcoma, which as a family tends to resist radiation; the aggressive component of your tumor is the more radiation-responsive part, so the expectation is tempered rather than zero. And the sequencing rule is strict: irradiating a broken bone that has not been surgically repaired can stop it from ever healing, and a hip socket that never heals is not a recoverable situation. So any radiation here waits until the surgery decision above is settled, and the radiation and surgical teams should make that call together rather than in whatever order they happen to see you. One more interaction worth knowing: radiation to the pelvis also reaches bowel, bladder, and bone marrow, and marrow is what chemotherapy leans on, so the field and the timing need planning around the chemotherapy.

docs.title: Standard treatment 6 — clinical trial enrollment as a strategy
docs.text: Cancer guidelines say plainly that the best management of any patient with cancer is in a clinical trial, and trials are the one preference you actually stated. This entry is here because that principle is itself part of standard care in this disease, where the approved options are thin. But "join a trial" only becomes real as a specific seat, and the specific seats live on the experimental list below. All of them wait on the same two things: a fitness score somebody has actually measured, and the genetic panel. There is nothing to do under this heading beyond what those entries describe; it is on the list so the trial question shows up as a concrete plan rather than a slogan.

docs.title: Standard treatment 7 — ivosidenib, an IDH-blocking pill
docs.text:
This option is only available if the IDH test comes back positive. Ivosidenib blocks the protein made by a mutated IDH1 gene, and your tumor has not been tested for that mutation yet. About 7 in 10 tumors of your subtype carry an IDH mutation, so a positive result is genuinely likely, and guidelines carry IDH-blocking drugs for exactly that situation in your variant, which is why this sits on the standard list at all. If the test comes back negative, this entry closes, along with three entries near the bottom of the experimental list, and nothing else on either list moves: the chemotherapy, the surgery, the palliative care, the radiation, and every other trial seat stand exactly as ranked, because none of them depends on IDH. A negative test closes one drawer, not the plan.

Now the harder truth: a positive result buys less than the word "mutation" suggests. The encouraging response number attached to this drug, roughly 23 in 100, came entirely from a small group of patients with the conventional, slower-growing form of chondrosarcoma, where the responses were strikingly durable. The only published result in your subtype used a closely related drug, and the disease held for about six weeks on average before growing again. The working biological explanation is that by the time this cancer dedifferentiates, it may have outgrown its dependence on the pathway these drugs block. On top of that, the drug's official approval covers other cancers entirely, so this would be off-label prescribing, and the large ongoing trial of it in chondrosarcoma accepts the conventional form only. A positive IDH result is still worth having; it opens a real conversation and future trial doors. It is just not the targeted rescue it sounds like.

docs.title: Standard treatment 8 — pazopanib (set aside)
docs.text: This targeted pill was assessed and set aside. Its supporting evidence and its guideline position belong to the conventional, slower-growing form of chondrosarcoma; the study behind it excluded your subtype by design. As your diagnosis stands, both the evidence and the approval pathway point at a cancer you are stated not to have. It would come back into play only if the expert pathology review reclassified the tumor, which is exactly why that review is part of the workup.

docs.title: Standard treatment 9 — surgery or ablation for the lung nodules (set aside)
docs.text: Also assessed and set aside. Removing lung metastases surgically is a real and sometimes curative move in bone sarcoma, but only when there are just a few nodules that can all be taken out. Your scans show many small nodules scattered through both lungs, which is a different situation, and time spent on lung surgery that cannot clear the disease is time taken from the whole-body treatment the lungs actually need. It is recorded here so you can see the question was asked.

docs.title: The top of the experimental list is a test, not a treatment
docs.text:
The first entry on the experimental list is not a drug. It is one comprehensive genetic panel, reading both the tumor's DNA and its RNA, run on the biopsy tissue you have already had taken. No new procedure, no side effects, no risk. It leads that list because eleven of the fourteen tumor features this review tracked have never been measured, and one order answers most of them at once.

The request should specify two things: that the lab test the aggressive, dedifferentiated part of the tumor (the pathologist carves that region out of the specimen, which is called macrodissection), and that the report state which lesion was sampled, because the genetics of the hip tumor and the lung nodules are not guaranteed to match. In fact the IDH mutation can be lost as this disease spreads, so if the result will drive a treatment decision later, retesting a metastatic sample is a fair question.

One test, several doors. It settles the IDH question, which governs the ivosidenib entry on the standard list and three entries at the bottom of the experimental list. It measures tumor mutational burden and something called microsatellite instability, two markers that, if high, would make an approved immunotherapy officially available to you after chemotherapy. It looks for the alterations that gate a trial seat for abemaciclib and the entry requirement for a nationwide drug-matching study. A negative result closes doors too, and closing them honestly is worth almost as much as opening them.

Timing matters in both directions. The full panel takes roughly two to three weeks to come back; a targeted IDH-only test can answer in about three to ten days. Treatment should not wait for either. This test runs alongside the start of your care, never instead of it: ordering it this week and starting treatment on its own schedule are both possible, and both should happen. If hip surgery goes ahead, tissue from the operation should be tested as well.

And to say it once, plainly: if the IDH test comes back negative, four entries close (ivosidenib on the standard list, and the three IDH-dependent entries on the experimental list). Everything else on both lists is untouched.

docs.title: The experimental options, ranked 1 to 22
docs.text: This is the second list: trial seats, off-label possibilities, and ideas with no route to you yet. Its number 1 is the genetic test you just read about, so the entries below start at 2. These options sit alongside and mostly after the standard treatments above; none of them replaces chemotherapy, and several exist precisely to be ready for the line after it. Many are here so you can see what was considered and set aside, with reasons, rather than wondering what was missed.

docs.title: Experimental option 2 — IACS-6274, a metabolism-blocking drug (the recommendation is a phone call)
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. This is a trial-only option. IACS-6274 blocks an enzyme called glutaminase, which tumor cells use to feed on a nutrient called glutamine. Laboratory studies found that high-grade chondrosarcoma cells make more of this enzyme and that blocking it kills chondrosarcoma cells in a dish. That is the entire evidence base. No drug of this kind has ever produced a documented response in a person with chondrosarcoma.

So why does it rank ahead of the other experimental options? Availability, not evidence, and that is worth being blunt about. The trial testing it is an early-phase, dose-finding study (everyone gets the drug, there is no comparison group, and the study's main goal is measuring side effects, not benefit), and it is the one open trial in this entire search that names chondrosarcoma as its own group and accepts people who have not had prior treatment. Seats like that are rare. What is actually recommended right now is not taking the drug; it is making the screening call, which costs nothing, comes back in days, and tells you whether the seat is real.

If the seat turns out to be real, the decision gets harder, and it is yours. Entering a dose-finding trial as your first treatment would spend your one window of proven chemotherapy response on a dose that nobody involved may expect to work. Whether "all possible options" points toward that trade or away from it is exactly the unresolved question from the preferences section. Two practical barriers: the trial requires a measured fitness score of 0 or 1, so the assumed 2 has to be replaced by a real measurement that comes back better, and the trial runs at a single hospital in Houston, so travel is a real question nobody has asked you.

docs.title: Experimental option 3 — abemaciclib, a trial seat set up now for the line after chemotherapy
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. This is a trial-only option. Abemaciclib is a pill already approved for breast cancer that blocks proteins called CDK4 and CDK6, which push cells to divide. A trial is testing it in sarcomas whose tumors carry alterations in that pathway, and it names your subtype as eligible. Of everything in this search, this trial has the cleanest design: it checks the tumor's biology with a centrally reviewed test before letting anyone in, instead of explaining results afterward.

The honesty that has to sit next to that: no drug of this class has any published result in chondrosarcoma, in anyone. The supporting evidence is laboratory work, including a mouse study where a sister drug slowed chondrosarcoma growth in bone. A well-built trial is not the same thing as a signal.

Three gates stand between you and a seat, and none can be cleared retroactively: a qualifying tumor alteration plus a positive companion stain (both come from the panel plus one extra test, neither ordered yet), a measured fitness score of 0 or 1, and the practical reality that the seat fits the line after first-line chemotherapy. The move now is ordering the tests so the seat is live if you want it later. Known side effects of the drug class: diarrhea, low white blood cell counts, fatigue, and blood clots.

docs.title: Experimental option 4 — pembrolizumab, an immunotherapy for second line, if the tumor tests the right way
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Pembrolizumab releases a brake on the immune system's T cells so they can attack the tumor. Here is the entire forward-planned trial experience of drugs like this in chondrosarcoma: five patients, one of whom responded. There is also one response among five patients in a look-back series and one published case of a response lasting two years. Real signal or luck, nobody can say from numbers that small; with groups of four and five people, the honest uncertainty runs from nearly nothing to nearly everything.

The practical path runs through the genetic panel. If it shows a very high mutation count or the marker called microsatellite instability, pembrolizumab becomes officially approved for you after prior treatment, no trial needed. The catch: only around 4 in 100 sarcomas test that way, and chondrosarcoma usually is not among them. So this is a long-shot lottery ticket that costs nothing extra, because the panel is going out anyway. It should be checked, not planned around.

The genuine open question with all immunotherapy in this disease: chondrosarcoma tumors are dominated by a different immune cell type, macrophages, rather than the T cells this drug unleashes, and animal work suggests the T-cell brake may not be the lever that matters here. On the other side of the ledger, this drug's side effects (immune attacks on the lungs, glands, or kidneys, plus anemia and low blood counts) are the best understood of anything non-chemotherapy on this page, with years of management playbooks every oncology unit already runs.

docs.title: Experimental option 5 — TAPUR, a nationwide study matching approved drugs to tumor genetics
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. This is a trial-only option. TAPUR is a registry-style study at roughly 180 US hospitals. If your genetic panel finds an alteration that matches one of its drug groups, you receive an already-approved drug, used outside the cancer it was approved for, with your outcome recorded. Two things earn it a slot here. Its fitness bar (0 to 2) is one of the very few in this search you may already clear even as your chart reads today. And it realistically fits the line after first-line chemotherapy, which in this disease arrives in months, so registering interest now is what a trials-forward plan looks like in practice.

The caveat is that this option carries no benefit estimate at all. There are no chondrosarcoma results from it, and this cancer's genome is often quiet: the panel may simply find nothing matchable, in which case the seat never materializes. Hear that plainly now rather than discovering it later. The only cost of keeping it open is the panel you are already ordering.

docs.title: Experimental option 6 — sunitinib plus nivolumab, off-label, the most disputed entry on this page
docs.text:
This option carries caveats, more than anything ranked above it. This combines a targeted pill (sunitinib) with an immunotherapy (nivolumab), both off-label. It is on the page because of one fact no other immunotherapy option can claim: in a 40-person trial that included four people with your exact subtype, one of those four responded. That is the only checkpoint-immunotherapy dataset anywhere in which a dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma shrank.

Now the other half of the ledger, from the same trial. One of the 40 patients died of lung inflammation caused by the treatment, and 17 in 100 stopped because of side effects. Severe problems included low white counts, high blood pressure, and liver enzyme spikes. The trial is closed, so taking this route would mean prescribing both drugs off-label: available at first progression without waiting for anything, and stripped of every trial safeguard, with a likely insurance fight on top.

What is contested is not the numbers; the numbers are accepted. It is whether a one-in-four signal justifies accepting a small but real risk of a fatal complication that you have never actually been shown and asked about. Your file lists no side effects you would refuse, but that list is empty because nobody asked, and an unfilled form is not the same as a yes. There is also a biology concern pointing the wrong way: the same macrophage-dominated immune environment described under the pembrolizumab entry, which may blunt or even invert what the immunotherapy half is trying to do. This entry stays visible so you can see the full trade, not because the page urges it.

docs.title: Experimental option 7 — CAR-T cell therapy aimed at B7-H3
docs.text: This option carries caveats. This is a trial-only option. Your own T cells would be collected, engineered to attack a protein called B7-H3 on tumor cell surfaces, and returned to you. The concept is real, and B7-H3 shows up on most sarcomas. The problem is dose of target: these therapies work best when the target protein is abundant, and in the one study that measured levels across sarcoma types, chondrosarcoma carried the lowest of any of them. Low levels mean a weak attack and an escape route for the tumor. Before this option means anything, the tumor would need a special stain (not a standard order, and not yet requested) showing a genuinely high level; a middling result should end the conversation, without regret. Further catches: the trial gives chemotherapy and a vaccine alongside the cells, so even a response could not be credited to the CAR-T; no safety data exist for this therapy in chondrosarcoma; the single site is overseas; fast-progressing disease is excluded; and manufacturing the cells takes weeks a fast tumor may not give back. Known risks of the class include severe immune-activation reactions and neurologic side effects.

docs.title: Experimental option 8 — antibody-drug conjugates aimed at B7-H3, as a class
docs.text: This option carries caveats. An antibody-drug conjugate is a guided missile: an antibody that finds B7-H3 on tumor cells and delivers a chemotherapy payload directly to them. Four separate companies are running four separate programs (the next four entries), which matters because it means the approach is not a single-company bet. But the same concerns apply across all of them: no results in chondrosarcoma for any, the same low-target-level worry as the CAR-T entry, and a payload class that can inflame the lungs, which matters in someone with nodules in both lungs. None of the four accepts a patient who has not yet had treatment, and most require a fitness score of 0 or 1. The realistic shape of this option: get the B7-H3 stain at some point, and if it comes back high, revisit this class in a later line of treatment.

docs.title: Experimental option 9 — ifinatamab deruxtecan
docs.text: This option carries caveats. The first of the four programs under the class entry above. Its trial accepts sarcomas and does not require the B7-H3 stain for entry, but it takes only patients whose disease has progressed on standard treatment, with a fitness score of 0 or 1. A later-line possibility, nothing sooner.

docs.title: Experimental option 10 — HS-20093
docs.text: This option carries caveats. The second program. Its trials are the most sarcoma-friendly of the class, and one arm even takes untreated patients alongside chemotherapy, but that arm names soft-tissue sarcoma and osteosarcoma, not chondrosarcoma, so eligibility would have to be asked, not assumed. The sites are in China, which only matters because nobody has asked you about travel.

docs.title: Experimental option 11 — MGC026
docs.text: This option carries caveats. The third program, and the one with no fitness cutoff published anywhere on the record, so the eligibility question has to be put to the trial site directly. It requires tumor tissue and excludes major surgery within four weeks, both of which interact with the hip operation on the standard list. Otherwise everything said about the class applies.

docs.title: Experimental option 12 — risvutatug rezetecan
docs.text: This option carries caveats. The fourth program, and the Western arm of the same molecule as HS-20093, listed mainly so you and your team can see the pipeline has depth beyond one company. Entry would sit well after first-line treatment.

docs.title: Experimental option 13 — enasidenib
docs.text: This option is only available if the IDH test comes back positive, and even then, it was considered but not recommended. The one open trial of this IDH2-blocking drug that accepts chondrosarcoma restricts enrollment to tumors arising in the skull base or sinuses, and requires prior treatment besides. Yours arises in the pelvis. No test result changes anatomy, so this door is closed no matter what the panel says. As a reminder, a negative IDH test closes only this entry, the next two, and the ivosidenib entry on the standard list; everything else on this page stands.

docs.title: Experimental option 14 — LY3410738
docs.text: This option is only available if the IDH test comes back positive, and it was considered but not recommended. On paper this would have been the best-fitting IDH trial in the whole search, with chondrosarcoma named and no subtype restriction. Its enrollment closed in 2023, before any results were published. There is nothing to join. One useful detail survives it: that trial accepted a blood-based IDH test for chondrosarcoma, which supports asking whether your IDH status could be checked from blood if tissue runs short.

docs.title: Experimental option 15 — olaparib plus ceralasertib
docs.text: This option is only available if the IDH test comes back positive, and it was considered but not recommended. The idea, that IDH-mutant tumors have a DNA-repair weakness these drugs can exploit, was directly tested in chondrosarcoma cells in the laboratory, and it failed. The trial has also closed to new patients. Both the science and the logistics point the same way.

docs.title: Experimental option 16 — PD-1 / PD-L1 immunotherapy as a class
docs.text: This option carries caveats. This is the drug family pembrolizumab belongs to, listed once so the same trials are not rediscovered over and over. The practical version of this idea is the pembrolizumab entry above. Worth knowing: the trials combining first-line chemotherapy with immunotherapy in sarcoma all exclude cartilage tumors, one of them naming chondrosarcoma in its first exclusion criterion, so that seemingly obvious route is closed.

docs.title: Experimental option 17 — nivolumab plus ipilimumab, a double immunotherapy
docs.text: This option was considered but not recommended. There are no results for this combination in your disease, it carries a heavier immune side-effect burden than single-drug immunotherapy, and the same macrophage-biology concern applies. It is recorded here so you can see the double-immunotherapy question was asked rather than silently skipped.

docs.title: Experimental option 18 — mifamurtide, an immune stimulator aimed at macrophages
docs.text: This option carries caveats. Of everything in this search, this drug's mechanism fits your tumor's biology best: it works on macrophages, the immune cell type that actually dominates chondrosarcoma, rather than on T cells. It came close to ranking higher, and what stopped it was access, not biology. It is approved only in Europe, only for osteosarcoma in young people, and there is no route to it in the US. No person with chondrosarcoma has ever received it on record; the supporting evidence is one animal study of it combined with doxorubicin. If your care ever crosses paths with a trial of it, the question is worth reopening.

docs.title: Experimental option 19 — belzutifan, a pill targeting the tumor's low-oxygen survival machinery
docs.text: This option carries caveats. One laboratory study suggests the target matters in high-grade chondrosarcoma, and no patient with this cancer has ever received the drug. It is on the page so you can see the idea was considered rather than missed, and that is the honest extent of it. If the genetic panel happens to show amplification of the relevant gene, the conversation sharpens a little, which is one more small return on the test.

docs.title: Experimental option 20 — engineered T cells against NY-ESO-1
docs.text: This option was considered but not recommended. Two tests that would even establish whether you are a candidate (a tissue-type blood test called HLA typing, and a tumor stain for the target) have not been ordered, the open trial enrolls soft-tissue sarcoma rather than bone sarcoma, and manufacturing engineered cells takes weeks that a fast-moving disease may not give back. Unassessable today rather than proven useless, but not a live option.

docs.title: Experimental option 21 — tebentafusp
docs.text: This option was considered but not recommended. Its target is a melanoma protein that cartilage tumors do not make, so in your cancer the drug has nothing to bind, and its trial enrolls a different sarcoma entirely. It stays on the page for one side reason: its trial has the most permissive fitness bar in this entire search (it accepts a score of 2), and it is the argument for drawing your HLA tissue type now, since that one blood test decides whether any future medicine in this whole category is even discussable for you.

docs.title: Experimental option 22 — proton or carbon-ion radiation to the hip tumor
docs.text:
This option was considered but not recommended, and of everything on either list, this was the firmest no in the whole review. That deserves a careful explanation, because particle radiation genuinely is a celebrated treatment for chondrosarcoma, and you may well read about it.

The celebrated results come from a different situation: tumors at the base of the skull, mostly lower grade, in patients whose cancer had not spread, treated with the goal of cure. Those numbers do not transfer to a fractured, weight-bearing pelvis in metastatic disease. Both trial routes for particle therapy exclude patients whose cancer has spread, so there is no seat to be had regardless. The safety picture in your specific anatomy is severe: among long-term survivors of similar high-dose radiation to the acetabular region, about half developed nerve damage, about half suffered pelvic fractures, and about a third developed bone death in the head of the femur. And there is a mechanical problem stacked on top: irradiating a broken bone that has not been surgically repaired can prevent it from ever healing. If radiation to the hip has a role for you, it is the conventional palliative radiation on the standard list, after surgical stabilization, not particle therapy.

docs.title: Questions to ask your oncologist
docs.text:
1. For my hip: do you expect surgical repair to leave me stronger for treatment, or to cost me recovery time I will not get back? What does the operative date do to trial eligibility windows, and can tumor tissue be banked during the operation for the genetic testing?
  2. Can my ECOG fitness score be formally assessed and written in my chart now, with my pain control and walking status recorded next to it, and reassessed after my hip is treated? Which trial doors does the honest answer open or close?
  3. For chemotherapy: which response numbers would you quote for my exact subtype, and why? Would you recommend doxorubicin alone with early rescans and agreed stop rules, or doxorubicin plus a second drug, and what heart, kidney, and liver testing do I need first?
  4. Has the comprehensive DNA and RNA panel been ordered on my existing biopsy tissue? Will the lab test the aggressive (dedifferentiated) part specifically, will the report say which lesion was sampled, and is the faster IDH-only test worth ordering in parallel?
  5. If the IDH test comes back negative, do you agree that the only things that change are the ivosidenib option and the three IDH-dependent experimental entries, and that everything else stands? If it comes back positive, would you still hold ivosidenib back given how thin its results are in my subtype, and if not, why?
  6. Should any radiation to my hip wait until after the bone is surgically stabilized, and will the radiation and surgical teams decide that together?
  7. Can a palliative-care team be involved from the start for pain and symptom control alongside treatment, rather than later, and can we talk about it as support rather than as a change of goals?
  8. Can we make the screening call for the metabolism-drug trial this week, and can the same referral move my care to a high-volume sarcoma center? And since travel has never come up: how far is realistic for me?

docs.text: A forward-looking horizon scan: candidate drugs, compounds, and treatment strategies that are earlier than clinical development (or not yet developed) but plausibly target this patient's stated features. Separate from the board's clinical recommendations, and not reviewed by the virtual tumor board.

Reading the columns

These are candidate ideas that are earlier than clinical development, or not yet developed at all. Stage is how far the candidate has progressed (conceptual through IND-enabling). Evidence strength is the qualitative weight of the preclinical support. Counter-productive MoA is the mechanism-level risk that the candidate's own pathway could blunt its therapeutic goal. None of these options is enrollable today; they are a horizon scan, not the ranked clinical recommendations on the Recommendations table.

docs.title: Standard of care options — chondrosarcoma-mets-acetabular-fx-idh-unknown-y34r
docs.text: The treatment strategies that are standard for this patient's situation, meaning a regulator approved them for a population that includes this patient or a major academic or clinical-society guideline carries them. This is one of the case's two therapeutic tables and frequently carries its primary recommendation; the experimental ranking is the other, and neither narrows the other.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
• Standard of care options (offline HTML) — the same standard-of-care assessment, self-contained HTML that opens offline
  • Standard of care options (PDF) — print-friendly, grouped by next step

9 standard options assessed: 6 to consider now, 1 behind an open gate, 0 already received.

Nine standard options were screened for this treatment-naive metastatic dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma, six can be weighed now, and the table carries its own ranking, 1 to 9, ordered on expected benefit and fit. First is doxorubicin-based chemotherapy, the unanimous first choice of all five board personas and the only option here with an on-label footing (the FDA doxorubicin label names metastatic bone sarcomas); its first-line response expectation stays contested, 9% in a modern multi-institutional cohort against 20.5% in an older locally-assessed series. Second is orthopaedic fixation of the fractured acetabulum, the sequencing keystone: irradiated bone heals poorly, so radiotherapy to that field waits on the fixation call. Third is early specialist palliative care alongside active treatment, the best-evidenced item on this page: a strong ASCO recommendation resting on randomised data, costing no line of therapy. Pre-treatment referral to a high-volume sarcoma centre, palliative radiotherapy, and trial enrollment as guideline-carried management complete the actionable six.

Nothing standard has been spent: there is no prior therapy on file.

One option sits behind a gate. Ivosidenib is carried by NCCN for IDH-mutant dedifferentiated disease but waits on the IDH1 sequencing the ranked workup already orders, and its FDA label does not yet include chondrosarcoma. Pazopanib and pulmonary metastasectomy were assessed and set aside because their guideline populations, conventional histology and oligometastatic lungs, are not hers.

This report is additive. Its ranking is its own 1 to 9, beside the Experimental table's separate 1 to 22; neither continues the other, and nothing here narrows or reorders that ranking. Ivosidenib and the trial-enrollment strategy now live on this table only, filed by regulatory maturity, while the ranked table keeps the protocol seats and the profiling row that closes the ivosidenib gate. Where two options share a line, the rows name the trade instead of resolving it.

docs.title: Assessed and set aside
docs.text:
2 option(s) screened against this patient and set aside

Screened against this patient and found not to apply. Listed for the audit trail.

  • Pazopanib (carried for the conventional-chondrosarcoma population, which this is stated not to be): Carried so the chondrosarcoma pathway reads complete rather than because it fits: pazopanib's guideline position and its phase 2 evidence are in conventional chondrosarcoma, and that trial excluded dedifferentiated histology. It would only enter consideration if the pending expert bone-sarcoma pathology review reclassified the tumour, and that review is a hardening item, not an open fork.
  • Pulmonary metastasectomy or local ablation of lung metastases: Standard in bone sarcoma only for oligometastatic lung disease, and the profile places this presentation outside that population on its face. Assessed and set aside so a reader who knows metastasectomy is sometimes curative in bone sarcoma can see it was weighed rather than missed; systemic control is the operative question for these lungs.

docs.title: How these sit alongside the experimental options
docs.text:
These options and the experimental ranking are two co-equal tables, and nothing here changes that ranking. What this section adds is the sequencing: where a standard option and an experimental one compete for the same line, and where taking one would close the door on the other.

Competes for the same line of therapy

  • Doxorubicin-based chemotherapy (doxorubicin alone or with ifosfamide or cisplatin): First-line chemotherapy and the IACS-6274 phase 1 seat occupy the same window: that protocol has no prior-therapy requirement, and the board noted a first-line dose-escalation slot would spend the one line with a proven response signal in this histology. Several ranked options (abemaciclib on NCT04040205, TAPUR, sunitinib plus nivolumab) are pre-positioned for the line after an anthracycline, so receiving it is also what opens them. The trade is named here, not resolved. (interacts with: glutaminase-inhibition, cdk4-6-inhibition, tapur-genomically-matched-agents, sunitinib-plus-nivolumab, tam-directed-therapy)
  • Ivosidenib, conditional on an IDH1 mutation being found: The Experimental table no longer carries its own ivosidenib row: the PI deduplicated the agent to this table, so this row is where ivosidenib lives on the case page. The gate is unchanged, the untested IDH1 status that the ranked table's rank-1 profiling row exists to close. If sequencing returns a susceptible IDH1 mutation, ivosidenib would occupy the same mutation-directed line as the ranked IDH-gated rows, LY3410738 at rank 14 and olaparib plus ceralasertib at rank 15. Its regulatory limits stand: no chondrosarcoma indication on the FDA label, and the phase 3 route, CHONQUER NCT06127407, enrols conventional histology only. (interacts with: comprehensive-dna-rna-profiling, ly3410738, parp-inhibition)

May foreclose a targeted option

  • Palliative radiotherapy to the acetabular lesion: Photon radiotherapy to the acetabulum would complicate any later particle-therapy course to the same field. The ranked particle-therapy row is currently not enrollable for her (both protocol routes exclude distant metastases), so the overlap is named for completeness rather than as a live conflict. (interacts with: particle-therapy)

Comes before the targeted options

  • Orthopaedic stabilisation (fixation) of the pathologic acetabular fracture: Fixation before any irradiation of the fracture site is the standing sequencing constraint on this case (irradiated bone forms atrophic non-unions in the preclinical model), which reaches the ranked particle-therapy row and this table's palliative radiotherapy row alike. Whether fixation improves or spends the measured ECOG also bears on the ECOG 0-1 gates of the ranked trial seats; the board split on that and the split is preserved, not resolved. (interacts with: particle-therapy, glutaminase-inhibition, cdk4-6-inhibition)

Can run alongside the targeted options

  • Early referral to a specialist interdisciplinary palliative care team, alongside active treatment: Runs alongside every ranked option and forecloses none. The board's critic observed that this recommendation is the best-evidenced single item put in front of the board, and it carries randomised data where the rest of the case rests on retrospective cohorts.
  • Referral to a high-volume sarcoma centre with a bone-sarcoma multidisciplinary team, before first treatment: An expert centre is also where the ranked workup (comprehensive DNA plus RNA profiling on the dedifferentiated component) and most protocol seats are reachable, so this option widens rather than competes with the experimental track. (interacts with: comprehensive-dna-rna-profiling)
  • Clinical trial enrollment as a management strategy: The ranked table on this case page is the concrete instantiation of this row: it holds the ranked protocol seats. This row records only that guideline text itself points to trials in metastatic chondrosarcoma; it does not rank among them or substitute for them.

Independent of the targeted options

  • Pazopanib (carried for the conventional-chondrosarcoma population, which this is stated not to be):
  • Pulmonary metastasectomy or local ablation of lung metastases:

Reading this report

An option earns a row here only if a regulator approved it for a population that includes this patient, or a major society's guideline carries it. What makes it standard names the endorsing body and, next to it, whether that endorsement was written for this patient's situation or for a different population. Fit to this patient is judged against the case profile alone, so an option the patient has already had and progressed on is marked rather than re-offered. This page is additive: it runs alongside the ranked recommendations and does not narrow, rerank, or filter the targeted options that ranking surfaces.

Back to case · Recommendations · Target validation · Biomarker survey · Trials · Evidence · Access guide · Board

Decision support, not medical advice

Libby is experimental. Standard of care is set by a treating team using the full clinical record, not by this page. Guideline versions and approvals move, eligibility here is inferred from a scrubbed profile rather than an examination, and nothing on this page is a recommendation to start, stop, or sequence a treatment. See PHI policy.

docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences essentialIDH1 codon 132 and IDH2 codons 140/172 mutation testing by DNA sequencing (comprehensive NGS panel or targeted hotspot assay), not R132H immunohistochemistryconfirmatoryNGS_panelArchival FFPE block or 10-15 unstained slides cut from the dedifferentiated component3-10 days for a targeted hotspot assay; 2-3 weeks if it rides on the comprehensive panelIvosidenib or olutasidenib and entry to IDH1-directed trials, each of which requires a documented mutation by sequencing.Sequencing decides whether an IDH-directed drug or trial is available at all, and it is the highest-yield untested item in the case: IDH1/IDH2 mutations were present in 71 percent of dedifferentiated chondrosarcomas in a paired series against 36 percent of conventional tumours (pmid:36926116). docs.title: Unmeasured molecular landscape
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences essentialComprehensive tumour DNA plus RNA next-generation sequencing panel covering IDH1/IDH2, TP53, CDKN2A/B, TERT promoter, NTRK1-3, RET and BRAF, reporting TMB in mutations per megabase and an MSI callco-mutationNGS_panelOne FFPE block or 10-20 unstained slides containing the dedifferentiated component2-3 weeksTumour-agnostic options (TRK and RET inhibitors, dabrafenib plus trametinib, pembrolizumab for TMB-H or MSI-H) and genotype-matched trial entry.One order answers the IDH question and every tumour-agnostic one at the same time, which is what a patient with no molecular testing needs. Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma is enriched for TP53, TERT promoter and CDKN2A/B alterations relative to conventional disease (pmid:36926116), while TMB of 10 or more per megabase and MSI-high are rare in sarcoma at 3.9 percent and 0.7 percent respectively (pmid:35705558, pmid:42531431) but each opens approved checkpoint therapy. Specify a validated comprehensive panel with RNA fusion coverage; a small hotspot panel prints a TMB figure it is not sized to call, and a DNA-only panel can miss a fusion whose breakpoint sits in a large intron.Foundation Medicine · FoundationOne CDx preferredtest info · 400 Summer Street, Boston, MA 02210 · 888-988-3639Preferred: FDA-approved companion diagnostic claims, validated TMB and MSI reporting, and the widest sponsor acceptance for trial screening.Caris Life Sciences · MI Cancer Seek (whole exome plus whole transcriptome) UStest info · 3600 W Royal Ln, Irving, TX 75063 · 888-979-8669Choose this instead if fusion depth matters most; the whole transcriptome is the stronger fusion assay in sarcoma.Mayo Clinic Laboratories · OncoHeme / solid tumour comprehensive panel UStest info · 3050 Superior Drive NW, Rochester, MN 55901 · 800-533-1710NeoGenomics Laboratories · NeoTYPE Sarcoma Profile UStest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 239-768-0600 option 3Tempus AI · Tempus xT plus xR UStest info · 600 West Chicago Avenue, Chicago, IL 60654PMID 36926116PMID 35705558PMID 42531431 essentialPathology block review for tumour cellularity and dedifferentiated-component representation, with macrodissection instructions and a written tissue-allocation plan across the panel, the immunohistochemistry set and any reflex stainsheterogeneityotherExisting diagnostic block; a repeat image-guided core only if tumour content is insufficient2-4 daysWhether the archival block can carry the whole work-up, or whether a repeat core is needed before any molecular result can be trusted.Everything else on this list runs off one block, and dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma is biphasic by definition, so a core that sampled only the low-grade cartilage returns a falsely reassuring molecular and PD-L1 result; PD-L1 positivity in this subtype was confined to the dedifferentiated component (pmid:27312065), and the two components differ in mutational and copy-number profile even though they share early events (pmid:36926116). Ask the pathologist to confirm the block holds enough high-grade non-cartilaginous tumour, to macrodissect it, and to cut once for the panel and once for the stains rather than piecemeal. If the block falls short, schedule a repeat image-guided core of the acetabular mass now instead of waiting for a stabilisation procedure.—PMID 27312065PMID 36926116 highFour-antibody mismatch-repair IHC (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6), with MSI by PCR or NGS if any stain is equivocalorthogonal validationIHC4 unstained slides from the block cut for the immunohistochemistry set2-5 daysTumour-agnostic pembrolizumab or dostarlimab in a later line if mismatch-repair protein loss is found.Days rather than weeks, and an orthogonal read on the MSI call the sequencing panel will produce. MSI-high appeared in 0.7 percent of sarcomas in the largest clinically sequenced cohort (pmid:42531431), so a proficient result is the expected one, but a loss of staining would put approved tumour-agnostic checkpoint blockade in front of a patient with no other approved targeted option. Loss of a mismatch-repair protein also raises a Lynch syndrome question for her and her relatives, and reflexes to MLH1 promoter methylation testing.NeoGenomics Laboratories · MMR IHC panel preferredtest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 239-768-0600 option 3Preferred among reference labs for a validated four-antibody panel with sarcoma experience; a treating hospital's own histology laboratory is usually faster and equally validated if it offers the panel.ARUP Laboratories · MMR IHC panel UStest info · 500 Chipeta Way, Salt Lake City, UT 84108 · 800-522-2787Labcorp Oncology · MMR IHC panel UStest info · 358 South Main Street, Burlington, NC 27215Mayo Clinic Laboratories · Mismatch repair protein IHC UStest info · 3050 Superior Drive NW, Rochester, MN 55901 · 800-533-1710Quest Diagnostics · MMR IHC panel UStest info · 500 Plaza Drive, Secaucus, NJ 07094PMID 42531431 highPD-L1 IHC with the clone and scoring system recorded explicitly (22C3 pharmDx with CPS, or SP263 per the protocol in play), read on a section containing the dedifferentiated componentmicroenvironmentIHC1-2 unstained slides from the immunohistochemistry-set block3-7 daysEnrichment for checkpoint-inhibitor trials; it does not gate an approved drug in sarcoma.This is a subtype-specific finding rather than a generic sarcoma prior: PD-L1 was positive in 9 of 22 dedifferentiated chondrosarcomas and in none of 119 conventional, 19 mesenchymal or 20 clear-cell tumours, with staining confined to the dedifferentiated component and tracking with T-cell infiltrate (pmid:27312065); a second cohort found comparable positivity in dedifferentiated disease (pmid:33912442). No sarcoma indication is keyed to PD-L1, and SARC028 showed limited activity in bone sarcoma cohorts (pmid:28988646), so treat the result as trial-enrichment information rather than a prescription. Stain a section that actually contains dedifferentiated tissue, or the result will be falsely negative for the wrong reason.NeoGenomics Laboratories · PD-L1 IHC (22C3, SP263, 28-8) preferredtest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 239-768-0600 option 3Preferred: carries all the major PD-L1 clones under one order, which matters because a result generated with one companion diagnostic does not transfer to another protocol's cutoff.ARUP Laboratories · PD-L1 IHC UStest info · 500 Chipeta Way, Salt Lake City, UT 84108 · 800-522-2787Labcorp Oncology · PD-L1 IHC UStest info · 358 South Main Street, Burlington, NC 27215Mayo Clinic Laboratories · PD-L1 IHC UStest info · 3050 Superior Drive NW, Rochester, MN 55901 · 800-533-1710Quest Diagnostics · PD-L1 IHC UStest info · 500 Plaza Drive, Secaucus, NJ 07094PMID 27312065PMID 33912442PMID 28988646 mediumCD3 and CD8 tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte density plus tumour HLA class I expression by IHC, read on the dedifferentiated componentmicroenvironmentIHC2-3 unstained slides from the immunohistochemistry-set block1-2 weeksContext for checkpoint and cell-therapy discussions; not an eligibility criterion anywhere.Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma carries T-cell infiltrate and retained HLA class I far more often than the other subtypes, and PD-L1 positivity travels with both (pmid:27312065, pmid:33912442). Loss of tumour HLA class I would undercut any T-cell-redirecting approach even with the right host genotype and a positive antigen stain, which is the one thing the HLA blood draw cannot tell you. No protocol enrolls on these numbers, so they belong on the same block cut as the other stains and not on a separate requisition.NeoGenomics Laboratories · CD3 / CD8 immunohistochemistry preferredtest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 239-768-0600 option 3Preferred: CD3 and CD8 are standard catalogue stains here; HLA class I clone availability varies and should be confirmed when the order is placed.ARUP Laboratories · CD3 / CD8 immunohistochemistry UStest info · 500 Chipeta Way, Salt Lake City, UT 84108 · 800-522-2787Mayo Clinic Laboratories · T-cell subset immunohistochemistry UStest info · 3050 Superior Drive NW, Rochester, MN 55901 · 800-533-1710PMID 27312065PMID 33912442 mediumGermline cancer-predisposition panel from blood or saliva, reflexed if the tumour panel returns a BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2 or TP53 variant at an allele fraction suggesting germline origingermlinegermline_panel5-10 mL whole blood in EDTA, or a saliva collection kit2-4 weeksFamily screening, and radiotherapy planning if a germline TP53 variant is confirmed.The cartilage phenotype itself does not point to a germline syndrome: no germline IDH1 or IDH2 mutations were found across roughly 1200 mesenchymal tumours in the founding series, and the multiple-enchondroma syndromes are mosaic rather than inherited (pmid:21598255). The germline question here therefore rides on what else the tumour panel turns up, and homologous-recombination deficiency appeared in 2.5 percent of sarcomas in a large profiling cohort (pmid:35705558). A confirmed germline BRCA1/2 or TP53 finding changes screening for her relatives and, in the TP53 case, how radiotherapy is considered.Myriad Genetics · MyRisk Hereditary Cancer Test preferredtest info · Salt Lake City, UTPreferred: large US commercial laboratory with established insurance pathways for a reflex germline order, which matters when the test is not on the critical path.Ambry Genetics · CustomNext-Cancer UStest info · Aliso Viejo, CAGeneDx · Hereditary cancer panel UStest info · Stamford, CTLabcorp Oncology · Hereditary cancer panel UStest info · 358 South Main Street, Burlington, NC 27215Mayo Clinic Laboratories · Hereditary cancer multi-gene panel UStest info · 3050 Superior Drive NW, Rochester, MN 55901 · 800-533-1710PMID 21598255PMID 35705558

docs.title: Large acetabular lesion with pathologic fracture
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences essentialOrthopaedic oncology assessment of the periacetabular fracture with thin-slice bone-algorithm pelvic CT and MRI of the hemipelvis, addressing stabilisation or resection options and their timing against systemic therapyfunctional assayimagingNone; imaging plus clinical reviewimaging within days; surgical opinion at the same visitTiming of orthopaedic stabilisation or radiotherapy against first-line systemic therapy, and the surgical-washout window for trial entry.The hardening question at this site is structural rather than molecular: whether the joint needs fixation or resection, and whether that happens before, alongside or after chemotherapy. A primary pelvic sarcoma with a pathologic fracture is a different surgical problem from an acetabular metastasis, since fracture haematoma contaminates compartments and periacetabular resection and reconstruction is a specialist decision (pmid:41289179, pmid:34500044). The sequencing carries a concrete cost: the phase 3 ivosidenib protocol excludes major surgery within 4 weeks of randomisation (nct:NCT06127407), and comparable washouts are standard, so an unplanned operation can close trial doors for a month.—PMID 41289179PMID 34500044NCT06127407 essentialDocumented ECOG performance status scored in clinic, recorded alongside weight-bearing status, ambulatory aids and analgesic requirementfunctional assay—None; clinic assessmentsame dayChemotherapy intensity, and eligibility for protocols that cap performance status at ECOG 0-1 or 0-2.The ECOG of 2 in the profile was assumed at intake from the pathologic fracture and has never been measured, yet it carries more weight than any other number in the case: most protocols cap eligibility at 0-1 or 0-2, and full-dose anthracycline plus ifosfamide is a fitness decision. A score driven by a mechanically unstable hip is not the same as one driven by disease burden, and stabilisation or adequate analgesia may move it. Until someone scores it, every eligibility statement made downstream rests on a guess.——

docs.title: Multiple dispersed pulmonary metastases
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences highBaseline contrast-enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis with thin-section lung reconstructions, read for RECIST 1.1 measurability and for whether the nodule distribution leaves any role for local therapyconfirmatoryimagingNone; imagingdaysEntry to any protocol requiring RECIST-measurable disease, and whether a local pulmonary approach is on the table.Two questions get settled in one acquisition: whether any nodule reaches 10 mm in longest diameter and is therefore measurable under RECIST 1.1 (pmid:19097774), which trial protocols including the phase 3 ivosidenib study require, and whether bilateral dispersed disease genuinely rules out metastasectomy or SBRT. Small scattered nodules are also the yardstick against which chemotherapy response will be judged, so the baseline has to exist before treatment starts rather than after the first cycle. Biopsy of a pulmonary nodule is worth doing only if the plan turns on tissue confirmation of metastasis or on the metastatic genotype.—PMID 19097774NCT06127407

docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences highHLA class I genotyping at 4-digit (allele-level) resolution by sequence-based typinggermlineNGS_panel5-10 mL whole blood in EDTA, or a buccal swab; no tumour tissue1-2 weeksWhether HLA-restricted TCR-T and ImmTAC programmes (afamitresgene autoleucel, uzatresgene autoleucel, IMA203, brenetafusp) can be pursued at all.A blood draw that spends no tumour tissue and decides whether the three cancer-testis antigen rows below are worth staining at all. docs.title: MAGE-A4 (HLA-A*02:01-restricted)
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences mediumMAGE-A4 expression by IHC or RT-PCR on the dedifferentiated component, ordered only after HLA-A*02:01 is documented; RNA expression from a whole-transcriptome panel is an acceptable first passconfirmatoryIHC1-2 unstained slides from the immunohistochemistry-set block; reflex only1-2 weeks after typingMAGE-A4-directed TCR-T referral; afamitresgene autoleucel is synovial-sarcoma labelled, uzatresgene autoleucel is trial-only.The sequence is what makes this tractable: type first, stain only if HLA-A*02:01 is present, because an expression result cannot be interpreted for eligibility without the restricting allele. Expectations should be modest; in the largest cancer-testis antigen survey of bone and soft tissue sarcomas MAGE-A4 was found in about 40 percent of osteosarcomas and a third of undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcomas, while chondrosarcomas showed little expression overall (pmid:40152485), and the approved product is licensed for synovial sarcoma alone (pmid:38554725). Sponsors re-test centrally with their own antibody and cutoff, so a local result triages the referral rather than qualifying her for it.Caris Life Sciences · MI Cancer Seek whole transcriptome (MAGEA4 expression) preferredtest info · 3600 W Royal Ln, Irving, TX 75063 · 888-979-8669Preferred first pass: if the whole transcriptome is already being run for the fusion question, MAGEA4 expression comes off it without spending another slide.NeoGenomics Laboratories · Custom immunohistochemistry UStest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 239-768-0600 option 3Tempus AI · Tempus xR RNA expression UStest info · 600 West Chicago Avenue, Chicago, IL 60654PMID 40152485PMID 38554725

Note the trial does not require a B7-H3 IHC result to enter, so a negative or absent stain would not itself exclude her later. ——2025—NCT072436262Advanced soft tissue sarcoma, first line1L (no previous systemic treatment)none required25Single-arm phase 2Envafolimab plus doxorubicin and ifosfamide—Progression-free survival————single-arm, single-country——nonecross-tumormonoclonal antibodyphase 2 activeSecond Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine—Included as a documented exclusion rather than an option: the regimen is exactly the doxorubicin-ifosfamide-plus-PD-L1 combination her histology invites, and it requires patients be systemically untreated, which she is — but exclusion criterion 1 names chondrosarcoma explicitly, alongside osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma. That pattern repeats across the first-line sarcoma chemo-immunotherapy trials I screened, where the enrolling histology lists are soft-tissue and cartilage tumours are carved out. The histology gate is the problem: cohort 1 is soft tissue sarcoma and cohort 2 is osteosarcoma, and chondrosarcoma is named in neither. The histology is the wall — clear cell sarcoma only, and gp100 is a melanocytic antigen with no expected expression in a cartilage tumour. The row stays in the dossier because it is the only active IDH2-directed protocol that takes chondrosarcoma at all, so it would matter if an IDH2 mutation turned up and the site restriction were ever waived. ——2024—NCT064228063Metastatic or unresectable dedifferentiated liposarcoma, undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma and related poorly differentiated sarcomas1L (no prior systemic therapy for advanced disease)none required365Randomised phase 3Doxorubicin plus pembrolizumabDoxorubicin aloneProgression-free survival————randomised, low risk of bias by design; results pending——weakcross-tumormonoclonal antibodyphase 3 activeNational Cancer Institute (NCI)—Mechanically this is the pairing her tumour biology argues for — first-line anthracycline plus PD-1 blockade in a chemo-responsive, PD-L1-expressing high-grade sarcoma — and it is one of the few sarcoma protocols that requires patients be treatment-naive rather than pretreated. docs.title: Research question
docs.text: A working artist in her 60s has stage IV EGFR L858R lung adenocarcinoma. She got 22 months out of first-line osimertinib (PR), and now she is progressing. The tumor is T790M-negative but MET-amplified at GCN 8.2 by FISH. What should the next line of therapy target, given that she needs her hands, prefers oral therapy, and is open to trials?

docs.title: Patient profile (scrubbed)
docs.text:
• Primary site / histology: lung adenocarcinoma
  • Stage: IV
  • Performance status: ECOG 1
  • Age band: 60-69
  • Biomarkers: EGFR L858R (present); EGFR T790M (absent); MET amplification (GCN 8.2 by FISH); PD-L1 TPS 10%
  • Prior therapy: 1L osimertinib, PR x 22 months — now progressed
  • Targetable features: EGFR L858R (sensitizing); MET amplification (likely on-target resistance)

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text:
• Efficacy/toxicity weight: 0.55 (slight efficacy lean)
  • Toxicity vetoes: severe neuropathy, cardiotoxicity, alopecia
  • Modality constraints: oral preferred; no inpatient infusion; minimize IV chair time
  • Free text: "working artist — manual dexterity in hands matters more than typical"
  • Trials preferred: yes

docs.title: Target validation paths
docs.text: EGFR L858R, MET amplification (GCN 8.2), and T790M-absent are all confirmed at decision-relevant resolution, so no diagnostic test gates the savolitinib + osimertinib trial enrollment (SAFFRON / SACHI). The validation work here is about resistance characterization at progression, not target confirmation. The goal is to make sure the case really is MET-amplified bypass resistance and not something more complicated wearing the same imaging signature.

docs.title: EGFR L858R
docs.text: The most consequential miss right now would be SCLC histologic transformation, which is the highest-PPV resistance pattern that no liquid biopsy can confirm. Tumor NGS including TP53 and RB1 status is the screen: co-loss is the strongest predictor of transformation, with reported rates of 3–14% across post-osimertinib cohorts. If imaging morphology shifts or co-loss is detected, fresh re-biopsy with a neuroendocrine IHC panel (chromogranin, synaptophysin, INSM1, Ki-67) is the only way to confirm. ctDNA covering EGFR C797S and exon-20 inserts is the parallel on-target resistance check; a positive C797S result reframes the next-line conversation toward fourth-generation EGFR-TKIs or combination strategies.

docs.title: MET amplification
docs.text: The FISH GCN 8.2 result clears SAFFRON's enrollment threshold (≥ 6) cleanly, but MET amplification can be focal, and primary-vs-metastatic discordance is a documented confounder in this setting. A second-site FISH (or a matched archival block) refines confidence that the dominant disease, not just the biopsied site, is the amplified one. MET IHC (clone SP44) is the orthogonal-modality complement to the SAFFRON eligibility profile. A comprehensive NGS panel that picks up HER2 / BRAF / FGFR co-alterations frames durability expectations and the next-line plan.

docs.title: Biomarker plan
docs.text:
Recommended assay Rationale Suggested assay provider Tissue requirements ctDNA panel including EGFR C797S, T790M, and exon 20 insertions After osimertinib progression, the resistance landscape divides cleanly between on-target EGFR mutations (C797S, exon-20 inserts, less commonly T790M) and bypass mechanisms. Detecting C797S in cis vs trans changes whether a fourth-generation EGFR-TKI or a combination strategy is the rational next move. Skipping ctDNA at progression risks treating the case as bypass-resistance-only when the biology is mixed. Guardant Health (Guardant360 CDx) · test info · 505 Penobscot Drive, Redwood City, CA 94063 · 1-855-698-8887 10–20 mL whole blood; archival tissue not required Tumor NGS including TP53 and RB1 status TP53 + RB1 co-loss is the strongest predictor of small-cell histologic transformation as a resistance mechanism in EGFR-mutant NSCLC progressing on osimertinib. The probability of transformation is non-trivial (3–14% across cohorts), and missing it changes the next-line conversation entirely; chemotherapy backbones and platinum-etoposide enter the picture. Pair this with re-biopsy guidance below. Foundation Medicine (FoundationOne CDx) · test info · 150 Second Street, Cambridge, MA 02141 · 1-888-988-3639 archival FFPE; if exhausted, ctDNA broad panel Re-biopsy with neuroendocrine IHC panel (chromogranin, synaptophysin, INSM1, Ki-67) if imaging morphology shifts Histologic small-cell transformation is the most consequential resistance pattern that no liquid biopsy can confirm. When TP53/RB1 are co-lost or imaging shows new visceral / explosive growth atypical for adenocarcinoma, fresh tissue with a neuroendocrine IHC panel is the only way to confirm. Without this, a transformed case can be treated as adenocarcinoma indefinitely. Mayo Clinic Laboratories · test info · 200 First Street SW, Rochester, MN 55905 · 1-800-533-1710 fresh biopsy of the most-active site MET FISH on a second site (metastatic biopsy or matched archival block) MET amplification can be focal and discordant between primary and metastatic sites in EGFR-resistant NSCLC. The patient's GCN 8.2 from a single block clears SAFFRON's threshold, but a second-site test rules out the scenario where one biopsy hits a focal amplicon and the dominant disease is unaffected. Without it, a positive trial enrollment can rest on a non-representative result. NeoGenomics Laboratories · test info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 1-866-776-5907 second-site archival FFPE if available; not gating MET IHC (clone SP44) for orthogonal expression confirmation FISH-confirmed MET amplification at GCN 8.2 is the load-bearing finding, and SAFFRON enrollment accepts FISH or IHC 3+. IHC adds an orthogonal modality and surfaces protein-level MET expression; concordance increases confidence that the FISH result reflects active MET signaling. Discordance (FISH-amp without IHC overexpression) is a soft signal worth flagging but does not foreclose the trial. Mayo Clinic Laboratories · test info · 200 First Street SW, Rochester, MN 55905 · 1-800-533-1710 archival FFPE; same block as prior testing Comprehensive NGS for HER2 amp, BRAF, KRAS, FGFR1-3, and bypass-pathway alterations Bypass amplifications co-occur with MET amp in roughly 10–20% of post-osimertinib cases and modify expected response to MET-directed therapy. Detecting co-bypass alterations doesn't foreclose savolitinib + osimertinib but reframes the durability expectation and informs subsequent-line planning. Pair this with the TP53 / RB1 panel if running comprehensive NGS; same blood draw / block.
