docs.title: INCB161734, KRAS G12D-selective inhibitor (1L parent NCT06179160; phase 3 DAWN-303 NCT07522073) (incb161734)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker4lowA second sponsor's allele-matched agent with a 37% monotherapy ORR and 78% DCR in heavily pretreated G12D PDAC, and notably the monotherapy toxicity was GI-only with rash and stomatitis absent, which is a cleaner profile than the pan-RAS skin signature. The upside is a G12D-selective oral drug that spares the mucosal toxicity while still delivering a high response fraction, with 1L combination cohorts already open. It sits behind the top picks only because the response data are second-line-plus and the enrollable chemo-combination cohort carries ~40% grade >=3 neutropenia.37% ORR is from patients with >=2 prior lines; the 1L number is untested; the gem/nab-paclitaxel combination cohort ran ~40% grade >=3 neutropenia; PFS and DoR were not reached at ~5 months, so durability is unquantified conservative3moderateThe monotherapy AE picture is the reason this ranks above the other combination agents: phase 1 GI toxicity ran 50-60% but stayed grade 1-2, and rash and stomatitis were notably absent, so it does not stack skin toxicity onto a chemo backbone the way the pan-RAS agents do. The grade >=3 neutropenia (~40%) clustered in the chemo-combination cohort and reads as chemo-driven, with no treatment-related deaths. DAWN-303 is a randomized double-blind chemo +/- INCB161734 design, so the added-agent toxicity is measured against placebo+chemo rather than assumed. Confidence is moderate-to-low: the supporting efficacy is a 37% ORR in a heavily pretreated single-arm set (n=41), and the neutropenia rate in combination warrants an explicit growth-factor and monitoring plan before I would call it managed in a 79-year-old.~40% grade >=3 neutropenia in the chemo-combination cohort needs a defined growth-factor/monitoring algorithm; in a 79-year-old this is the load-bearing safety question, not the agent's own low-grade GI profile; Efficacy anchor is single-arm, pretreated, n=41 (ORR 37%); the front-line survival case is extrapolated; Retifanlimab-containing cohorts exist in the parent phase 1 — an anti-PD-1 pairing I would not endorse given MSS/TMB 8.6, where checkpoint benefit is low and irAE risk is not offset critic——did not pick— concensusite3moderateDAWN-303 (NCT07522073) requires KRAS G12D and enrolls previously untreated metastatic PDAC, so it fits his allele, tumor type, and line, and adds a second sponsor to the front-line G12D field. It is guideline-consonant as a trial under NCCN Pancreatic v2.2025, again with no consensus category. The phase-1 monotherapy read is the strongest single-agent G12D-PDAC response surfaced here (ORR 37%, DCR 78%, doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.654), which is what motivates the front-line combination test.Phase-1 population was heavily pretreated (>=2 prior lines); extrapolating that response to first line is an assumption.; Grade >=3 neutropenia clustered around 40% in the chemo-combination cohort, which matters more in a 79-year-old on a chemo backbone.; No mature PFS or randomized comparison yet. advocate5moderateThis has a strong single-agent signal on his driver, 37% ORR and 78% disease control, and as monotherapy the GI toxicity stayed grade 1-2 with rash and stomatitis notably absent, which is a good fit for an older patient. prefers_trials is served: DAWN-303 (NCT07522073) requires KRAS G12D and enrolls previously untreated metastatic PDAC, and the phase 1 parent (NCT06179160) takes him at his line too, both oral. It lands at rank 5 only because the recruiting front-line trial reads out as inhibitor-plus-chemotherapy, and grade 3 or worse neutropenia clustered near 40% in that combination cohort, which is the number I would put in front of him before he chose this over the cleaner zoldonrasib route.prefers_trials and oral modality both met, but the recruiting 1L arm bundles chemotherapy and ~40% grade >=3 neutropenia in that cohort works against a 79-year-old the neutral weight does not protect; the 37% ORR comes from heavily pretreated patients (all >=2 prior lines); mPFS and mDoR are immature, so first-line durability is unproven

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment criticconcensusitequalifiedevidence_qualityRanking INCB161734 above GFH375 on line-fit is reasonable, but the efficacy under it is an uncontrolled n=41 phase 1 abstract at 2L+ (all >=2 prior lines), ORR 37% with no CI and mPFS/mDoR not reached at ~5 months (doi:10.1200/JCO.2026.44.2_suppl.654). That is a response rate with no time-to-event anchor, which is exactly the surrogate I discount, and DAWN-303's front-line combination benefit is extrapolated across both line and setting. Keep it as an enrollable trial; do not let the 37% read as a durability estimate it does not carry.

docs.title: zoldonrasib (RMC-9805), KRAS G12D(ON)-selective inhibitor, first-line (RASolute 305, NCT07621718) (zoldonrasib)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker5lowThe G12D(ON)-selective RAS(ON) agent that maps to the patient's exact allele, with a 30% ORR and 80% DCR and, importantly, a well-tolerated profile at 1200 mg/day with no grade 4-5 treatment-related events. The bet is that pairing a clean-tolerability selective inhibitor with chemotherapy in the double-blind 1L RASolute 305 gives durable disease control in an older patient who cannot absorb much toxicity. It ranks last of the KRAS agents only because its 30% ORR trails the 37-41% seen with INCB161734 and GFH375, not because of any safety concern.ORR 30% is the lowest of the selective agents and PFS/DoR were not reported in the abstract; RASolute 305 is placebo-plus-chemo controlled, so there is a chance of assignment to chemo alone; the response data are second-line, so the 1L signal is inferred not observed conservative2lowZoldonrasib maps to the exact G12D allele and carries the cleanest single-agent tolerability signal I have: phase 1 at 1200 mg/day showed no grade 4 or 5 treatment-related events, GI toxicity that stayed grade 1-2 (nausea 27%, diarrhea 20%), and only a 1% grade 3 ALT rise. The catch is maturity — that read is an ASCO GI 2025 abstract, n=40, with PFS and DoR not reported, so the drug-specific long-tail is genuinely unknown. The enrollable front-line RASolute 305 adds it to mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel against placebo+chemo, which means the incremental grade >=3 burden the patient takes on is the known chemotherapy backbone rather than a novel signature. I rank it second, not first, because the phase 3 efficacy is unproven and the safety base is 40 patients deep.Safety base is a single 40-patient phase 1 abstract; no mature grade >=3 union rate or per-term G3+ breakdown published yet; The placebo-controlled design keeps the chemo backbone honest, but a treatment-naive 79-year-old still absorbs full-intensity mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel toxicity on top of the investigational agent; Efficacy for the combination is not yet demonstrated — the front-line survival benefit is a hypothesis built on a 30% single-agent ORR critic2moderateThis is the one place I credit biology over data: it hits G12D directly, which is a cleaner target rationale than daraxonrasib's pan-RAS extrapolation. But the clinical read is a single-arm phase 1 abstract, n=40, ORR 30% with no reported confidence interval and no PFS or DoR, so what I have is an unreplicated surrogate endpoint from a conference abstract, not a durability estimate. The front-line RASolute 305 (NCT07621718) is a registered double-blind phase 3, which is the correct design to settle this, but it has produced no readout yet, so ranking it here rests on the allele match plus a promising-but-immature response rate. I put it second because the target fit is genuine, not because the evidence is.ROBINS-I: single-arm, no comparator, so the 30% ORR has no control to net against and no CI to bound it; surrogate-only endpoint: PFS and DoR were not reported in the ASCO GI abstract, so durability is unknown; abstract-stage reporting, not a peer-reviewed full paper; I have not seen the RoB profile of the primary analysis concensusite2moderateZoldonrasib maps to his exact allele, and RASolute 305 (NCT07621718) requires KRAS G12D and enrolls treatment-naive metastatic PDAC, so it matches him on allele, tumor type, and line. As a trial it is guideline-consonant under NCCN Pancreatic v2.2025, with no consensus category yet since the agent is investigational and the front-line efficacy read is still open. The phase-1 signal (ORR 30%, DCR 80%, doi:10.1200/JCO.2025.43.4_suppl.724) is thinner than daraxonrasib's randomized data, which is why it sits second.The efficacy base is a single-arm phase-1 abstract with no mature PFS or DoR; the first-line phase 3 has not read out.; RASolute 305 randomizes against placebo plus mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel, and mFOLFIRINOX is a demanding backbone in a patient this age.; Tissue-documented G12D is required for entry. advocate3moderateIf I weight for the man rather than the depth of the data, this is the gentlest agent on his exact allele: at 1200 mg/day no grade 4 or 5 treatment-related events, and the common toxicities were grade 1-2 GI (nausea 27%, diarrhea 20%, vomiting 15%, rash 10%). The free_text flags that a 79-year-old likely warrants more toxicity-aversion than the neutral 0.5 allows me to encode, and this tolerability profile is exactly what that unstated preference would reward. prefers_trials is honored: RASolute 305 (NCT07621718) requires KRAS G12D and is recruiting at first line. It sits behind the two agents above because the base is a single-arm phase 1 of n=40 with no CI on the 30% ORR and no mature PFS, so I cannot tell him how durable it is.cleanest tolerability in the set, which is what I would lead with for an older patient, but the neutral 0.5 weight does not formally let me upweight it over the better-evidenced GFH375 and daraxonrasib; the recruiting 1L trial adds chemotherapy to zoldonrasib and the combination toxicity table is not published, so additive myelosuppression at 79 is unquantified

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment conservativerisktakerendorsetoxicityYou rank this last but say plainly it is not on safety grounds, and I want the tolerability read on the record as the right instinct for this patient. At 1200 mg/day the phase 1 showed no grade 4 or 5 treatment-related events, GI toxicity that held grade 1-2 (nausea 27%, diarrhea 20%), and a 1% grade 3 ALT rise. For an age-79 patient the missing safety datum is the combination arm, not the single agent, since RASolute 305 layers it onto full-intensity mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel. concensusitecriticqualifiedguideline_fitWe land the same order, so this is a framing note rather than a disagreement. You rank zoldonrasib second on "biology over data" and flag the n=40 abstract as thin, which is fair on the numbers, but the guideline-consonant reason it belongs at rank 2 is concrete: RASolute 305 (NCT07621718) is a registered double-blind front-line phase 3 requiring KRAS G12D, so it is the correct design to settle the allele question rather than a mechanistic bet. NCCN Pancreatic v2.2025 gives no category to any of these, so a registered 1L phase 3 in progress is the strongest guideline-fit signal available short of a readout. advocateconservativequalifiedpreference_fittoxicity_vetoes is empty so I raise no veto, and your rank-2 for zoldonrasib is close to where the patient's toxicity lens points too: no grade 4 or 5 events, rash only 10% (doi:10.1200/JCO.2025.43.4_suppl.724). My one qualifier is that the enrollable RASolute 305 slot (nct:NCT07621718) adds the agent to mFOLFIRINOX or gem/nab-paclitaxel, so the clean monotherapy signal is not what he actually takes on; the combination toxicity at 79 is unpublished, and that belongs in front of him.

docs.title: ceralasertib (AZD6738), ATR inhibitor — ARID1A-stratified basket (NCT03682289) (ceralasertib)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker——did not pick— conservative5lowI carry the ARID1A synthetic-lethal axis at rank 5 rather than any pan-KRAS or checkpoint-vaccine option because the ATR-inhibitor class has a well-characterized and manageable toxicity — cytopenias (anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia) with established dose-hold and transfusion algorithms, and no treatment-related deaths in the ARID1A-deficient phase 2. The efficacy is honestly weak for this tumor: 14% ORR across the full ARID1A-deficient set, with activity concentrating in gynecologic histologies and the non-gynecologic (PDAC-relevant) signal thinner. This slot is conditional: entry gates on BAF250a/ARID1A protein loss by IHC, and only ~two-thirds of ARID1A-mutant tumors show that loss, so the ctDNA frameshift call alone does not confirm eligibility. I would not move on it until IHC confirms loss and the treating team has a chemotherapy backbone decided.PDAC-relevant efficacy is weak — 14% ORR overall, activity skewed to gynecologic tumors; Per-term grade >=3 cytopenia rates were not broken out in the abstract, so the class signature is known but the trial-specific G3+ magnitude is not; the ATR class reference (camonsertib grade 3 anemia ~26%) sets expectations; Eligibility is IHC-gated on BAF250a loss; without confirmed protein loss the frameshift call does not secure a slot critic5lowI keep this on the list as a mechanistically independent second axis, not because the in-indication evidence supports it. The phase 2 (NCT03682289, n=29) returned 14% ORR across the full ARID1A-deficient population, and every response clustered in gynecologic histology; there is no PDAC responder in the data, so the pancreatic case is pure cross-tumor extrapolation. Enrollment is gated on BAF250a IHC loss, and only about two-thirds of ARID1A-mutant tumors show protein loss, so the frameshift call alone does not confirm eligibility. It ranks last on the evidence: a banked axis worth validating with IHC, but the current PDAC signal is absent, not merely weak.no PDAC responder in the clinical ARID1A data; case_match is cross_tumor_only, so PDAC activity is extrapolated; eligibility depends on BAF250a IHC loss that the frameshift does not reliably predict (~67% concordance), so the patient may screen-fail the target; class ATR-inhibitor cytopenias (anemia in particular) are dose-limiting and matter more at 79 concensusite5lowHis ARID1A frameshift is a real secondary axis, and NCT03682289 assigns treatment by ARID1A/BAF250a status while accepting pancreatic cancer, so it is a trial-enrollment option consonant with NCCN Pancreatic v2.2025 for a pretreated patient once the KRAS-directed slots are exhausted. There is no consensus category, and the clinical read is honest about its limits: the phase-2 signal concentrated in gynecologic histologies with a weak non-gynecologic showing (ORR 14% overall, pmid:41686845). Entry turns on BAF250a loss by IHC, which only about two-thirds of ARID1A-mutant tumors show, so the frameshift alone does not confirm eligibility.No PDAC responder in the reported data; the pancreatic signal rests on cross-tumor extrapolation.; BAF250a IHC is the real gate, and it has not been done — a plausible screen-fail.; This is a later-line consideration, not a first move while front-line G12D trials are open. advocate——did not pick—

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment concensusitecriticendorseguideline_fitAgreed on rank 5 and the reason. There is no NCCN Pancreatic v2.2025 category for an ARID1A/ATR agent, and germline testing came back negative, which also closes the one DDR route that does carry a category here, the BRCA/PALB2 olaparib POLO maintenance line (NCCN category 2A). So the synthetic-lethal axis is a later-line, IHC-gated trial option with no PDAC responder, exactly as you place it, not a front-line contender.

docs.title: ATR inhibition in ARID1A-deficient tumors (VE-821 / VX-970, ATR-class proof of concept)
docs.text:
intervention_id: ceralasertib · 1 row(s)

docs.title: What this page is
docs.text:
Libby read your tumor's genetic profile and gathered the treatment options that aim at the specific features driving this cancer. It ranked them and wrote down the promise and the problems for each one. This is the plain-language version of that work, written for you and the people helping you decide rather than for a specialist.

Before you go further, one thing to hold onto. This page only covers treatments that target the molecular features found in your tumor. The standard chemotherapy that almost everyone with this diagnosis is offered first is a separate conversation with your oncologist. Some of the trials below build on that chemotherapy, so it comes up as a backbone, but it is not ranked here and your care team owns that decision.

docs.title: What we know about your cancer
docs.text:
You have pancreatic cancer of the ductal adenocarcinoma type, and it has spread. There is a large mass in the pancreas itself and several tumors bigger than a centimeter in the liver. A gene-expression test placed your tumor in the "basal-like" group, which tends to behave more aggressively than the other main subtype, and that plays into which chemotherapy partner your team would choose.

The genetic testing turned up a handful of things that shape the options:

  • A change in a gene called KRAS, the G12D version. This is the main engine of the cancer and the most useful target found. Most of the options below aim straight at it.
  • A loss-of-function change in a gene called ARID1A. This is a second, separate target, less established but real.
  • A single change in a DNA-repair gene called MLH1. On its own, that can look like the kind of cancer that responds to immune-unleashing drugs. The rest of your profile points the other way, though: the tumor is "microsatellite stable" and its overall mutation count is on the lower side. So immune-checkpoint drugs by themselves are probably low-yield here. A simple tissue test (MMR protein staining, sometimes called IHC) settles the question, and it is worth running before anyone reaches for that kind of drug.
  • A few other changes (in SMAD4, TP53, and some incidental genes) that mostly speak to prognosis rather than pointing at a drug. One of them, in a gene called ASXL1, may actually be coming from your blood cells rather than the tumor. A paired blood test can sort that out so it is not mistaken for a tumor target.

Your markers were read from a blood-based test, a liquid biopsy. Most of the trials will want the KRAS finding confirmed on an actual tissue sample before they enroll you, so getting a tissue biopsy looked at is a practical first errand, and the same tissue can run the MMR stain at the same time.

docs.title: What you told us matters most
docs.text:
You did not give us specific goals or priorities, so we set the balance between fighting hard and going easy on side effects right in the middle. You did tell us you are open to clinical trials, and that matters a great deal here, because every targeted option for this cancer is currently available only through a trial.

One honest flag: you are 79. In someone's late seventies, the side-effect cost of a treatment usually weighs heavier than a neutral setting captures. We have not tilted the ranking on a preference you did not state, but it comes up repeatedly below, because the best-studied option and the gentlest option are not the same drug. If you and your oncologist decide that being easier on your body is the priority, the order near the top could reasonably shift. That is worth saying out loud in the room.

docs.title: The options
docs.text: These are ranked, but the gaps among the first three are narrow and partly a matter of what you value. Further down, the options get more uncertain, and the last few are on the page as things that were weighed rather than things to reach for now.

docs.title: Option 1 — daraxonrasib (a KRAS-blocking pill)
docs.text:
This is the option to discuss first. It is a pill that blocks the KRAS protein driving your cancer, and it covers the broader RAS family, not just the single G12D spot. Of everything on this page, it has the strongest evidence behind it: a large randomized trial of about 500 people, where some got the drug and some got chemotherapy, so the comparison is a real one.

In that trial, run in people who had already had one prior treatment, the results were striking. People on daraxonrasib lived a median of about 13 months, against about 7 months on chemotherapy. Put another way, at the point the researchers analyzed the data, the drug roughly cut the risk of dying by about 60% compared with chemo. The cancer also shrank in about a third of people, versus about one in nine on chemo, and the serious side effects were actually fewer than chemo caused in the same trial.

Here is the catch, and it matters. That trial was in people who had already had a first treatment. You would be starting this as your first treatment, and the trial testing it in that earlier setting (called RASolute 303) has not reported yet. So the benefit at your stage is expected, based on how the drug worked later on, but not yet proven. The survival numbers above also come from a mix of KRAS subtypes; your exact G12D version sat inside that group but was not analyzed on its own.

The main side effects are a skin rash and mouth sores, severe in roughly one in seven people, plus the general side effects any cancer drug brings. For an older person, the rash and mouth-sore problem is the thing to watch, because managing them sometimes means cutting the dose, and a lower dose can mean less benefit. The trial team has a playbook for handling these. It is a pill you take continuously, it fits your openness to trials, and the first-line trial accepts your KRAS type.

docs.title: Option 2 — GFH375 (also written VS-7375), a KRAS pill given with an antibody called cetuximab
docs.text:
This is a second KRAS-blocking pill, and it is built to hit your exact G12D version. Of all the options here, it posted the loudest tumor-shrinkage number: in an early study of about 59 people with your exact mutation, the cancer shrank in roughly 41%, and it was held in check in nearly everyone. That is the highest single-drug response on your specific mutation anywhere on this page.

Two things keep it from the top spot. First, that study had no comparison group, it was run at a single center in China, and most of the people in it had already been through two or more prior treatments, while you would be starting fresh. A response rate from that kind of study is a weaker footing than Option 1's randomized survival result. Whether the 41% carries over to a first-line patient is genuinely unknown until the first-line group reports. Second, the trial you would enter pairs this pill with cetuximab, an antibody given by IV. The pill's own side effects (some low blood counts, diarrhea) have known management routes, but the two together have never had their own safety report in pancreatic cancer, so how the combination sits with a 79-year-old is uncharacterized. That combination piece is the open question.

It matches you on the mutation and on your openness to trials, and the first-line slot is recruiting now.

docs.title: Option 3 — zoldonrasib (a more precisely targeted KRAS pill)
docs.text:
This is another KRAS-blocking pill built to hit your exact G12D mutation, and it is the gentlest drug on this whole page. In an early study of about 40 people with your mutation, the cancer shrank in about 30% and was held in check in about 80%. There were no severe (grade 4 or 5) side effects at the dose used; what did show up (nausea, some diarrhea, a little rash) was mostly mild.

So why third and not first? Because that 30% comes from an early study where everyone got the drug, with no comparison group, and only 40 people. We do not yet know how long the benefit lasts, because that has not been measured and reported. A response rate without any read on durability is weaker evidence than a randomized survival result. That is the open question here: real activity in your exact mutation, but staying power that nobody has measured yet.

For a 79-year-old, the tolerability is a real point in its favor. If going easy on your body is your priority, this is the drug a careful person would put forward first. The first-line trial (RASolute 305) adds it on top of chemotherapy, and the combined side effects of that pairing have not been published on their own, so the bone-marrow risk of the combination at your age is not yet a known quantity.

docs.title: Option 4 — INCB161734 (another precise KRAS pill, given with chemo)
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here is the tradeoff to weigh. This is a fourth KRAS-blocking pill, from a different company, also aimed at your G12D mutation. On the response numbers it looks the strongest of the single agents: in an early study of about 41 people (all heavily pretreated), the cancer shrank in about 37%. On its own, its side effects stayed mild, and it notably did not cause the rash and mouth sores the others can.

The caveat is about how you would actually receive it. The first-line trial (DAWN-303) does not give this pill by itself; it stacks it on top of full chemotherapy. In the early combination data, about 40% of people had a serious drop in their infection-fighting white blood cells. That is the concern for a 79-year-old: the chemo-plus-pill combination hits the bone marrow harder, and there is no dedicated safety study of that combination yet. The favorable side-effect profile is real for the drug alone, but the version you would enroll in bundles in the chemotherapy and its risks.

On effectiveness, the 37% here and the 30% for Option 3 are close enough to be within the noise of two small studies, so this does not clearly beat Option 3. It sits a notch lower mainly because the route you would take carries that documented marrow hit.

docs.title: Option 5 — HRS-4642 (a KRAS drug given by IV with chemotherapy)
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here is the tradeoff to weigh. This is a KRAS drug aimed at your G12D mutation, given by IV alongside chemotherapy, and its front-line number is the highest on this page. In an early study of 30 people starting treatment for the first time, the cancer shrank in about 63%. On paper that is the loudest first-line result here.

The tradeoff is severe, and there are two parts to it. The first is safety. In that study, about 90% of people had a serious (grade 3 or higher) side effect, mostly low blood counts, and there was one death from treatment in the wider safety group. For a 79-year-old, that is a heavy burden, and it runs against the general lean toward gentler treatment at your age. The second part is that the 63% number is hard to credit to the drug itself. It was given on top of chemotherapy, and chemotherapy alone shrinks these tumors in roughly a fifth of people. When this same drug was given by itself, without chemo, the response was only about 21%. So a large share of that 63% is the chemotherapy you would receive anyway, and there was no comparison group to separate the two. What the drug actually adds, on its own, is the open question.

There is also a practical wall right now: the trial that would offer this is not yet enrolling. It could become a real conversation for someone who put the highest possible response ahead of tolerability, but that is not where an unstated preference for a 79-year-old naturally points. It is on the page because Libby shows what was weighed, and this one was weighed and set aside for now on the strength of that safety profile.

docs.title: Option 6 — a group of brand-new pan-KRAS drugs still in first-in-human testing
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here is the tradeoff to weigh. These are four very early drugs (BBO-11818, BLU-924, PF-07934040, and LY3962673) that block KRAS broadly and would cover your G12D mutation. They are on the page because they aim squarely at your main target and some have recruiting slots.

The honest problem is that there is almost nothing to go on yet. These are first-in-human studies, the earliest stage of testing, where the goal is mostly to find a safe dose. None of them has a real response rate published. The only public hint is a single patient on one of these drugs whose tumor shrank, with no larger group behind that one case, and no safety tables yet for any of the four. Ranking them any higher would be ranking novelty, not evidence. Think of these as worth keeping an eye on for later, with the first meaningful readout expected in the second half of this year, rather than as something to act on now.

docs.title: Option 7 — ceralasertib (a pill aimed at the ARID1A loss, your second target)
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here is the tradeoff to weigh. This one aims at your other target, the ARID1A loss, through a completely different mechanism than the KRAS drugs. We keep it on the page because it is a genuinely independent second shot if the KRAS route does not work out. It is also the thinnest evidence here, with several real problems.

In the study that exists, across a mix of ARID1A-deficient cancers, the tumor shrank in about 14% of people, and the responses clustered in gynecologic cancers. No pancreatic cancer responded in that data. So applying it to your pancreatic cancer is an educated guess from the biology, not something shown to work in this disease.

Getting in is not even certain. The trial requires a specific tissue stain (BAF250a) to confirm the ARID1A protein is genuinely gone, and only about two-thirds of tumors with this gene change show that loss, so your genetic result alone does not guarantee eligibility. The main trial for it is currently not enrolling. The drug's class is also known for lowering blood counts, especially anemia, which is harder to tolerate at 79. This is here as a documented backup, not something to act on now.

docs.title: A note on immune therapies and KRAS vaccines
docs.text: You may have read about immune treatments and KRAS vaccines for this kind of cancer, so it is worth saying plainly why they are not on the list. The published KRAS-targeted cell therapy that made headlines only works in people with a particular immune-system type (a specific HLA marker), and your immune type is different, so it cannot recognize your tumor the way it needs to. The vaccine approaches that do not depend on immune type were studied in people whose cancer was caught early and largely removed by surgery, not in cancer that has spread the way yours has, so those results do not carry over. And the immune-checkpoint drugs are unlikely to help here, for the DNA-repair reasons above. None of this is a target your KRAS options are missing; those particular immune routes just do not fit your case.

docs.title: Questions to ask your oncologist
docs.text:
• For Option 1 (daraxonrasib), what is the plan for catching and managing the skin rash and mouth sores early, and at what point would we cut the dose?
  • The strongest evidence for Option 1 comes from people who were further along in treatment than I am. How much should we lean on it when I would be starting first-line?
  • Given that I am 79, should we lean toward the gentler pill (Option 3) even though it has less evidence behind it? How do you weigh that for me specifically?
  • Option 2 pairs its pill with an IV antibody, and Option 4 pairs its pill with chemotherapy. What extra side effects does each pairing add, and how would we watch for them?
  • For Option 4, the combination caused a serious drop in white blood cells in about 40% of people. How would we monitor my blood counts, and what is the threshold for backing off?
  • Option 5 had a very high rate of serious side effects and is not yet enrolling. Is there any scenario where it would be worth waiting for, or is it off the table for me?
  • Can we get a tissue biopsy reviewed to confirm the KRAS finding, since most of these trials need that before I can enroll?
  • Is it worth running the MMR protein stain on my tumor to settle the immune-therapy question one way or the other?
  • For the ARID1A option (Option 7), can we order the confirming stain (BAF250a) now so we know whether it is even a real fallback, and are any trials for it actually open?

Reading the columns

Toxicity burden is patient-level G3+ AE severity (Low / Moderate / High) summarized from trial publications. Counter-productive MoA is the mechanism-level risk that the intervention's own pathway could blunt the therapeutic goal — distinct from patient AEs. The board's endorse / dissent / veto state appears as pills under each intervention; full per-persona rationale lives on the board page.

docs.title: Research question
docs.text: In recurrent KRAS G12R pancreatic adenocarcinoma after adjuvant FOLFIRI (ECOG 1, MSS, TMB 4.1, with CDKN2A loss and CCND3 co-alteration), what interventions could target KRAS G12R or the CDKN2A/CCND3 cell-cycle axis?

docs.title: Patient profile (scrubbed)
docs.text:
• Primary site / histology: pancreas — pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
  • Stage: recurrent, post-resection and post-adjuvant chemotherapy
  • Performance status: ECOG 1
  • Age band: 50-59
  • Sex: unknown
  • Biomarkers (all confirmed on NGS):
    • KRAS G12R — mutated, NGS. Confirmed. The lead driver.
    • TP53 — inactivating mutation, NGS. Confirmed. Co-mutation context; variant class (missense vs truncating) not annotated on file.
    • CDKN2A — loss, NGS copy-number / IHC. Confirmed. The secondary cell-cycle axis.
    • CCND3 — alteration, NGS. Confirmed. Reinforces CDK4/6 dependency.
    • MSI status — MSS, NGS/IHC MMR panel. Confirmed. Forecloses tumor-agnostic ICI on the MSI-H label.
    • TMB — 4.1 mut/Mb. Confirmed. Below the 10 mut/Mb tumor-agnostic pembrolizumab threshold.
  • Prior therapy: FOLFIRI (adjuvant), best response PD. Irinotecan-based, so the patient is platinum-naive and oxaliplatin-naive.

docs.title: Target validation paths
docs.text: All six biomarkers in this case read as confirmed on the local report, so the workup here hardens the calls rather than gates a fresh diagnosis. The single essential row is orthogonal KRAS G12R confirmation by plasma ctDNA plus a second-platform tissue NGS: pan-RAS and RAS(ON) sponsors re-test the variant on plasma at screening regardless of the local report, and the same draw seeds the baseline VAF used for on-treatment monitoring at cycle 2 and cycle 4. This re-test gates trial entry for daraxonrasib (RMC-6236, NCT05379985), the daraxonrasib + chemo combination platform (NCT06445062), and the zoldonrasib (RMC-7977) + ivonescimab program (NCT07397338). Five high-priority workups run in parallel: a comprehensive germline panel, p16 IHC on the CDKN2A call, CCND3 alteration-class refinement, KRAS co-mutation NGS (SMAD4 / KEAP1 / STK11 / GNAS / ARID1A), and MTAP reflex testing on the 9p21 locus. Six medium-priority workups round out the dossier.

docs.title: KRAS G12R
docs.text:
Essential: orthogonal NGS plus baseline ctDNA. Pan-RAS / RAS(ON) trial central labs re-test KRAS G12X on plasma at screening; the orthogonal call locks eligibility for daraxonrasib monotherapy (NCT05379985), daraxonrasib + chemo (NCT06445062), and the RMC-7977 + ivonescimab combination (NCT07397338). Reference platforms are Guardant360 CDx, FoundationOne Liquid CDx, Tempus xF+, Natera Signatera, and Caris Assure; the FDA-approved CDx platforms are the safest choice for trial-entry documentation. G12R is biologically distinct from G12C and G12D (RAS-GTP-binding-deficient per Hobbs 2020), so G12C-specific covalent agents are not the relevant class. Turnaround is one to two weeks.

Three high-priority companions ride on the same NGS order. Co-mutation profiling for SMAD4, KEAP1, STK11, GNAS, and ARID1A frames prognosis and weights any ICI-combination decision: SMAD4 loss in PDAC is the strongest single co-alteration linked to wider metastatic spread, and KEAP1 / STK11 predict diminished ICI benefit on KRAS-mutant backgrounds. A germline hereditary-cancer panel (BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, ATM, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM, CDKN2A, TP53, STK11) is NCCN-recommended for every PDAC patient regardless of family history. A pathogenic BRCA1 / BRCA2 or PALB2 result opens olaparib maintenance via NCT02184195 plus rucaparib as the platinum-induction-gated PARP follow-on. Germline turnaround is three to six weeks; order in parallel with a genetic-counseling referral.

Two medium-priority resistance reads sit alongside: KRAS copy-number annotation (baseline KRAS amplification and acquired wildtype-KRAS amplification are documented escape mechanisms on the pan-RAS class), and serial KRAS G12R ddPCR or tumor-informed MRD at cycle 2 and cycle 4 of any KRAS-directed therapy, which flags VAF rebound weeks ahead of RECIST imaging.

docs.title: TP53
docs.text: The local report annotates an inactivating mutation, but the functional class matters: pure loss-of-function (truncations, splice) reads differently from dominant-negative missense hotspots (R175H, R248W, R273H) and from gain-of-function variants, and any TP53-restoration or MDM2-axis strategy gates on the precise call. The workup is a same-day re-read of the existing NGS report against the IARC TP53 database for variant annotation in HGVS notation. Does not gate the KRAS axis; refines any downstream cell-cycle / DDR conversation.

docs.title: CDKN2A
docs.text:
Two confirmatory reads. p16 IHC (clone E6H4 on archival FFPE, one to two week turnaround) is the orthogonal protein-level check on the NGS copy-number call; CDK4/6-inhibitor trial central labs prefer p16-negative status or biallelic CDKN2A loss for enrollment in CDKN2A-loss-enriched arms. A discordance (NGS-loss but IHC-retained) suggests subclonal or assay-driven calls and tempers expectations for CDK4/6 monotherapy.

Multi-region p16 IHC on a second tumor block (primary plus metastatic site if available) reads PDAC clonal heterogeneity at the next tier. A patchy result does not gate enrollment, but it changes how a CDK4/6-inhibitor response is interpreted and may push the board toward combination strategies.

The 9p21 MTAP reflex (callable from the same NGS panel) is the other operational read: CDKN2A and MTAP are co-deleted in roughly 80 to 90 percent of CDKN2A homozygous deletions, and MTAP co-deletion is the eligibility threshold for the MTA-cooperative PRMT5 class (anvumetostat on NCT06360354, BMS-986504 on NCT07492680). Decisive for any decision on whether the dual-feature daraxonrasib + anvumetostat regimen is on the table.

docs.title: CCND3
docs.text: The local NGS report names a CCND3 alteration without specifying class. An amplification or activating mutation supports cyclin-D-axis dependency and CDK4/6 sensitivity; a passenger missense without copy gain carries weaker mechanistic weight. Cyclin-D-degrader and selective CDK4 programs (PF-07220060, fadraciclib, INCB123667) gate on copy-number gain or known activating mutations, so the class call frames whether these axes belong on the page at all. Usually returnable as an annotation re-read of the existing NGS panel; ask the molecular pathologist for the alteration class explicitly. Turnaround is two to three weeks if a fresh order is required.

docs.title: MSS
docs.text:
Two reads to confirm the negative ICI finding. MMR IHC (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 on archival FFPE, one to two week turnaround) is the orthogonal protein-level confirmation on the NGS call. NGS-derived MSI calls have known false negatives at low tumor purity, and most ICI-trial central labs accept MMR IHC on its own. A confirmed MSS by both NGS and IHC closes the door cleanly on the tumor-agnostic pembrolizumab pathway.

The tumor microenvironment workup (PD-L1 22C3, CD3 / CD8 TIL density, alpha-SMA or H and E stromal density) frames any ICI-combination strategy. PDAC is the textbook immune-cold, stromally dense tumor, and the dominant interpretive question is usually T-cell exclusion rather than PD-L1 score. Returnable on a multiplex IHC panel (NeoGenomics MultiOmyx covers PD-L1, CD3, CD8, and stromal markers on a single section).

docs.title: TMB
docs.text: Documentation review rather than a new order. TMB values are sensitive to panel size, mutation-call filters, and whether synonymous variants are included; 4.1 mut/Mb on a 500-gene panel may map differently against the FDA-approved tumor-agnostic pembrolizumab threshold than a whole-exome-derived value (Friends of Cancer Research TMB Project harmonization study). If the existing report is from FoundationOne CDx, this is a same-day documentation check on the bioinformatics methods section. Below the 10 mut/Mb threshold the tumor-agnostic pembrolizumab route is foreclosed; the read confirms that foreclosure cleanly.
