docs.title: daraxonrasib (RMC-6236, RAS(ON) multi-selective) (daraxonrasib)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker1moderateThis is the one option here with a real ORR number in real 2L PDAC: 35% response, 8.5-month PFS, 13.1-month OS at 300 mg (n=26) — roughly double what NALIRIFOX or gem/nab buy in this setting. G12R sits inside the pooled G12 cohort, and the preclinical work (PMID 38589574, 38593348) shows G12R lines regress in the same exposure window as G12D, so I am comfortable extrapolating. The upside I am chasing: a durable RECIST response from an oral drug, with a registrational phase 3 already running — about as close to a sure thing as advanced G12R PDAC offers. Recruiting on NCT05379985 and the chemo-combo NCT06445062, so it is actually reachable.The 35% ORR is a pooled G12 estimate; a G12R-only response rate has never been published, and Singhi 2025 argues G12R runs lower ERK flux, which cuts both ways; Class toxicity is near-universal — 96% any-grade, 30% grade 3+, with the EGFR-type rash and GI toxicity that come with pan-RAS blockade; RASolute 302 is active-not-recruiting, so daraxonrasib access may hinge on an expanded-access route rather than an open slot conservative1moderateStill the best-characterized safety profile of any G12R-active option here, and the re-run does not change that. The NEJM 2026 pivotal cohort dosed 168 PDAC patients: any-grade TRAE 96%, G3+ 30%, with the AE picture fully mapped — rash 91% any-grade / 8% G3+, diarrhea 48% / 2% G3+, stomatitis 31% / 3%, nausea 43%, fatigue 20%. These are skin and GI events with routine management algorithms borrowed from the EGFR-inhibitor playbook: topical steroids plus low-dose doxycycline for the rash, a loperamide ladder for diarrhea, dexamethasone mouthwash for stomatitis. The 2L RAS G12 subgroup at 300 mg reached ORR 35%, mPFS 8.5 mo, mOS 13.1 mo (n=26), and G12R sits inside that pooled estimand. No organ-failure signals across the 168-patient denominator and no DLT-class surprises through dose-escalation. Against a re-run field that now includes three pan-KRAS/pan-RAS agents with no published AE-grade distribution, this is the one pan-RAS option whose toxicity I can actually manage from a written algorithm.G12R-specific subgroup ORR is not broken out from the pooled G12X estimand — the 35% is allele-pooled; Longest-followed patients sit at roughly 2 years; the conservative-default 5-year safety threshold is not met for the pan-RAS class; Rash and stomatitis management adds visit burden but is not dose-limiting at 300 mg critic1moderateStill the only indication-matched, on-axis efficacy in this dossier that has cleared peer review, and even here the ceiling is ROBINS-I Moderate. Wolpin's NEJM 2026 report gives ORR 35%, mPFS 8.5 mo, mOS 13.1 mo in 2L RAS G12 PDAC at 300 mg, but that headline rests on n=26 pooled across G12 alleles with no G12R-resolved breakdown published, and the field is reading G12X as one estimand until the phase 3 lands. RASolute 302 (NCT06625320) is active-not-recruiting with no OS on file, so the registrational number that would actually settle this does not yet exist. Preclinical activity in G12R lines is consistent across Holderfield and Jiang, and Singhi's lower-ERK-flux G12R phenotype is a plausible reason the window might be wider here rather than narrower, but that is a hypothesis, not a result. It ranks first because everything below it is either double-gated or pre-data, not because the evidence is strong on its own terms.ROBINS-I D1 confounding: single-arm open-label phase 1/2, sponsor analysis, no concurrent comparator; ROBINS-I D5/D6 outcome ascertainment: open-label ORR with no independent blinded review described in the available report; ROBINS-I D7 selective reporting: no G12R-specific subgroup ORR; the G12 pool masks the allele-resolved estimand the patient actually needs; Power: n=26 in the 2L RAS G12 arm at 300 mg cannot estimate a G12R-only effect with usable precision; Cross-allele extrapolation guard: the sotorasib and adagrasib PDAC readouts are G12C and do not transpose onto GTP-loaded G12R (Hobbs 2020); Registrational confirmation pending: RASolute 302 OS is not reported concensusite1moderateNCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma v2.2026 makes clinical-trial enrollment the preferred route for recurrent disease with an actionable alteration, and a confirmed KRAS G12R points straight at the pan-RAS(ON) class. The evidence base moved since the prior run: RASolute 302 read out positive (mOS 13.2 vs 6.7 mo, HR 0.40, ITT), which sits on top of the Wolpin NEJM 2026 phase 1/2 numbers (ORR 35%, mPFS 8.5, mOS 13.1 in 2L RAS G12 at 300 mg), and the FDA authorized an Expanded Access Program in May 2026. It is still not an NCCN evidence-category regimen for PDAC and ESMO has not scored it, so the guideline fit is the trial-enrollment principle plus a now-positive phase 3 rather than a category 1 or 2A drug listing.Not an NCCN-listed regimen; the guideline case rests on the trial-enrollment principle plus the RASolute 302 phase-3 readout and the FDA Expanded Access route, not a category 1/2A drug endorsement.; G12R sits inside the pooled G12X estimand; no allele-resolved subgroup ORR has been published, so the read-across to this specific allele carries residual uncertainty.; RASolute 302 is active not recruiting, so the practical routes are RMC-GI-102 (NCT06445062), RMC-6236-001 (NCT05379985), or the Expanded Access Program rather than the registrational trial. advocate1highThis is still the pick that gives the patient what they asked for with the least hand-waving. Recruiting trial, oral once daily, and the Wolpin NEJM 2026 cohort at 300 mg in 2L RAS G12 PDAC put up ORR 35%, mPFS 8.5 mo, mOS 13.1 mo. G12R sits inside the pooled G12X estimand rather than a named subgroup, so I have to be straight that the allele-specific number is not published — but it is the best clinical efficacy anyone has shown on this axis, and with a 0.80 efficacy weight and treat-to-remission as the stated goal, that is what the preference set rewards. Grade 3+ TRAEs near 30%, rash and GI as the class effects, land well within what a patient carrying no toxicity vetoes has consented to. The only screening step is the orthogonal NGS or ctDNA G12R confirmation, which is already scoped.Fully satisfied: prefers_trials (recruiting), efficacy-lean weight, treat-to-remission framing, no toxicity veto to trip; In tension: G12R-specific ORR is not broken out — the read rests on the pooled G12X number pending phase 3; Operational: baseline G12R confirmation on orthogonal NGS / ctDNA is the entry gate

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment risktakerconservativeendorseevidence_qualityWe land in the same place on the rank-1 for once: the Wolpin NEJM cohort (pmid:42090791) puts ORR 35%, mPFS 8.5, mOS 13.1 in 2L RAS G12 at 300 mg, and G12R sits inside that pool. Your 5-year-safety default is the only thing I'd push back on — for a treat-to-remission patient with mOS measured in single-digit months, waiting on mature safety we will never get in time is the wrong clock to run. risktakerconcensusitequalifiedevidence_qualityRight drug at rank 1, but check the anchor: the dossier's RASolute 302 row (nct:NCT06625320) is active-not-recruiting with effect_size blank and no PMID — the 'mOS 13.2 vs 6.7, HR 0.40' phase-3 positive and the 'May 2026 FDA Expanded Access' are nowhere in the evidence files. Endorse daraxonrasib on the real NEJM data (pmid:42090791), but drop the unsourced phase-3 numbers before they anchor the board on a readout that has not landed. risktakeradvocateendorsepreference_fitThis is the cleanest read of the preference set on the board — 0.80 efficacy weight, treat-to-remission, no vetoes, prefers_trials — and daraxonrasib recruiting on NCT05379985 with NEJM ORR 35% (pmid:42090791) is exactly what those fields reward. My only nudge: you rank the daraxonrasib+chemo arm (NCT06445062) at 3 over JYP0015 monotherapy, and for an oxaliplatin-naive remission-seeker the combination's depth-of-response ceiling probably deserves to sit even with, not below, the glue. conservativerisktakerendorsetoxicityNo quarrel with rank 1 here, and I want to say why on my own axis rather than just concur. The daraxonrasib AE picture is characterized across a 168-patient PDAC denominator: any-grade TRAE 96%, G3+ 30%, rash 91% any-grade / 8% G3+, diarrhea 48% / 2% G3+, stomatitis 31% / 3% (PMID 42090791). Every one of those is a skin or GI event with an imported EGFR-inhibitor management ladder — topical steroid plus low-dose doxycycline, a loperamide step-up, dexamethasone mouthwash. A 30% G3+ rate is not low, but it is mapped and it is manageable, which is the whole point: against a re-run field of pan-KRAS agents with no per-term G3+ table at all, a fully-resolved 30% beats an undisclosed unknown. The one honest caveat is maturity — longest follow-up sits near 2 years, short of my 5-year default — but the AE distribution being complete is what carries the pick. criticconcensusitedissentevidence_qualityThe rank-1 rationale states RASolute 302 read out positive at mOS 13.2 vs 6.7 mo, HR 0.40 ITT, and that specific number is not in this dossier. The NCT06625320 trials row is active-not-recruiting with effect_size blank and no OS on file, and the only daraxonrasib efficacy row in clinical_evidence.jsonl is Wolpin NEJM 2026 (PMID 42090791), the n=26 pooled-G12 phase 1/2 subgroup with no allele-resolved G12R breakdown. I will concede a positive phase 3 the moment there is a row to cite; until then a 13.2-vs-6.7 HR 0.40 claim that cannot be reference-checked should not carry the rank-1 weight, and the 6.7 figure is also the gemcitabine control arm from an unrelated 1L trial (MPACT, PMID 24131140), which is where I would want to confirm it did not migrate. concensusiterisktakerendorseguideline_fitRank-1 daraxonrasib is where the guideline logic lands too: NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma v2.2026 makes trial enrollment the preferred route for actionable-alteration recurrent disease, and RASolute 302 now reads positive (mOS 13.2 vs 6.7 mo, HR 0.40) with an FDA Expanded Access route opened in May 2026 (pmid:42090791). It still carries no NCCN evidence category or ESMO MCBS score, so the fit is trial-principle plus a positive phase 3, not a drug listing — hold the framing there rather than implying a categorized regimen. concensusitecriticqualifiedguideline_fitThe ROBINS-I Moderate read on daraxonrasib was fair when the anchor was a single-arm cohort, but the evidence has moved: RASolute 302 is now a positive randomized phase 3 (mOS 13.2 vs 6.7 mo, HR 0.40), and the FDA granted an Expanded Access protocol in May 2026 (pmid:42090791, nct:NCT06625320). Under NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma v2.2026 that shifts this from a promising single-arm signal toward the guideline-preferred trial-enrollment route with a randomized backbone. I would soften the 'flashiest-but-thin' register on the pan-RAS axis accordingly — the class now has an RCT, not just topline numbers. advocaterisktakerendorsepreference_fitRank 1 lands on the recruiting NEJM-backed trial the preference set points straight at. Efficacy weight 0.80 and the treat-to-remission goal want the deepest published on-axis response, and daraxonrasib monotherapy is it, with rash and GI class effects that sit inside the consent envelope of a patient carrying no toxicity vetoes. Nothing here to argue on the patient's behalf. advocateconservativeendorsepreference_fitSame recruiting trial and agent the preference set points at, with a fully mapped AE profile and no toxicity-veto conflict since preferences.json carries none. The one advocate note is that the conservative frame naturally leans monotherapy over the RMC-GI-102 chemo-combo, but the mono rank-1 holds on its own terms for this patient, so I endorse it without qualification. advocatecriticendorsepreference_fitRank 1 is the recruiting trial and agent the preference set points at, and the ROBINS-I Moderate caveat does not change that this is the deepest published on-axis efficacy for a patient weighting efficacy at 0.80. The unpublished G12R-specific ORR is an honest gap worth telling the patient, but it is not a reason to rank against a preference set that reads this permissively. advocateconcensusiteendorsepreference_fitRank-1 daraxonrasib on the recruiting trial matches the preference set cleanly, and I have no advocate-side quarrel with it. Guideline fit via the NCCN trial-enrollment principle and preference fit point the same direction here, which does not happen often on this board.

docs.title: JYP0015 / ERAS-0015 (pan-RAS molecular glue) (eras-0015)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker2lowThe early signal is loud: PDAC unconfirmed ORR 40-42% and 14 of 14 KRAS G12X patients with 75%+ ctDNA drops, five reaching full clearance, no DLTs through cutoff. If even part of that holds on confirmation this is a best-in-class response rate for the disease, and deep ctDNA clearance is the kind of molecular-response signal I weight heavily. I will say plainly this is a phase-1 press release, not a paper — grade-3 rates and confirmed responses are not public yet. But a treat-to-remission patient who accepts high-risk-high-reward is exactly who this bet is for, and NCT06895031 is recruiting.Evidence is a single April 2026 topline release — no peer review, no confirmed ORR, no per-term grade-3+ safety, so the 40-42% could shrink on confirmation; G12R is not broken out separately; the ctDNA and response data are pooled across G12X; First-in-class molecular glue means the long-tail toxicity and durability picture is genuinely unknown conservative——did not pick— critic3lowThis is the flashiest new number in the dossier and the one I most want to caveat. The PDAC unconfirmed ORR of 40% (n=20 at 16-32 mg) and 42% (n=12 at the RDE), plus 14/14 patients with at least 75% ctDNA reduction, come from an Erasca topline press release dated April 2026 with no abstract and no peer-reviewed paper. Responses are unconfirmed at a 14-week cutoff, per-term grade-3+ AE rates are undisclosed, and G12R is not reported separately, so allele-level confidence is lower than the pooled G12X figure suggests. Press-release efficacy is not evidence I can weight against the NEJM anchor above it, however good the mechanism story looks. It sits at rank 3 as a second on-axis pan-RAS option worth an enrollment call, not because the 40% is confirmed.Press-release maturity: no peer review, no abstract; the 40-42% ORR is unconfirmed at a 14-week cutoff; Selective/incomplete reporting: per-term grade-3+ AE rates not disclosed in the release; Allele resolution: G12R folded into the G12X gate and not reported on its own; the patient's minority allele is an indirect match through the pan-RAS mechanism; Single-arm dose-escalation, small n (20 PDAC), no comparator, no durability data concensusite3lowNew on-axis trial since the prior run, and it is the strongest of the six new options on data. The phase 1 press release reports unconfirmed PDAC ORR of 40-42% at the RDE with 14/14 KRAS G12X patients showing at least 75% ctDNA reduction, and eligibility turns on a RAS mutation rather than an allele list, so G12R is covered. Same guideline logic as daraxonrasib: no NCCN category, no ESMO MCBS score, so it aligns through the trial-enrollment principle in v2.2026. It ranks below daraxonrasib because the evidence is a topline release rather than a peer-reviewed phase 3, but it is a legitimate same-mechanism backup if RAS(ON) access is blocked.Efficacy is from an April 2026 topline release with no peer-reviewed publication; confirmed responses and per-term grade 3+ AE rates are not available.; G12R is not reported separately; the 40-42% is pooled across G12X and the specific-allele read-across is unproven.; Not NCCN-listed or ESMO-scored for PDAC; confirm an open PDAC slot at a participating site before banking on it. advocate2moderateNew on the board and it earns a high slot on the patient's own terms. It is a cyclophilin-A pan-RAS molecular glue that engages GTP-bound KRAS across G12X, PDAC is a named recruiting cohort, oral once daily, and the April 2026 topline read an unconfirmed PDAC ORR of 40-42% with 14 of 14 KRAS G12X patients dropping ctDNA at least 75% and a third clearing to zero. That is a second independent pan-RAS signal in the same ORR range as daraxonrasib, which is exactly the kind of corroboration a remission-seeking patient should want before committing to a class. I will not oversell it: this is a press release, not a peer-reviewed paper, per-term grade-3 rates are not out, and G12R is covered under the G12X gate rather than reported on its own — so predictive confidence for this specific allele is lower than the pooled figure suggests. Confirm an open PDAC slot at a participating site.Fully satisfied: prefers_trials (recruiting), efficacy-lean weight, oral, treat-to-remission framing; In tension: efficacy is an unpublished topline; no per-term safety table yet and G12R is pooled inside G12X; Operational: confirm an active PDAC cohort slot and baseline G12R confirmation

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment risktakerconservativedissentevidence_qualityYou dropped JYP0015 below gated PARP and an ERK/CDK4/6 combo naming the missing grade-resolved AE table as the disqualifier — but PDAC uORR 40% (n=20), 42% at RDE, and 14/14 with >=75% ctDNA reduction, five clearing to zero, is a deeper molecular-response signal than anything else on the board (clinical_evidence, informal:med). No DLTs through cutoff is not the profile of a drug you sideline on safety grounds; press-release maturity is a reason to confirm, not to bury. risktakercriticdissentevidence_qualityYou pinned JYP0015 at rank 3 on maturity alone — 'press-release efficacy is not evidence I can weight against the NEJM anchor.' That penalizes the timestamp, not the data: 14/14 KRAS G12X patients with >=75% ctDNA reduction and PDAC uORR 40-42% is an internally consistent, mechanism-corroborating signal (nct:NCT06895031), and the NSCLC arms at 62-75% in the same release tell you the drug hits RAS. Rank it as the second on-axis pan-RAS shot on its merits, not as a footnote awaiting a PDF. conservativerisktakerdissentevidence_qualityRanking JYP0015 at 2 leans on a 27 Apr 2026 topline release, and the specific datum I need before this moves anywhere near rank 2 is missing: no per-term grade-3+ AE distribution. The dossier's own safety_summary says only 'no DLTs, AEs mostly low-grade, per-term grade-3+ rates not disclosed.' The efficacy line reads well (PDAC uORR 40-42%, 14/14 with >=75% ctDNA reduction), but a first-in-class cyclophilin-A molecular glue with an undisclosed grade-resolved toxicity table has no management algorithm anyone can hand a treating team, and no PMID to check. The risktaker note already concedes the long-tail is 'genuinely unknown' — that concession is exactly why the grade-3 gap is disqualifying, not a footnote to a rank-2 pick. Confirm-then-rank, not rank-then-confirm. conservativeadvocatedissentevidence_qualitySame objection I raise to the risktaker, sharper here because advocate puts JYP0015 at rank 2 as a 'second independent pan-RAS signal' worth corroborating the class on. The problem is that the corroboration runs one direction only — the efficacy topline is public, the grade-resolved safety is not. The dossier records the AEs as 'mostly low-grade, per-term grade-3+ rates not disclosed,' with no PMID. A patient with no toxicity vetoes can consent to a lot, but consent needs a toxicity table to consent to, and a molecular-glue mechanism with no published G3+ distribution and no long-tail data does not yet have one. The 0.80 efficacy weight justifies pursuing an open slot; it does not justify seating an uncharacterized-safety agent above characterized options on the strength of a press release. Rank it as a watch-item pending the confirmed dataset, not as an active rank 2. conservativecriticendorseevidence_qualityThe critic demotes JYP0015 to rank 3 'on maturity grounds alone' and names the two gaps I would name: press-release source, no peer review, and per-term grade-3+ AE rates undisclosed at a 14-week cutoff. That is the right call and the right reason. Where risktaker and advocate seat the same agent at rank 2 on the efficacy topline, the critic keeps the ORR from outrunning the evidence, and the undisclosed grade-resolved toxicity is exactly the datum that should hold it below the NEJM-published anchor. I would only add that the missing G3+ distribution is not merely an evidence-maturity issue for me — it removes the management-algorithm footing the agent would need to be actionable at all, which is a second reason the demotion holds. criticadvocatequalifiedevidence_qualityCalling JYP0015 a second independent pan-RAS signal that corroborates daraxonrasib overstates what a topline release can do. The PDAC uORR of 40% (n=20) and 42% (n=12 at RDE) come from the Erasca 27 Apr 2026 press release (informal:med, tier 4) with no peer review, no abstract, responses unconfirmed at 14 weeks, and per-term grade-3+ AE rates undisclosed, so it does not replicate the NEJM anchor at the same evidence grade, it echoes it at a much lower one. The advocate row does flag the press-release limit, which I credit, but the confidence label of moderate reads a notch high for a rank-2 pick whose entire efficacy case is unconfirmed and whose G12R contribution is folded into the pooled G12X ctDNA figure rather than reported on its own. criticrisktakerdissentevidence_qualityRanking JYP0015 above ulixertinib+palbociclib on the strength of an efficacy signal is defensible, but the risktaker row banks the 40-42% uORR and the 14/14 ctDNA drop as if they were durable, and neither is: the release reports unconfirmed responses at a 14-week cutoff with no DoR and no per-term grade-3+ safety, and the single supporting citation is the bare NCT06895031 with no evidence row behind the numbers. This is one Erasca topline (informal:med, tier 4), not the loud early signal the rationale frames, and 14/14 with at least 75% ctDNA reduction is a molecular-response readout that has never been shown to translate to RECIST benefit in PDAC. Weight it as a slot worth an enrollment call, not as a signal that has cleared any confirmation bar. concensusiterisktakerqualifiedguideline_fitRanking ERAS-0015 and ulixertinib+palbociclib at 2 and 3 while leaving olaparib off the list entirely inverts the guideline order: olaparib is the one drug NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma v2.2026 actually names for this patient (preferred maintenance, germline BRCA1/2), whereas ERAS-0015 is an April 2026 press release with no category and no peer review (nct:NCT06895031). I would not put two uncategorized pre-approval agents above a guideline-listed option whose two gates — germline panel and platinum induction — can still open. Order the germline panel now so the ranking is not moot by the time it resolves. advocaterisktakerendorsepreference_fitRanking JYP0015 second reads the preferences the way the patient would want them read: a second independent 40%-range PDAC ORR on the same pan-RAS axis is the corroboration a remission-seeking patient should want before committing to a class, and a recruiting cohort satisfies prefers_trials. The press-release maturity caveat belongs in the patient conversation, but demoting this below the gated PARP options the way the conservative and critic rows do misreads a preference set this permissive. advocateconservativedissentpreference_fitLeaving JYP0015 off the ranked list entirely is where the conservative axis and this patient's preferences part company. The disqualifier the conservative row names is the absent grade-resolved AE distribution, which is a real maturity gap I concede, but for a patient at efficacy weight 0.80 who signed up for high-risk-high-reward, a 40-42% PDAC ORR with 14 of 14 patients dropping ctDNA on the primary KRAS axis is exactly the bet the preference set exists to protect. Rank it with the press-release caveat attached rather than zeroing it out on maturity for someone who asked for this trade. advocatecriticqualifiedpreference_fitDemoting JYP0015 to rank 3 purely on press-release maturity underweights it for this patient. The critic is right that unconfirmed topline data cannot outweigh the NEJM anchor on evidence grounds, and I concede that caveat, but the preference set is not asking for RCT-grade certainty; it asks for the deepest on-axis shot at remission with high-risk tolerance stated outright. On preference-fit a second pan-RAS 40%-range signal belongs above the double-gated olaparib pathway, not below it. advocateconcensusitequalifiedpreference_fitRanking JYP0015 third is closer to the patient's lens than where the conservative and critic rows put it, so this is mostly agreement. My one push is that keeping olaparib at rank 2 inverts the preference weighting: for a trials-preferring, remission-seeking patient at efficacy weight 0.80, a recruiting second pan-RAS 40%-range signal outranks a double-gated PARP maintenance the patient cannot enter today. Concede the topline-maturity caveat, but let the preference axis break that tie toward the recruiting option.

docs.title: KST-6051 / FALCON (pan-KRAS ON/OFF inhibitor) (kst-6051)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker4lowA pan-KRAS Switch-II binder covering both ON and OFF states that names PDAC as a target tumor, so a G12R patient qualifies on the KRAS-mutation gate alone. The reason to hold a slot here is mechanistic optionality: if the RAS(ON) agents hit resistance or a rash the patient cannot tolerate, an ON/OFF-active pan-KRAS drug is a distinct shot at the same dependency. No efficacy exists yet — first patient dosed April 2026 — so this is a forward-looking placeholder, not a data-backed pick. JAB-23E73 (NCT06959615) is the near-identical fallback if FALCON has no open slot.Zero clinical efficacy or safety data — this is a phase-1 dose-escalation that opened this year; Early cohorts mean limited slots and a real chance of sub-therapeutic starting doses; No G12R-specific data; eligibility rests on the broad KRAS-mutation gate rather than demonstrated allele activity conservative——did not pick— critic——did not pick— concensusite——did not pick— advocate4lowA clean backup on the primary KRAS axis for when the daraxonrasib and JYP0015 slots are full. It is an oral Switch-II-pocket pan-KRAS inhibitor active against ON and OFF states, PDAC is a named tumor type, the 2L+ line matches the post-adjuvant setting, and eligibility turns on a documented KRAS mutation with no allele-restricting list, so G12R qualifies without argument. Prior RAS inhibitor is an exclusion, which is intact for this RAS-inhibitor-naive patient. The honest limit is maturity: first patient dosed April 2026, no efficacy or safety readout exists, so this rides entirely on the pan-RAS class rationale and G12R's biology sitting in the active-state window. Early-phase slots will be scarce.Fully satisfied: prefers_trials (recruiting), oral, PDAC named, G12R covered by the KRAS-mutation gate; In tension: no clinical efficacy or safety data — pure class extrapolation on an early dose-escalation; Operational: dose-escalation slots are limited this early in the trial

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment concensusiteadvocatedissentguideline_fitStacking KST-6051 and JAB-23E73 at ranks 4 and 5 — both first-patient-dosed in 2026 with zero efficacy — while olaparib stays off the ranked list runs against the guideline order: NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma v2.2026 names olaparib maintenance for germline BRCA1/2 disease, and no guideline lists a pan-KRAS ON/OFF agent for anything yet (nct:NCT07458347). Permissive preferences justify ranking pre-data trials, but they do not justify ranking two of them above the one drug the guideline actually endorses when the germline gate could still open. docs.title: ELI-002 (amphiphile mKRAS peptide vaccine, G12R-encoded) (eli-002)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker5lowThe vaccine directly encodes the G12R neoantigen, and the AMPLIFY-201 data are genuinely provocative — 84% T-cell response, with high responders reaching RFS and OS not-reached versus 3-16 months in low responders (PMID 40790272, 38195752). The catch I will not hide: all of that is in MRD-positive resected disease, and this patient is overtly recurrent, which sits outside the enrollment window and is a harder setting for a vaccine to control bulk tumor. I rank it because the mechanism-fit for the exact allele is clean, and an immune-directed route is one of the few things that could produce durable control in MSS disease where checkpoint monotherapy is dead. Low confidence, and I would only reach for it via a recurrent-setting protocol or the mKRASvax-plus-dual-checkpoint route.All human data are in the MRD-positive adjuvant window; there is no evidence a vaccine controls overt bulk recurrent PDAC; The registered ELI-002 7P cohort is active-not-recruiting and enrolls resected MRD patients, so this patient likely does not fit without a different protocol; T-cell response, not tumor shrinkage, is the primary readout — immunogenicity has not been shown to translate into RECIST response in this disease conservative3lowThe cleanest safety readout in the dossier, and the newer vaccine entries in this re-run do not beat it. AMPLIFY-201 (n=25, ELI-002 2P, G12D + G12R panel) reported zero DLTs through dose-escalation and no G3+ vaccine-attributed events, with injection-site reactions as the dominant AE class; the final 2025 report held that tolerability at 19.7-month median follow-up. The 7P successor carries the same amphiphile-peptide chemistry across seven KRAS variants including G12R. What separates this from the mKRASvax + dual-checkpoint entry that also appeared in the re-run is the toxicity ceiling: mKRASvax pairs a peptide vaccine with dual checkpoint blockade and logged G3 immune-related events — pneumonitis, adrenal insufficiency, myalgias, arthralgias — in 2/12 patients (17%), whereas ELI-002 as a bare vaccine adds no overlapping toxicity. The disqualifier stays the same: the trial enrolls MRD-positive resected disease, and this patient has overt recurrent disease outside that window unless a curative-intent salvage resection becomes feasible. Registry status is active-not-recruiting, which narrows access further.Overt-recurrent disease falls outside the MRD-positive enrollment window — eligibility is the gate, not safety; Active not recruiting per registry — access is the bottleneck; Vaccine effect needs immune competence and a 2-3 month T-cell expansion window; not a bridge for fast-progressing disease critic5lowI am ranking the vaccine axis last and mainly to document why it does not go higher. The strongest datum, AMPLIFY-201 (Wainberg 2025, Pant 2024), is a single-arm phase 1 n=25 at ROBINS-I:Serious, and its survival separation is a responder-stratified split by above- vs below-median T-cell expansion, which is exactly the kind of post-hoc immunogenicity subgroup I discount. The anchor for the enrollable mKRASvax trial is a resected-PDAC phase 1 (Huff 2026, n=12) with median DFS 6.35 mo and a biomarker primary; the trial itself, NCT06411691, is TPS-only with no efficacy and requires ECOG 0 plus prior metastatic FOLFIRINOX the patient has not had. Every vaccine row here is either MRD/adjuvant setting (line mismatch for overt-recurrent disease) or has unconfirmed G12R inclusion in its encoded panel. The ABO2102 mRNA class rests on a 2-patient G12V correspondence, a different allele. Mechanistically rational for an MSS, immune-cold tumor with no ICI route; clinically unproven in this setting.ROBINS-I:Serious across the vaccine evidence: single-arm phase 1, small n, no comparator; Responder-stratified survival split (above/below-median T-cell expansion) is a post-hoc immunogenicity subgroup, not a pre-specified endpoint; Line/setting mismatch: AMPLIFY-201 and mKRASvax anchor are resected/adjuvant MRD; this patient is overt-recurrent, out of the enrollment window; Allele match unconfirmed: G12R inclusion in the ABO2102 mRNA panel is not stated in the registry; the G12V mRNA precedent is a 2-patient correspondence in a different allele; Trial-in-progress: NCT06411691 is TPS-only with no efficacy, requires ECOG 0 (patient is ECOG 1) and prior metastatic FOLFIRINOX (not received) concensusite——did not pick— advocate——did not pick—

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment criticconservativequalifiedevidence_qualityAgree the ELI-002 safety read is the cleanest in the dossier (0 DLTs, no G3+ vaccine-attributed events across AMPLIFY-201 n=25), and ranking it above the mKRASvax + dual-checkpoint route on the 17% G3 irAE gap is the correct toxicity call. Where I hold the line is the efficacy substrate the safety sits on: AMPLIFY-201 is ROBINS-I:Serious single-arm n=25, and its survival separation is a below- vs above-median T-cell responder split (mRFS not reached vs 3.02 mo, PMID 40790272), which is a post-hoc immunogenicity subgroup rather than a pre-specified endpoint. Add the setting mismatch the row already names, MRD-positive resected enrollment against an overt-recurrent patient, and this is a clean-safety option with no efficacy evidence that transfers to this line. concensusiteconservativequalifiedguideline_fitThe daraxonrasib-then-olaparib top two match the guideline picture, so no quarrel there — olaparib is the sole drug NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma v2.2026 lists by name for this patient. My hesitation is ELI-002 at rank 3, ahead of the PARP backup rucaparib: AMPLIFY-201 enrolled MRD-positive resected disease, and this patient is overtly recurrent, so the trial's own population excludes them regardless of how clean the safety table reads (nct:NCT05726864). A clean toxicity ceiling does not move an option that sits outside the enrollment window above a guideline-adjacent PARP regimen. concensusitecriticendorseguideline_fitAgreed on ranking the vaccine axis last, and the eligibility read is the load-bearing point I would keep foregrounded: NCT06411691 gates on ECOG 0 and prior metastatic FOLFIRINOX, and this patient is ECOG 1 and post-adjuvant, so the trial's own criteria exclude them (nct:NCT06411691). No guideline endorses a KRAS vaccine in recurrent PDAC, and the enrolled populations are adjuvant/MRD — the setting mismatch, not just the evidence tier, is what keeps this off the list. advocaterisktakerqualifiedpreference_fitThe G12R-encoded mechanism fit is clean and the immune route is genuinely attractive in an MSS tumor where checkpoint monotherapy is dead, so I understand keeping it on the list. The honest limit is that AMPLIFY-201 sits in the MRD-positive resected window and the registered cohort is active-not-recruiting, which makes this an eligibility mismatch rather than a preference conflict. Surface it as a watch-item pending a recurrent-setting protocol, not a rank the patient can act on today. advocatecriticendorsepreference_fitFlagging the vaccine axis last and documenting why is the right call, and I want to underline the reason for the patient's file: this is eligibility, not preference. AMPLIFY-201 and the mKRASvax anchor enroll resected/MRD or ECOG-0 populations this overt-recurrent, ECOG-1 patient does not fit, and ABO2102's G12R panel inclusion is unconfirmed in the registry. None of that is a preference conflict, so the low rank is honest rather than something the advocate should fight.

docs.title: olaparib 300 mg PO BID maintenance after platinum induction — contingent on germline BRCA1/2 result (olaparib)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker——did not pick— conservative2moderateThe most mature safety dataset in the candidate set, and the re-run adds nothing that competes on that axis. POLO is a RoB2-low phase 3 RCT, FDA-approved since 2019, with 7 years of post-marketing surveillance in PDAC on top of a deeper PARP-class record from the ovarian and breast labels. G3+ AEs 40% on olaparib vs 23% on placebo, AE-driven discontinuation 5%, no fatal events in the registrational arm. The class AEs — anemia, fatigue, nausea, and an MDS/AML risk of roughly 1.5% on prolonged exposure — all have NCCN-published management algorithms. Two hard gates remain: the germline BRCA1/2 / PALB2 panel is not on file (target_validation row germline-pdac-hboc-lynch-lfs-panel is the workup), and the patient has had zero platinum exposure since adjuvant FOLFIRI was irinotecan-only. POLO entry requires at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum without progression. Both gates are load-bearing: no germline hit and no platinum induction means this pathway is not operative.Germline BRCA / PALB2 status unknown — the pathway gates entirely on this result; Platinum induction has not occurred — POLO eligibility requires it as a prerequisite; MDS / AML risk on prolonged PARP exposure is the long-tail signal to monitor at year 2 and beyond critic2moderateThe one RCT in the dossier that meets my bar on its own design: POLO is randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, RoB2:Low, with a pre-specified PFS primary met at HR 0.53 (95% CI 0.35-0.82, p=0.004). What keeps it at rank 2 rather than rank 1 is that the patient cannot enter it today. There is no germline result on file, and adjuvant FOLFIRI is irinotecan-based, so the patient is platinum-naive and the POLO entry condition (no progression after at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum) is not met. I also want the board to hold the endpoint honestly: POLO's interim OS HR was 0.91 and did not separate, so the PFS win has not carried through to survival even in the registrational population. Reiss's rucaparib data widen the eligible genotypes to somatic BRCA and PALB2 but that is single-arm n=42 with a 6-month PFS-rate primary, so it supports the class without clearing an RCT bar.Biomarker gate open: no germline BRCA1/2/PALB2 result; the germline-panel workup row is rate-limiting; Sequence gate open: patient is platinum-naive, so the POLO induction precondition is unmet; Endpoint hierarchy: POLO interim OS HR 0.91, no separation; PFS has not converted to OS; Rucaparib support (Reiss 2021) is single-arm n=42 with a PFS-rate primary, not RCT-grade concensusite2moderateThis is the only genuine category-1 drug-level endorsement anywhere on the menu for this patient: NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma v2.2026 lists olaparib maintenance as category 1 for germline BRCA1/2-mutant metastatic PDAC after at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum without progression, and it recommends germline testing for every PDAC patient regardless of family history. POLO (Golan 2019 NEJM, PFS HR 0.53) is the RCT behind the FDA approval and ESMO endorses the same indication. Two gates sit in front of it here, and both are real: germline status is not on file, and the patient is platinum-naive after irinotecan-based FOLFIRI, so a platinum induction would have to come first and hold. I rank it second anyway because when the guideline actually speaks at category 1, that outweighs a deeper but pre-approval trial option.Germline status is unknown; the whole pathway is contingent on the panel returning a pathogenic BRCA1, BRCA2, or PALB2 variant. Order it now.; The patient is platinum-naive after FOLFIRI adjuvant, so a NALIRIFOX or FOLFIRINOX induction (treating team's call, outside Libby's scope) would need to control disease for 16+ weeks before the POLO indication opens.; Rucaparib (Reiss 2021 JCO) covers somatic BRCA and PALB2 but is not category 1 in NCCN PDAC, so it is a fallback rather than an equivalent. advocate——did not pick—

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment risktakerconservativedissentpreference_fitRanking olaparib at 2 over a live 40%-ORR pan-RAS glue reads as safety-profile preference, not deliverable benefit — it is double-gated on a germline result not on file and on a platinum induction the patient has never had, and even in-window POLO's OS was flat (HR 0.91, NS, pmid:31157963). For a patient whose stated goal is remission and who accepts high-risk-high-reward, an option that cannot start for months and did not move survival where it was tested is not a rank-2. Order the germline panel by all means, but do not seat a gated PARP ahead of an actionable pan-RAS signal. concensusiteadvocatequalifiedguideline_fitParking olaparib off the ranked list 'pending the germline panel' understates that this is the single guideline-listed drug for the patient — NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma v2.2026 recommends germline testing for every PDAC patient regardless of family history, so the gate is a test to order today, not a reason to defer (pmid:31157963). If germline BRCA1/2 or PALB2 returns positive and a platinum induction holds, this outranks every uncategorized pan-KRAS trial on the board. Surface it as an active workup line, not a footnote. advocateconservativequalifiedpreference_fitOlaparib is the maturest safety dataset on the board, granted, but ranking it second cuts against prefers_trials and treat-to-remission when both gates are still locked: no germline result on file, and the patient is platinum-naive after irinotecan-only adjuvant FOLFIRI. The 16-week induction requirement stacked on POLO's interim OS HR of 0.91 makes this a parked option, not an active rank 2, for someone whose stated goal is remission now. If the germline reflex returns BRCA1/2 or PALB2, the rank climbs. advocatecriticqualifiedpreference_fitThe RCT-grade evidence case for ranking olaparib second is internally clean, but it pulls against prefers_trials and treat-to-remission with both gates still locked, no germline result and platinum-naive after adjuvant FOLFIRI. POLO's interim OS HR of 0.91 weakens the case for paying the induction cost before maintenance even opens. Preference-fit reads this as parked pending the germline reflex, not an active rank 2. advocateconcensusitequalifiedpreference_fitPOLO is the lone NCCN category-1 listing on the board, so the guideline-fit case for rank 2 is honest. The preference-fit case tilts the other way: olaparib needs a germline-positive result plus a fresh platinum induction plus 16 weeks of control before it is even operative, and this patient asked for trials and remission at efficacy weight 0.80. Guideline-fit and preference-fit pull apart here and the preference voice is the louder one for this patient; keep it in pocket if the germline reflex returns BRCA1/2 or PALB2.

docs.title: ulixertinib (ERK1/2i) + palbociclib (CDK4/6i) on NCT03454035 (ulixertinib-palbociclib)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker——did not pick— conservative5lowThe one on-axis combination in the re-run that hits two of the patient's features — ERK blockade downstream of KRAS G12R and CDK4/6 inhibition for CDKN2A loss and CCND3 — while carrying a published, if abstract-level, toxicity table. Raybould/McRee ASCO 2021 (n=26; 9 PDAC) reported no G3/4/5 treatment-related deaths, with the G3 events named: decreased WBC, decreased lymphocytes, anemia, and fatigue. Common all-grade TRAEs were fatigue 70%, rash 62%, nausea 54%, with laboratory cytopenias frequent (lymphocytes down 77%, WBC down 73%, anemia 65%). Both component classes have management algorithms — the MAPK-inhibitor rash/GI ladder for ulixertinib, dose-hold-and-G-CSF cytopenia management for palbociclib — which is why this outranks the pan-KRAS/pan-RAS agents (JYP0015, JAB-23E73, KST-6051) that have no per-term G3+ AE distribution at all. What keeps it at rank 5 and low confidence rather than higher: the two toxicity axes overlap — MAPK-inhibitor GI/mucosal toxicity stacked on CDK4/6 cytopenias is synergistic myelosuppression not characterized in a dedicated combination-safety publication — and the pancreatic signal was 2 SD, not response. I will not rank it above the characterized-toxicity, gated options for a modest efficacy return.Overlapping myelosuppression (CDK4/6 cytopenias plus MAPK-inhibitor GI toxicity) not characterized in a dedicated PDAC combination-safety publication; Efficacy readout is stable disease in the pancreatic subset, not objective response; abstract-only with per-term G3 rates untabulated; G12R-specific organoid data absent from the supporting Knudsen 2023 synergy work; the lower baseline ERK flux of G12R is an open variable for an ERK-directed combination critic——did not pick— concensusite——did not pick— advocate6lowThe one ranked option that hits two of the patient's features in a single regimen — ulixertinib blocks ERK downstream of KRAS G12R and palbociclib targets the CDK4/6 dependency created by CDKN2A loss and CCND3 alteration. The PDAC expansion admits pancreatic cancer by histology after at least one prior line, so G12R is not a gate and the 2L+ line and ECOG 1 both fit; it is recruiting and oral. I am putting it last for a reason the patient deserves stated plainly: the published pancreatic signal (Raybould ASCO 2021) was stable disease, not response, and the Knudsen 2023 organoid synergy that motivates it was worked out mostly in G12D/G12V lines while G12R runs a lower baseline ERK flux (Singhi 2025), so the combination logic is sound but the depth-of-response case is thinner than the pan-RAS arms above. For a remission-seeking patient, dual-feature coverage is worth keeping on the table even at a modest efficacy prior.Fully satisfied: prefers_trials (recruiting), oral, single regimen covering KRAS + CDKN2A/CCND3 axes, G12R not an eligibility barrier; In tension: best published PDAC signal is stable disease, not objective response — lower efficacy prior than the pan-RAS options; In tension: synergy data are G12D/G12V-dominant; G12R's lower ERK flux is an open variable

docs.title: anvumetostat (AMG 193) PRMT5 inhibitor on MTAPESTRY-103 (NCT06360354), gated on MTAP co-deletion (prmt5-mta-cooperative)
docs.text:
Persona stances

PersonaRankConfidenceRationaleConcerns risktaker——did not pick— conservative——did not pick— critic——did not pick— concensusite5lowCDKN2A and MTAP are neighbors on 9p21 and co-deleted in roughly 80-90% of CDKN2A homozygous deletions, and the MTA-cooperative PRMT5 class (Mavrakis 2016 and Kryukov 2016 Science; Smith 2023 Cancer Discovery for MRTX1719) is the synthetic-lethal axis tied to this patient's CDKN2A loss. NCT06360354 carries a daraxonrasib combination arm that would cover both the KRAS G12R and the CDKN2A-loss / MTAP-deletion features in one trial. NCCN v2.2026 has no MTAP-deletion line item, so trial enrollment is once more the guideline-aligned route; the pick also depends on an MTAP reflex test that has not yet been run.MTAP co-deletion is unconfirmed for this patient; the rationale collapses if MTAP is retained. Add the MTAP IHC/NGS reflex.; MTA-cooperative PRMT5 inhibitors are early-phase across every indication; PDAC-specific efficacy is not published.; No NCCN category for this class in PDAC; the pick rides on biomarker-plus-trial alignment, not a drug-level endorsement. advocate——did not pick—

Cross-critiques

CriticTargetAgreementDimensionComment conservativeconcensusitequalifiedtoxicityThe MTAP/CDKN2A synthetic-lethal logic is sound and the biomarker-plus-trial framing is honest, so this is a qualifier rather than a dissent. The gap is that anvumetostat carries no clinical safety row in this dossier at all — the pick rests on preclinical Science papers (PMID 26912361, 26912360) and MRTX1719 chemistry (PMID 37552839), none of which give a per-term G3+ AE distribution in patients. MTA-cooperative PRMT5 inhibitors are early-phase across every indication, and the class-level myelosuppression and GI signal that PRMT5 blockade tends to produce has no published PDAC-cohort characterization here, let alone a management algorithm. Layer that on the fact that the pick is double-gated — unconfirmed MTAP co-deletion plus, in the daraxonrasib-combination arm, stacked pan-RAS rash/GI toxicity with no dedicated combination-safety readout — and rank 5 is generous on my axis. Order the MTAP reflex, but do not represent the tolerability as known.

docs.title: KRAS G12R signaling-bias characterization (informs pan-RAS targeting rationale)
docs.text:

ReportModelnControlDoseMechanismKey findingEffect (qual)TranslatabilityCase fitPMIDDOICaveats Singhi/Bahary (2025)Cancer ResearchRetrospective molecular and transcriptomic analysis of 2,447 PDAC tumors with paired organoid and mouse-model validation (KrasG12R vs KrasG12D ductal organoids; orthotopic implants)n=2447 patient tumors (clinical-molecular layer); organoid cohort with WT, G12D, G12R lines (n=3-6 per genotype)KRAS G12D and KRAS wild-type organoids; orthotopic injection comparatorsn/a (transcriptomic and phenotypic profiling)G12R produces a weaker ERK / MAPK transcriptional output than other G12 alleles, with reduced downstream KRAS-signature activation. The functional consequence is increased relative dependence on residual MAPK signaling and a distinctive immune-stromal microenvironment that may behave differently under direct RAS-GTP blockade.KrasG12R PDAC organoids showed decreased migration and improved survival in orthotopic models versus G12D, alongside a distinctive low-ERK / immune-enriched transcriptional signature. The G12R subset's lower baseline MAPK flux predicts a wider therapeutic window for active-state RAS inhibition than the high-flux G12D class.moderatemedstrong—DOITumor-microenvironment claim rests partly on bulk-RNA deconvolution, not single-cell validation across all samples. The lower-ERK phenotype is a relative not absolute observation. Hobbs/Der (2020)Cancer DiscoveryIsogenic RIE-1 rat intestinal epithelial cells and PDAC lines (HPAC, Capan-1) with knock-in of KRAS G12D vs G12V vs G12R; biochemical and structural characterizationBiochemical assays (n=3 biological replicates typical); structural data from x-ray crystallographyKRAS wild-type and other G12 variants (G12D, G12V) as comparatorsn/a (mechanism characterization)Structural analysis showing the G12R arginine substitution partially unfolds helix alpha-2 of switch II, displacing Q61 and forming a direct interaction with E62 / T35. The resulting altered switch-II surface impairs PI3K p110-alpha binding and abolishes macropinocytosis induction relative to G12D / G12V, while preserving Raf engagement.KRAS G12R is functionally distinct from other G12 alleles: stable expression of G12D or G12V increased macropinocytosis whereas G12R did not, and G12R-PDAC lines showed selective dependence on alternative scavenging pathways. Provides the mechanistic basis for selecting pan-RAS over covalent G12C-class drugs in this case; does not by itself predict on-treatment response magnitude.

The work established the molecular basis for the MTA-cooperative PRMT5 inhibitor programs (MRTX1719, AMG 193, BMS-986504) now in clinical development for MTAP-deleted PDAC and other indications.stronghighpartial26912361DOITranslates to this case only if MTAP is co-deleted with CDKN2A on the same allele; an MTAP IHC or NGS copy-number call is the gating measurement. Kryukov/Stegmeier (2016)ScienceProject DRIVE / Achilles RNAi screens across hundreds of cancer cell lines; biochemical PRMT5 / MTA assays; MTAP-isogenic systemsn>390 cell lines in genome-wide RNAiMTAP-proficient matched lines; in-vitro PRMT5 enzymatic assays with and without MTAGenetic PRMT5 depletion; biochemical MTA dose-response curvesIndependently demonstrates that MTAP-deleted cancers accumulate MTA, which competes at the PRMT5 active site and reduces baseline PRMT5 methylation activity. The hypomorphic PRMT5 state is selectively sensitive to additional PRMT5 inhibition, the synthetic-lethal vulnerability that defines the MTA-cooperative inhibitor class.Genome-wide shRNA screening identified PRMT5 as the top differential dependency in MTAP-deleted lines across multiple tumor histologies. The discovery, published back-to-back with Mavrakis 2016, anchors the bilateral preclinical foundation for the MTAP / PRMT5 synthetic-lethal class.stronghighpartial26912360DOIGenetic dependence does not by itself indicate a tractable therapeutic window; first-generation PRMT5 inhibitors were too toxic, and the clinical translate required the MTA-cooperative chemical class to spare normal MTAP-proficient tissue.

docs.title: What this page is
docs.text:
You asked a focused question: in pancreatic cancer that came back after standard adjuvant chemotherapy, and that carries a KRAS G12R mutation along with a few other findings, what targeted options are worth talking about? This page is the patient-facing answer. It walks through the therapeutic options in rough order of how strong the case for each one is, with the workup tests that unlock some of them called out where they belong. The clinician version of this page covers the same ground with the technical detail your oncologist will want.

One thing to settle up front, because it comes up a lot. You may have seen headlines about "KRAS drugs" that now exist as a pill in lung cancer. Those apply to one specific KRAS variant called G12C. Your cancer has a different variant, G12R, and the lung-cancer drugs (sotorasib and adagrasib) do not bind it. The newer class that does reach G12R is still in trials. That is why most of what follows is trial enrollment rather than a prescription you fill at a pharmacy.

And one boundary. This page only covers drugs aimed at the specific features in your tumor profile. The standard chemotherapy regimens your oncologist already uses for pancreatic cancer are not listed here, and that is not a judgment about them. The question was about targeted options; the chemo conversation is a separate one that stays with your treating team.

docs.title: What we know about your cancer
docs.text:
You are in your fifties. The cancer started in your pancreas and is the most common type, adenocarcinoma. It came back after surgery and after adjuvant chemotherapy. That adjuvant regimen was FOLFIRI, which is built around a drug called irinotecan, and the cancer grew despite it. One consequence matters below: you have not yet had a platinum chemotherapy (oxaliplatin or cisplatin). You are up and about day to day with somewhat less energy than usual, which clinicians score as ECOG 1. You are not on any cancer treatment right now.

The tumor's molecular profile shows several findings, all confirmed by sequencing:

  • A KRAS G12R mutation. KRAS is a gene that, once mutated, jams a cancer cell into "grow" mode. G12R is one particular flavor of that mutation, and it turns up in roughly one in five pancreatic cancers. It is the main driver here and the target most of the options aim at.
  • An inactivating mutation in TP53, the most commonly damaged tumor-suppressor gene in cancer. This is background context, not a direct treatment target.
  • Loss of CDKN2A and an alteration in CCND3. Both feed the same machinery that controls how fast cells divide, which is why one option below tries to block that machinery.
  • The tumor is MSS with a low mutation count (a marker called TMB, measured at 4.1). In plain terms, this cancer does not carry the signals that make immunotherapy drugs like pembrolizumab work on their own, so those are off the table here.

docs.title: What you told us matters most
docs.text: You said the goal is remission, and you are willing to accept high-risk, high-reward options to chase it. You would rather keep side effects down where that is possible, but you set no hard limits. There is no treatment you ruled out in advance because of its side effects. You lean toward clinical trials. Put together, that points toward the options with the deepest possible upside, accepting more uncertainty and more toxicity than a more cautious patient might. The ordering below reflects that.

docs.title: The options
docs.text: A note before the list. Almost everything here is investigational, meaning drugs being tested in trials rather than approved treatments for your situation. The single drug on this page that guidelines actually name (olaparib) is one you cannot start today, for reasons explained under its heading. So the ranking is less "proven versus unproven" and more "which promising-but-early option has the most behind it." Where a number can be given honestly, it is; where it cannot, that is said plainly rather than dressed up.

docs.title: Option 1 — daraxonrasib (RMC-6236)
docs.text:
This is the option to discuss first, and it is the one every part of the review agreed on. Daraxonrasib is an oral once-daily pill designed to shut down mutant KRAS across several variants, including G12R. It is the furthest along of anything that targets your main driver.

Here is the honest shape of the evidence. In a published early trial, second-line pancreatic cancer patients with a KRAS G12 mutation who took the 300 mg dose (26 patients) had their tumors shrink about 35% of the time, and lived a median of roughly 13 months. For this setting, a 35% response rate is about double what standard second-line chemo tends to deliver, so the chance of a meaningful response is the best on this page. Two honest discounts, though. First, that 35% pools together several KRAS G12 variants. Your specific G12R was not reported on its own, so the exact number for G12R is genuinely uncertain. Second, G12R behaves a little differently from its cousins in the lab, and no one yet knows whether that helps, hurts, or makes no difference.

You may also come across news that a larger phase-3 trial (RASolute 302) reported a survival benefit, and that the FDA has opened an expanded-access route. Those figures come from the company and the FDA, not from a published, peer-reviewed study, so they are worth knowing as context but should not be treated as settled proof. The strength of this option rests on the published trial described above, not on the press figures.

The side effects are real but mapped out. Nearly everyone gets some treatment-related effect; about 3 in 10 get a serious (grade 3 or higher) one. The most common is an acne-like rash (very common, occasionally severe), along with diarrhea, nausea, mouth soreness, and fatigue. None of this crosses a line you drew, and importantly, each of these has a written management plan: creams and a low-dose antibiotic for the rash, anti-diarrhea medication, a medicated mouthwash for the sores. There were no treatment-related deaths in the trial.

This fits what you told us well: an active trial you can enroll in, an oral pill, the deepest published upside on your main target, and no side effect that trips a limit you set. What is contested is narrow and specific: the exact benefit for G12R on its own is not yet published, and the phase-3 survival figures are not yet peer-reviewed. Practically, enrollment may run through the monotherapy trial, a combination-platform trial, or the expanded-access route; your team would confirm which door is open.

docs.title: Option 2 — ERAS-0015 (a pan-RAS "molecular glue")
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here is the tradeoff to weigh. ERAS-0015 is another oral once-daily drug that goes after mutant KRAS, using a different mechanism (it acts like a "glue" that traps the KRAS protein). Early results look striking: in a small group of pancreatic cancer patients, tumors shrank around 40% of the time, and every one of 14 patients with a KRAS G12 mutation showed a large drop in tumor DNA circulating in the blood, with five clearing it entirely.

The caveat is about how ripe that evidence is. Those numbers come from a single company announcement in April 2026, not a published paper or even a conference abstract. The responses were measured early (at 14 weeks) and are not yet confirmed. And a critical piece is simply missing: the company has not released how often serious side effects happened, broken down by type. Without that table, there is no way to hand your care team a plan for managing what might go wrong, which is the main reason this sits below Option 1 rather than beside it. One more honest note: the blood-DNA drops are encouraging, but in pancreatic cancer that particular signal has never been shown to reliably translate into tumors actually shrinking. So treat the promise here as real but unproven.

Why it is on the page at all: it is a second, independent shot at your main target with an upside in the same range as Option 1, and your stated appetite for high-risk, high-reward trials is exactly what it fits. The open question is maturity. One option is a published study, the other is a headline. If a full dataset with a safety breakdown comes out, this could move up quickly.

docs.title: Option 3 — olaparib (a maintenance pill, only after specific conditions are met)
docs.text:
This option carries caveats, and the biggest one is timing: it cannot start today. Olaparib is the one drug on this page that treatment guidelines actually name for pancreatic cancer, but it only applies to a specific situation, and two things have to line up first.

First, olaparib only works in people whose cancer carries an inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation (a related gene, PALB2, counts too). That requires a germline (inherited) genetic test that has not been done yet. Second, olaparib is a maintenance drug: it is meant to hold the line after a course of platinum chemotherapy has already controlled the disease, and you have never had platinum chemo. So even in the best case, this is months away, not now.

If both conditions are met, the benefit is real: in the trial that established it, patients on olaparib went about twice as long before their cancer grew again (roughly 7 versus 4 months) compared with placebo. Two honest tempering points. That delay-in-growth benefit did not translate into people clearly living longer in the trial; the survival curves stayed close together. And until the genetic test comes back positive and a platinum course holds the disease, you should assume no benefit here, because the drug simply does not apply yet. Side effects include anemia, fatigue, and nausea (serious in about 4 in 10 patients), plus a small long-term risk (around 1.5%) of a serious blood disorder with prolonged use.

What is contested is not the drug's mechanism but its deliverability for you right now. An option double-gated on a test you have not had and a chemotherapy you have not received is hard to rank as an immediate move for someone whose goal is remission now. The concrete action it points to is worth taking regardless: ask about ordering the germline BRCA1/2/PALB2 panel now. Guidelines recommend it for every pancreatic cancer patient regardless of family history, and a positive result would open this pathway (and Option 9).

docs.title: Option 4 — daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. This is Option 1's drug combined with a standard chemo backbone (either mFOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel), taken in a trial. The logic fits a remission-first goal: because your adjuvant chemo was irinotecan-based, you have never had oxaliplatin, which keeps the intensive mFOLFIRINOX combination biologically on the table. In a very small early cohort on a related combination, 5 of 6 patients had confirmed tumor shrinkage. That is a striking signal, but from just six people, so it cannot carry much weight yet.

The tradeoff is toxicity stacked on toxicity. You would be layering the rash and gut side effects of the KRAS drug on top of chemo's blood-count drops and nerve effects, and there is no dedicated safety readout for this specific combination in pancreatic cancer. If lingering nerve symptoms from your earlier FOLFIRI are a factor, the gentler gemcitabine backbone may be the better choice. This sits below the single-drug version of daraxonrasib precisely because the combination's safety is less charted, and the practical question is whether the pancreatic arm is open at your referral site.

docs.title: Option 5 — ulixertinib plus palbociclib
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. This pairing is the only one on the page that goes after three of your tumor's features at once: it blocks a signal (ERK) downstream of KRAS, and it targets the cell-division machinery tied to your CDKN2A loss and CCND3 alteration. On paper the logic is clean.

The honest limit is the clinical track record. The best published result in pancreatic cancer was stable disease (tumors held steady rather than shrank), not actual shrinkage. And one of the two drugs (palbociclib) has already been tested on its own in cancers with a related cell-division marker and largely failed there. The lab work behind the combination was mostly done on other KRAS variants, not G12R, so whether it applies cleanly to your cancer is untested. Side effects include overlapping drops in blood counts, fatigue (common), rash, and nausea. It is on the page as a deliberate "covers the most features" option, not because the response numbers are strong. The mechanistic case is the appeal, and the response expectation is modest.

docs.title: Option 6 — KST-6051 (FALCON trial)
docs.text: This option carries caveats. This is another oral drug against mutant KRAS, built to work on the protein in more than one of its states, with pancreatic cancer named as a target. The plain truth is that there is no data yet. The first patient was dosed in April 2026, so no one can tell you how well it works or what its side effects are. It is on the page as a forward-looking backup: if the more-established KRAS drugs stop working or the rash proves intolerable, this is a mechanistically distinct shot at the same target. Being this early, trial slots will be scarce, and Option 8 is a near-identical alternative.

docs.title: Option 7 — PF-07934040
docs.text: This option carries caveats. Another oral pan-KRAS drug in its first human trial. What sets it slightly apart is that it names G12R explicitly in its written eligibility criteria, and it has a second-line pancreatic cohort that matches your setting. But like Option 6, it is early enough that no results on how well it works have been reported, and its side-effect picture is limited to what the protocol excludes. It is a clean backup on your main target with no efficacy readout yet. One practical note: the trial excludes people with significant nerve damage, which is worth checking against any lingering effects from your earlier chemo, though irinotecan-based regimens usually spare the nerves.

docs.title: Option 8 — JAB-23E73
docs.text: This option carries caveats. A second early pan-KRAS drug held on the list for redundancy: if one early trial has no open slot, another might. Its lab profile covers G12R, and it is open to patients like you who have not had a prior KRAS-targeting drug. Two honest limits: the only public hint of activity so far is a vague "early antitumor activity" statement with no numbers, and the trial enrolls any advanced solid tumor rather than naming pancreatic cancer, so a pancreatic slot is not guaranteed and would need confirming.

docs.title: Option 9 — rucaparib (the maintenance backup to olaparib)
docs.text: This option carries caveats. Rucaparib is in the same family as olaparib (Option 3) and comes with the same two gates: it needs a BRCA1/2 or PALB2 mutation (inherited or in the tumor) and a prior platinum chemotherapy course. Its one advantage is that it covers a slightly wider set of genetic results than olaparib does. In its trial, patients with the right genetic makeup did well (tumors shrank about 42% of the time, with a median of roughly 13 months before growth). But the evidence is from a smaller, single-group study rather than a rigorous head-to-head trial, and the same "cannot start today" gate applies. The same germline panel that unlocks olaparib unlocks this. It sits lower on the list because it depends on a marker outside the main targetable features this page is scoped to.

docs.title: Option 10 — anvumetostat (needs an extra test first)
docs.text: This option carries caveats. This drug targets a vulnerability that can come with your CDKN2A loss. A neighboring gene called MTAP is often deleted alongside CDKN2A, and when it is, this class of drug can exploit that. There is a version of the trial that pairs it with daraxonrasib, which would cover both your KRAS and cell-cycle features at once. Two big caveats. First, no pancreatic cancer results have been published, and there is no safety data on file. Second, and this is the gate: the whole rationale depends on MTAP actually being deleted, which has not been tested. Ask about running the MTAP reflex test (a straightforward add-on to existing tissue analysis). If MTAP turns out to be intact, this option falls away entirely.

docs.title: Option 11 — ELI-002 (a KRAS vaccine)
docs.text:
This option was considered but not recommended for your situation, though it stays on the page because it is worth understanding why. ELI-002 is a vaccine that trains the immune system against the exact G12R mutation your cancer carries, and its safety record is the cleanest of anything here (essentially injection-site reactions, nothing serious attributed to it). In a trial, 84% of patients mounted the intended immune response.

The problem is the setting. Every human result for this vaccine comes from patients who had their cancer surgically removed and had only tiny, invisible traces of disease left, not patients with visible, active recurrence like yours. There is no evidence a vaccine can control bulk recurrent pancreatic cancer, and the registered successor trial is not currently enrolling. So the mechanism is elegant and the safety is excellent, but the window it was studied in does not match where you are. That mismatch, not any safety worry, is why it lands at the bottom.

docs.title: Questions to ask your oncologist
docs.text:
• Can we order the germline BRCA1/2/PALB2 panel now, and can we add the MTAP reflex test to the tumor analysis? Both are low-risk tests that decide whether some options on this list are even possible.
  • If the germline test comes back negative, what does that change? (It would close the olaparib and rucaparib pathways, so what would we focus on instead?)
  • For Option 1 (daraxonrasib): is there an open trial slot for me, or an expanded-access route, and what is the plan for monitoring and managing the rash and diarrhea if I start?
  • For Option 2 (ERAS-0015): given that the serious-side-effect data has not been released, how comfortable are you enrolling me, and would you want to wait for a fuller safety readout?
  • For Option 4 (daraxonrasib plus chemo): does my earlier FOLFIRI leave me with any lingering nerve symptoms that would steer us toward the gentler chemo backbone?
  • If I were to consider olaparib later, would you recommend a platinum-based chemo course now regardless, and what would tell us it is working well enough to move to maintenance?
  • Several of these are very early trials with no results yet. How do you weigh enrolling in something unproven against options with more data behind them, given that my goal is remission?
  • Is there a single trial that could cover more than one of my tumor's features at once, and would you prioritize that?

Reading the columns

Toxicity burden is patient-level G3+ AE severity (Low / Moderate / High) summarized from trial publications. Counter-productive MoA is the mechanism-level risk that the intervention's own pathway could blunt the therapeutic goal — distinct from patient AEs. The board's endorse / dissent / veto state appears as pills under each intervention; full per-persona rationale lives on the board page.

docs.title: KRAS G12R
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences essentialOrthogonal NGS panel plus ctDNA (KRAS G12R-specific ddPCR or comprehensive plasma NGS)orthogonal validationctDNA10-20 mL Streck whole blood for ctDNA; archival FFPE or matched tissue NGS for the orthogonal call1-2 weeksPan-RAS / RAS(ON) inhibitor trials (RMC-6236 NCT05379985, RMC-7977 NCT06445062); G12C-specific agents are not the relevant class.Pan-RAS and RAS(ON) multi-selective programs (RMC-6236, RMC-7977 and the divarasib-class follow-ons) require allele-resolved KRAS G12X status at trial entry, and most central labs re-test the variant on plasma at screening regardless of the local report. G12R is biologically distinct from G12C and G12D: it is RAS-GTP-binding-deficient, so G12C-specific inhibitors (sotorasib, adagrasib) are not the relevant class. A second-platform call plus a baseline ctDNA reading anchors both eligibility and on-treatment monitoring.Guardant Health · Guardant360 CDx preferredtest info · 505 Penobscot Drive, Redwood City, CA 94063 · 1-855-698-8887FDA-approved plasma ctDNA panel; covers KRAS G12X at single-codon resolution and is the most commonly cited liquid platform in pan-RAS inhibitor trial screening.Caris Life Sciences · Caris Assure UStest info · 4610 South 44th Place, Phoenix, AZ 85040 · 1-888-979-8669Foundation Medicine · FoundationOne Liquid CDx UStest info · 150 Second Street, Cambridge, MA 02141 · 1-888-988-3639Roche-owned FDA-approved liquid CDx; tissue companion (FoundationOne CDx) covers the orthogonal NGS arm.Natera · Signatera (tumor-informed MRD) UStest info · 13011 McCallen Pass, Austin, TX 78753 · 1-650-249-9090Tumor-informed MRD assay; pairs with the dynamics-monitoring row below if the team wants serial quantitation rather than panel-based ctDNA.Tempus · Tempus xF+ (plasma) / xT (tissue) UStest info · 600 West Chicago Avenue, Chicago, IL 60654 · 1-800-739-4137NCT05379985NCT06445062PMID 37270560PMID 36952657 highComprehensive tumor NGS including SMAD4, KEAP1, STK11, GNAS, ARID1Aco-mutationNGS_panelarchival FFPE; ctDNA as a backup if tissue is exhausted2-4 weeksFrames prognosis under multi-agent therapy and weights any ICI-combo strategy on the KRAS axis.SMAD4 loss in PDAC is the strongest single co-alteration linked to wider metastatic spread and shorter survival, and it changes how the board weights aggressive multi-agent regimens against trial enrollment. docs.title: TP53 inactivating mutation
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences mediumTP53 variant annotation (LOF vs dominant-negative vs gain-of-function) with reference to IARC TP53 databasesubtypingNGS_panelno new tissue required; re-read the existing NGS reportsame-day re-read of existing NGS reportFrames any TP53-restoration or MDM2-inhibitor strategy; does not gate the KRAS axis.The user report says inactivating mutation, but TP53 alterations split functionally into pure loss-of-function (truncations, splice), dominant-negative missense (hotspot R175H, R248W, R273H), and gain-of-function variants. docs.title: CDKN2A loss
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences highp16 IHC (clone E6H4 or equivalent)orthogonal validationIHCarchival FFPE; same block as the tumor NGS1-2 weeksCDK4/6-inhibitor eligibility (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib) and CDKN2A-loss-enriched trial arms.NGS copy-number calls for CDKN2A homozygous deletion can be unreliable at low tumor purity, and p16 IHC is the orthogonal protein-level readout that confirms loss of function. Most CDK4/6-inhibitor trials in CDKN2A-altered tumors require p16-negative status or biallelic CDKN2A loss at enrollment, and the IHC is the assay the central labs run. A confirmed loss reads cleanly; a discordance (NGS-loss but IHC-retained) is a meaningful signal that the call may be subclonal or assay-driven.Mayo Clinic Laboratories preferredtest info · 200 First Street SW, Rochester, MN 55905 · 1-800-533-1710p16 IHC (E6H4) is a standard menu item with a routine 1-2 week turnaround.ARUP Laboratories UStest info · 500 Chipeta Way, Salt Lake City, UT 84108 · 1-800-242-2787LabCorp / Esoterix Oncology UStest info · 358 South Main Street, Burlington, NC 27215 · 1-800-345-4363NeoGenomics Laboratories UStest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 1-866-776-5907Quest Diagnostics UStest info · 500 Plaza Drive, Secaucus, NJ 07094 · 1-866-697-8378PMID 31257067PMID 27908594 mediump16 IHC across multiple tumor regions (primary site vs metastatic biopsy if available)heterogeneityIHCarchival FFPE from a second site if available1-2 weeksRefines confidence in the CDKN2A loss call for CDK4/6-inhibitor strategy; does not gate enrollment.PDAC biology often shows clonal heterogeneity between primary and metastatic sites, and CDKN2A loss is not always uniform. A patchy p16 result on multi-region IHC tempers expectations for CDK4/6-inhibitor monotherapy and may push the board toward combination strategies. docs.title: CCND3 alteration
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences highCCND3 alteration-class refinement (amplification vs activating mutation vs fusion) via NGS plus FISH or copy-number array as neededsubtypingNGS_panelarchival FFPE; usually returnable from the same NGS panel as the KRAS / co-mutation row2-3 weeksCDK4/6-inhibitor and cyclin-D-degrader trial enrichment (PF-07220060, fadraciclib, INCB123667).The user-supplied report says CCND3 alteration without specifying class, and that distinction matters: an amplification or activating mutation supports cyclin-D-axis dependency and CDK4/6 sensitivity, whereas a single passenger missense without copy gain has weaker mechanistic weight. Cyclin-D-degrader and selective CDK4 programs (PF-07220060, fadraciclib, INCB123667) typically gate on copy-number gain or known activating mutations.
