docs.title: What this page is
docs.text:
Libby is a research tool that looks at the specific features of one person's cancer and pulls together the treatment options that target those features, along with the trials that offer them. This page is the plain-language version of that work. It walks through what we found out about your cancer, what you said mattered to you, two tests worth doing first, and then the options themselves — ranked, with the upside and the catch of each laid out as plainly as we can manage.

It is not a treatment plan, and it is not a substitute for your oncologist. Think of it as a well-organized starting point for the conversation you'll have with your care team.

docs.title: What we know about your cancer
docs.text:
You have triple-negative breast cancer that started in the right breast and has spread — to a lymph node under the same arm, and to a single spot in the liver, about 1.5 cm across. This was found all at once, at diagnosis, and you have not had any cancer treatment yet.

A few features of the tumor shape the options below:

  • A BRCA1 mutation. BRCA1 is a gene that normally helps cells repair damaged DNA. When it's broken, the cancer becomes vulnerable to certain drugs — a class of pills called PARP inhibitors, and platinum-based chemotherapy. This is the single most useful thing we know about your tumor for picking treatment. One open question the lab still needs to answer: whether the mutation is one you were born with (inherited) or one that showed up only in the tumor. More on why that matters below.
  • "Basal-like" and immune-active. The tumor's overall pattern is the aggressive, fast-growing subtype most common in triple-negative disease. But it also has a lot of immune cells packed into it, and a high number of DNA mutations — both signs that immune-boosting treatment may work here.
  • A single, small liver spot. Cancer that has spread to just one place is called oligometastatic. It's part of why a cure is even worth talking about in your case: one small, controllable spot is very different from disease scattered through the body.

docs.title: What you told us matters most
docs.text:
You didn't spell out detailed preferences, so these are reasonable defaults for your situation rather than things you said word-for-word — worth confirming or correcting with your team:

  • Lean toward the strongest treatment, accept more side effects to get it. With a single liver spot and a real shot at long-term control, the priority is hitting the cancer hard rather than staying maximally comfortable. That's the balance reflected below.
  • Open to clinical trials. Several of the most interesting options for your particular tumor live inside trials, and your situation makes you a strong candidate for many of them. So trials are surfaced wherever they fit, not treated as a last resort.

docs.title: First steps: two tests to run before anything is prescribed
docs.text:
Before any treatment decision is final, two lab tests should be ordered — they don't hurt, they don't cost you treatment time, and they decide which version of the top options is available to you. Neither one takes a whole option off the table; they decide whether an option is used on-label (the standard, well-covered way) or off-label, and which lane you enter. Both can be started this week, in parallel with everything else.

  • A PD-L1 test (called "22C3 CPS") on the breast tumor. This measures a protein that predicts how well immune-boosting treatment will work. The result comes back in about a week. If it's high enough (a score of 10 or more), the top option below — the pembrolizumab combination — is the on-label, proven choice. If it comes back low, that specific benefit doesn't apply, and the plan leans on the other options. One technical note worth raising with your team: the test should be run on the breast tumor, because the breast and liver samples can disagree with each other maybe a fifth to a third of the time.
  • A blood or saliva test to check whether the BRCA1 mutation is inherited (germline testing). This takes two to three weeks. If the mutation is inherited, the PARP-inhibitor pills below are on-label and routinely covered. If the mutation turns out to be in the tumor only, those same pills still make biological sense against your cancer — but getting them covered becomes more of a paperwork fight, and the cleanest route may shift to a trial built for that situation. This test also matters for your family: an inherited result means relatives may want testing too, so it's worth pairing with a genetics counseling visit.

These aren't delays for their own sake. They're the difference between guessing and knowing, and the answers reshape the ranking below.

docs.title: The options
docs.text: Nine options came out of the analysis, in the order below. The top four are the well-established standards — backed by large, high-quality trials. From the fifth down, the options lean more on early or trial-stage evidence, and each is flagged for what's still unsettled about it.

docs.title: Option 1 — Pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy (carboplatin and gemcitabine)
docs.text:
This pairs an immune-boosting drug (pembrolizumab) with two chemotherapy drugs, one of which — carboplatin, a platinum drug — is exactly the kind your BRCA1 tumor is unusually sensitive to. So this regimen works on two fronts at once: it wakes up the immune system against the cancer and hits the DNA-repair weakness the mutation creates.

This is the option to discuss first. It has the strongest long-term survival evidence of anything on this page for newly diagnosed metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. In the trial that established it, among patients whose PD-L1 test was high, the ones who got this combination lived a median of about 23 months versus about 16 months on chemotherapy alone — and the treatment cut the death rate over the study period meaningfully. That's a real, measured survival gain, not a hoped-for one.

The catch is the PD-L1 test. That survival benefit was seen specifically in patients who scored 10 or higher. If your score comes back below that, the proven advantage of adding the immune drug goes away — and the tumor's other favorable features (the high mutation count, the immune cells) don't rescue it, because it's the PD-L1 score the evidence tracks. That's why the test comes first.

Side effects are real. The heaviest is a drop in infection-fighting white blood cells, which happens in roughly 4 out of 10 patients and needs monitoring. The immune drug can also, less often, turn the immune system against healthy organs — the thyroid, the liver, the lungs — which teams watch for and manage. Serious treatment-related deaths were very rare, well under 1 in 100.

This fits your lean toward strong treatment. It's the on-label standard when the PD-L1 test is high. And if you'd rather receive it inside a trial, Option 5 below offers exactly this regimen as its comparison arm.

docs.title: Option 2 — Olaparib (a PARP-inhibitor pill)
docs.text:
Olaparib is a once-or-twice-daily pill — no chemotherapy, no infusion chair — that targets the DNA-repair weakness your BRCA1 mutation creates. Cancer cells that can't repair their DNA properly, when you block their backup repair system too, tend to die.

In the trial behind it, in patients with a BRCA mutation, tumors shrank in about 60% of people on olaparib versus about 29% on standard chemotherapy, and the cancer stayed controlled noticeably longer. It's an oral, gentle-footprint treatment with a strong track record.

This option's availability depends on the germline test. If your BRCA1 mutation is inherited, olaparib is fully on-label and routinely covered. If it turns out to be in the tumor only, the drug still makes biological sense, but it moves off-label — meaning more work to get it approved, or a trial route instead.

The main side effect is anemia (low red blood cells), serious enough to need attention in about 1 in 6 patients — the gentlest blood-count profile of the pill options here, which is one reason it ranks ahead of the similar drug in Option 3. There's also a small long-term risk (roughly 1-2 in 100 over a year or two) of a serious bone-marrow problem, which is why blood counts get watched over time.

It's worth knowing this sits a step below Option 1 mainly because the pembrolizumab combination has direct evidence of helping people live longer in the first-line setting, which a PARP pill on its own hasn't shown as clearly. Some clinicians would argue that with two strong trials behind the PARP pills versus one behind the pembrolizumab combination, the pills have a case to lead — that's a genuine open question about sequencing, worth raising with your team.

docs.title: Option 3 — Talazoparib (the other PARP-inhibitor pill)
docs.text:
Talazoparib is a once-daily pill in the same family as olaparib, working the same way against the BRCA1 weakness. Its trial showed the deepest tumor-shrinkage of any single pill on this list — tumors responded in about 63% of BRCA-mutation patients versus about 27% on chemotherapy. That depth of response is the interesting part for you specifically: a treatment that shrinks the liver spot the most is the most plausible way to turn it into something a surgeon or radiation team could then remove or ablate, which is the curative-intent idea running through this whole page. That's a hypothesis to test (see Option 9), not a settled result — and this trial did not show a clear extension of overall survival.

Like olaparib, this depends on the germline test in the same way: inherited BRCA1 keeps it on-label; a tumor-only result moves it off-label, with a trial as the alternate route.

The reason it sits just below olaparib is side effects, not effectiveness — the two are considered equally strong. Talazoparib causes serious anemia in closer to 4 in 10 patients, more than double olaparib's rate, and more drops in other blood cells too. That matters more than usual for you, because you may need blood-count-taxing chemotherapy before or after, and there's only so much marrow reserve to spend. Same effectiveness, heavier cost to the blood counts — that's the whole difference between this and Option 2.

docs.title: Option 4 — Carboplatin plus gemcitabine (chemotherapy)
docs.text:
This is a two-drug chemotherapy combination built around carboplatin, the platinum drug your BRCA1 tumor is especially sensitive to. In BRCA-mutation patients, carboplatin shrank tumors in about 68% versus about 33% for a common alternative chemo — a strong signal, though it comes from a small slice of a trial (43 patients), so the exact number is less certain than the headline suggests.

Here's why this one earns its spot despite ranking below the others: it's the one option that no pending test can take away from you. It doesn't need a high PD-L1 score, and it doesn't care whether your BRCA1 mutation is inherited or tumor-only. If both tests come back in a way that limits the options above, this is the dependable ground to stand on. It also works as a foundation you can build on — many teams use platinum chemo first, then move to a PARP pill to maintain the response.

Side effects are the usual chemotherapy ones — mainly drops in white cells and platelets — which are well understood and manageable with dose adjustments. The tradeoff versus Option 1 is that you give up the added survival edge the immune drug brings if your PD-L1 score turns out high. It ranks below the pills because it means infusions rather than a chemo-free pill, and rests on somewhat less definitive trial evidence.

docs.title: Option 5 — Datopotamab deruxtecan (with or without durvalumab), on a clinical trial
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here's the tradeoff to weigh.

This is a clinical trial. It tests a newer targeted drug — datopotamab deruxtecan, which homes in on a protein called TROP2 that sits on basal-type breast cancer — sometimes combined with another immune drug. The trial is open to newly diagnosed patients whose PD-L1 score is high.

The appealing part, given your openness to trials, is how the trial is built: its comparison arm is exactly the pembrolizumab-plus-chemo regimen from Option 1. So one arm of the trial delivers the proven standard, and the other arm adds an experimental drug on top of that floor. Enrolling can't drop you below standard care.

Now the honest catch, and it's a real one. First, there are no results yet — the experimental arm is an unproven bet, not a measured benefit. Second, because the trial assigns you at random, you might land in the comparison arm and simply receive the standard regimen you could get off-trial anyway. Third — and this is the substantive concern — the experimental drug works through the TROP2 protein, not through the BRCA1 DNA-repair weakness. For a tumor like yours, where that DNA-repair weakness is the clearest thing to attack, spending the crucial early window on a mechanism that sidesteps it is a genuine tradeoff. This is a legitimate on-trial way to receive standard care plus a shot at something more — not a sign the experimental drug beats the standard. If your PD-L1 score comes back low, this trial isn't a fit, and a different set of trials would be the route.

docs.title: Option 6 — Niraparib plus pembrolizumab
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here's the tradeoff to weigh.

This combines a PARP-inhibitor pill (niraparib) with the immune drug pembrolizumab — a chemo-free pairing that, on paper, matches your tumor beautifully: the PARP pill damages the cancer's DNA in a way that creates targets, and the immune drug attacks those targets. The biology is a clean fit for a BRCA1, high-mutation, immune-active tumor like yours.

The problem is the evidence. The eye-catching number you'll see — tumors responding in about 47% of patients — comes from just 15 people in one arm of a small study with no comparison group. Across the fuller group, the response rate was about 21%, and with numbers that small, the true figure could sit almost anywhere in a wide range. A single small study without a comparison can't sort out how much credit goes to the PARP pill, the immune drug, or simply having a BRCA mutation.

On top of that, niraparib specifically isn't approved for breast cancer, so getting it paid for is harder than the approved pills in Options 2 and 3. The most realistic home for this chemo-free idea is later on — as a way to maintain a response after platinum chemotherapy — rather than as a first move. It stays on the page because the biology genuinely fits and the ceiling is high, but it isn't a front-line choice.

docs.title: Option 7 — A PARP1-selective inhibitor trial (HS-10502)
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here's the tradeoff to weigh.

This is a clinical trial of a newer kind of PARP pill designed to be gentler on the blood counts than olaparib and talazoparib — potentially sparing the anemia that limits the approved pills. For someone in their early 40s who may spend years on this class of drug, less strain on the marrow is a genuinely appealing goal.

Two honest limits. First, the encouraging response numbers you'll hear don't actually belong to the drug in this trial — they come from a related drug, reported only as a conference summary (not a full published study), in a mixed group of breast cancer patients that wasn't specific to triple-negative disease. The drug actually offered in this trial has no results of its own yet. Second, the whole selling point — that it's gentler on the blood — is a reasonable idea but an untested one: there's no detailed safety breakdown published to confirm it. That's precisely what a trial is meant to find out.

There's also a practical wrinkle: this trial expects you to have had a prior line of treatment, so it wouldn't be your very first step — it's an option for later. It stays on the page as a legitimate trial route for the gentler-on-the-blood bet, not because its effectiveness is established.

docs.title: Option 8 — Olaparib plus ceralasertib, on a clinical trial
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here's the tradeoff to weigh.

This trial adds a second drug (ceralasertib, which blocks another DNA-repair pathway) on top of the olaparib pill from Option 2 — aiming to push harder on the DNA-repair weakness your BRCA1 and TP53 mutations create. Of the newer combination trials, this one rests on the most solid published evidence, and it has an arm open to inherited-BRCA patients.

The reasons it ranks near the bottom are specific and worth understanding. The published response rate — about 17% — came from patients who'd already had other treatments, and that doesn't carry over cleanly to a newly diagnosed patient like you. More importantly, the one properly designed head-to-head trial built to prove that adding this second drug beats olaparib alone couldn't show a benefit. So the added drug brings extra side effects (more anemia, and high blood pressure) to buy an improvement that the strongest test couldn't confirm. It also requires a washout period that makes it a poor fit right now for someone starting fresh. It's a reasonable later-line trial slot, not a first move and not a replacement for the plain olaparib above it.

docs.title: Option 9 — Focused radiation to the liver spot, on a clinical trial
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here's the tradeoff to weigh.

This is about the liver spot directly. The idea — the one behind the curative-intent hope on this whole page — is that once the drugs have controlled the cancer everywhere, delivering precise, high-dose radiation (called SBRT) to that single small liver lesion might wipe out the last of it and give a shot at a lasting result. This trial offers that radiation on-protocol, after a scan at about 12 weeks confirms the breast and lymph node are under control. It's always layered on top of your drug treatment — it never replaces it.

Here's the honest part, and it's important. Two well-run studies tested exactly this idea — adding local treatment to a limited number of spread-out spots — and both came back negative: patients who got the local treatment did not do better overall than those who stuck with drugs alone. That's why removing or radiating your liver spot outside a trial is not a proven add-on, and shouldn't be done as a routine extra. The open, unanswered question is whether carefully selecting one small lesion in one person — as opposed to treating everyone with limited spread — changes that answer. That question is exactly what the trial exists to test, which is why the honest route to this is a trial rather than an off-trial procedure. It sits last because it doesn't attack the cancer's biology directly and isn't backed by a positive result — but it's here at all because your single small liver spot, and your hope for a cure, make it a fair thing to ask about.

docs.title: Questions to ask your oncologist
docs.text:
• Can we order the PD-L1 test on the breast tumor and the inherited-BRCA1 blood test this week, and how soon will each come back?
  • If the PD-L1 score comes back below 10, what does that change about the pembrolizumab option, and what would you recommend instead?
  • If my BRCA1 mutation turns out to be tumor-only rather than inherited, how does that affect whether I can get olaparib or talazoparib, and would a trial be the better route?
  • Between olaparib and talazoparib, given I may need chemotherapy that also lowers blood counts, how would you weigh talazoparib's deeper response against its heavier effect on my blood?
  • If we start with the pembrolizumab combination, what's the monitoring plan for the immune-related side effects — the thyroid, liver, and lung problems — and for the drop in white blood cells?
  • Am I a candidate for the datopotamab-deruxtecan trial, and if I enrolled, what's the chance I'd be assigned to the standard-care arm rather than the experimental one?
  • Is controlling the cancer enough to make the liver spot a candidate for focused radiation or removal, and would you support pursuing that only inside the trial rather than as a routine add-on?
  • Given my interest in trials, which of these are actually open and enrolling near me right now, and which would fit my situation as someone who hasn't had treatment yet?

single-arm, no comparator.Moderate (anemia, thrombocytopenia, immune-related AEs stacked)Moderate (In an MSS tumor a B2M/HLA-loss subclone would blunt the checkpoint half; critic dissented on the thin single-arm evidence base.)**A mechanistically clean chemo-free PARP+IO bet for this exact BRCA1/TMB/TIL phenotype, but the 47% is an n=15 subgroup and niraparib is off-label — a later-line maintenance question, not a 1L move.**PMID 31194225PMID 32771088 7PARP1-selective inhibitor trial — HS-10502 on NCT05740956 (saruparib/PETRA as class precedent), later-lineendorse: risktaker concensusite advocatedissent: conservative criticUncertain: class-precedent ORR 48.4% (saruparib PETRA, abstract, mixed HR+/TNBC); HS-10502's own activity unpublished.Not characterized (per-term G3+ table not released; mechanism predicts less anemia)Moderate (Critic and conservative dissented on the unproven toxicity-sparing claim; no per-term safety data to confirm PARP1-selectivity spares marrow.)**The enrollable toxicity-sparing PARP bet for a young patient facing years on the DDR axis, but the efficacy is cross-subtype abstract-level and the enrollable agent has no readout of its own.**NCT05740956PMID 28578601 8Olaparib + ceralasertib (ATR-i) on the recruiting germline-BRCA arm (NCT04090567) — later-lineendorse: critic advocatedissent: conservativeLow-to-moderate: TNBC ORR 17.1% (pmid:37773077), single-arm 2L+; the randomized VIOLETTE test did not beat olaparib alone.Moderate (anemia and hypertension added over single-agent olaparib)Moderate (Conservative flagged that the added ATR toxicity buys efficacy the randomized trial could not demonstrate over PARP monotherapy.)**The best-evidenced DDR-combination entry and a recruiting home for the BRCA1+TP53 ATR rationale, but VIOLETTE was negative over olaparib alone and it is 2L+ only.**PMID 37773077NCT04090567NCT03330847 9SBRT to the solitary liver lesion as consolidation on the MSK SABR trial (NCT05534438) — trial-only, after systemic responseendorse: advocateLow for durable benefit off-protocol: randomized consolidation was negative in unselected patients (NRG-BR002 HR 1.31, pmid:33885704); trial-only, biology-selected.Low (radiation modality; lesion-specific, no systemic AE profile)Low (No mechanism blunts the systemic goal; the risk is null benefit from consolidation, per the negative randomized readouts.)**The on-protocol route to the curative-intent framing the patient asked for, honestly tempered by two negative randomized consolidation trials — a trial-only layer on the systemic backbone, never a standalone.**NCT05534438PMID 33885704PMID 34995128

Reading the columns

Toxicity burden is patient-level G3+ AE severity (Low / Moderate / High) summarized from trial publications. Counter-productive MoA is the mechanism-level risk that the intervention's own pathway could blunt the therapeutic goal — distinct from patient AEs. The board's endorse / dissent / veto state appears as pills under each intervention; full per-persona rationale lives on the board page.

docs.title: BRCA1 mutation
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences essentialGermline BRCA1/2 sequencing plus del/dup, ideally on a hereditary breast/ovarian cancer panel that also covers PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, BARD1, RAD51C/D, BRIP1, TP53, PTEN, CDH1, STK11germlinegermline_panel5-10 mL whole blood (EDTA) or saliva kit2-3 weeksRisk-reducing surgery decisions (bilateral mastectomy, RRSO), cascade testing of first-degree relatives, and confirmatory eligibility for germline-BRCA-restricted trials.The tumor NGS call does not say whether the BRCA1 variant is germline or somatic, and the answer changes a 42-year-old patient's life: germline BRCA1 carriers face bilateral mastectomy and risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy decisions and trigger cascade testing of first-degree relatives, while a purely somatic BRCA1 still supports PARP-inhibitor and platinum sensitivity but does not drive surgical or family-screening choices. NCCN BINV/genetic-familial breast guidelines mandate germline testing in any patient diagnosed under 50 or with TNBC regardless of age. Skipping this means missing a near-certain risk-management conversation and leaving family members untested.Labcorp Genetics (formerly Invitae) · Invitae Hereditary Breast and Gyn Cancers Panel (Multi-Cancer Panel option) preferredtest info · 1400 16th Street, San Francisco, CA 94103 · 1-800-436-3037Highest-volume hereditary breast/ovarian panel in the US; broad payer acceptance and a financial-assistance program that meaningfully reduces patient out-of-pocket. The score does not gate PARP-inhibitor eligibility in BRCA1-mutated TNBC (that runs off the BRCA call itself), but it strengthens the platinum/PARPi rationale and frames any future HR-targeted trial discussion (pmid:33037126, pmid:32826325).Myriad Genetics · MyChoice CDx (HRD with Genomic Instability Score) preferredtest info · 320 Wakara Way, Salt Lake City, UT 84108 · 1-800-469-7423The only FDA-approved HRD companion diagnostic in the US; the most widely-recognized HRD assay in the literature and in trial protocols. docs.title: TP53 mutation
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences mediumComprehensive NGS review for replication-stress / DDR co-alterations (ATM, ATR, CHK1/2, CDK12, CCNE1 amplification) and TP53 variant-functional classificationco-mutationNGS_panelshared with the PIK3CA / PTEN / TMB block2-4 weeks if new panel; same-day if existing report covers these genesWEE1/ATR-inhibitor trial enrollment rationale; not gating for any approved therapy.TP53 mutation is near-universal in basal-like TNBC and not directly drug-gating, but it anchors the replication-stress phenotype that WEE1 inhibitors (adavosertib, debio-0123) and ATR inhibitors (ceralasertib, elimusertib) exploit. The actionability hinges on co-alterations: CCNE1 amplification, CDK12 loss, or ATM loss meaningfully shift the WEE1/ATR rationale, and TP53 missense vs nonsense vs hotspot R175H/R248Q/R273H functional class also affects experimental-trial enrollment (pmid:32499663, pmid:31754023). docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences essentialPIK3CA variant resolution to specific codon (therascreen PIK3CA RGQ PCR Kit hotspots or FoundationOne CDx) covering C420R, E542K, E545A/D/G/K, Q546E/R, H1047L/R/YconfirmatoryNGS_panel1 FFPE block or 10-20 unstained slides; archival acceptable2-4 weeks (tissue NGS); 7-10 days (therascreen PCR if used as a confirmatory)Alpelisib, inavolisib, and capivasertib eligibility; trial enrollment for PI3K/AKT-axis studies that require a hotspot-defined PIK3CA call.The profile says PIK3CA is mutated but does not specify the codon, and the FDA companion diagnostics for alpelisib (therascreen PIK3CA) and the F1CDx label for capivasertib (PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN) only call a tumor 'PIK3CA-altered' for the 11-variant hotspot set: C420R, E542K, E545A/D/G/K, Q546E/R, H1047L/R/Y. docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences mediumMYC FISH (8q24 break-apart / amplification probe set) or MYC IHC (clone Y69) on archival FFPEorthogonal validationFISH1 FFPE block or 4 unstained slides1-2 weeksRefines MYC-amplification call strength for BET/CDK7/CDK9 trial enrollment; does not gate approved therapy.MYC amplification by NGS copy-number is a reasonably specific call but the magnitude (low-level gain vs focal high-level amplification) varies by panel and tumor purity. docs.title: PTEN copy number loss
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences essentialPTEN IHC (clone 138G6 or SP218) with positive internal control, scored as deficient if <10% tumor-cell staining at any intensityorthogonal validationIHC1 unstained slide from archival FFPE5-7 business days once block is pulledCapivasertib + fulvestrant (HR+/HER2-) decision; trial enrollment for AKT-inhibitor protocols in TNBC where PTEN-deficient status is required by IHC.Copy-number loss on NGS does not always translate to PTEN protein loss; PTEN is frequently inactivated by promoter methylation, frameshift, or LOH not picked up by panels with limited copy-number resolution. The FDA approval of capivasertib (CAPItello-291) and the F1CDx companion-diagnostic label define 'PTEN-altered' on a DNA call, but the IHC re-stain with a <10% cutoff (validated in the 2025 Virchows Archiv series) is the orthogonal protein-level confirmation that pathologists and tumor boards expect before AKT-inhibitor discussion. docs.title: Basal-like molecular subtype
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences highPAM50 intrinsic-subtype assay (NanoString Prosigna or Agendia BluePrint) with concurrent Lehmann TNBCtype-4 (BL1/BL2/M/LAR) classification on RNA-seq datasubtypingRNA_seqFFPE block or 10 unstained slides2-3 weeksTNBC-subtype-directed therapy bias (AR-axis vs platinum/PARP vs ICI + taxane); trial-enrollment refinement for subtype-restricted protocols.Roughly 25% of TNBCs do not classify as PAM50 basal-like, and within basal-like the Lehmann TNBCtype-4 subdivision (BL1, BL2, M, LAR) carries divergent neoadjuvant pCR rates: BL1 ~52% versus BL2 ~0%, LAR ~10%, M ~23% under anthracycline-taxane backbones (pmid:29521352, pmid:21633166, pmid:31836816). The current 'basal-like' call should be locked to the assay that made it (PAM50 vs ad-hoc gene set), and the Lehmann layer adds therapeutic resolution that the basal/non-basal binary cannot: LAR enrichment shifts the conversation toward AR-directed agents, M/MSL shifts it away from KEYNOTE-style ICI + taxane, and BL1 reinforces the platinum/PARP backbone already supported by BRCA1.Veracyte (Prosigna / NanoString assets) · Prosigna PAM50 preferredtest info · 6000 Shoreline Court, Suite 300, South San Francisco, CA 94080 · 1-650-243-6300FDA-cleared PAM50 intrinsic-subtype call; the most defensible US assay for the basal-like-vs-non-basal question. docs.title: TMB-high (14 mut/Mb)
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences essentialTMB measurement on an FDA-cleared comprehensive genomic panel sized ≥0.8 Mb (FoundationOne CDx, MSK-IMPACT, or Tempus xT CDx), with the panel and threshold documented in the reportconfirmatoryNGS_panel1 FFPE block or 10-20 unstained slides; archival acceptable2-4 weeks if a new comprehensive panel is needed; same-day chart review if the existing report already names the panelTumor-agnostic pembrolizumab eligibility under KEYNOTE-158; TMB-restricted trial enrollment.The tumor-agnostic pembrolizumab approval (KEYNOTE-158) is anchored on FoundationOne CDx as the companion diagnostic at a ≥10 mut/Mb cutoff, and TMB values are not interchangeable across panels: smaller or differently-bioinformatic panels can over- or under-call TMB by 3-5 mut/Mb at the clinically-relevant threshold. A 14 mut/Mb value from a non-FDA-cleared assay near the 10 mut/Mb cutoff is exactly the situation where the call should be locked to a panel the FDA label recognizes before pembrolizumab is offered on a TMB-only basis. Confirmation also lets the tumor board document which panel made the call for prior authorization (pmid:32919526, guideline:fda-label-pembrolizumab-tmb-2020).Foundation Medicine · FoundationOne CDx preferredtest info · 150 Second Street, Cambridge, MA 02141 · 1-888-988-3639The only FDA-approved companion diagnostic for TMB at the ≥10 mut/Mb threshold used in the KEYNOTE-158 tumor-agnostic pembrolizumab label. If the existing TMB call came from another assay, this is the defensible re-run.Caris Life Sciences · MI Cancer Seek UStest info · 4610 South 44th Place, Suite 100, Phoenix, AZ 85040 · 1-888-979-8669Memorial Sloan Kettering Diagnostic Molecular Pathology · MSK-IMPACT UStest info · 1275 York Avenue, New York, NY 10065 · 1-212-639-2000Academic-center alternative; the panel size (~1.5 Mb) is well-validated for TMB but the assay is generally not available outside the MSK network.Tempus Labs · Tempus xT CDx UStest info · 600 W Chicago Avenue, Chicago, IL 60654 · 1-800-739-4137FDA-approved 648-gene panel; TMB methodology has been benchmarked against FoundationOne CDx but is not the panel named in the pembrolizumab label.PMID 32919526PMID 32540858fda-label-pembrolizumab-tmb-202002628067 mediumB2M and HLA class I IHC (B2M EP2978Y; HLA-ABC EMR8-5) on archival FFPE, plus B2M / HLA-A/B/C variant call review on the existing tumor NGS panelresistance markerIHC1-2 unstained slides; can share the PD-L1 / TIL block5-7 business daysPrimary-resistance risk for pembrolizumab and other PD-1/PD-L1 agents; refines the ICI rationale without gating it.B2M loss and HLA class I antigen-presentation defects are well-characterized primary-resistance mechanisms for ICI in TMB-high and MSI-H tumors; loss of cell-surface MHC class I removes the substrate that PD-1 blockade depends on (pmid:29070816, pmid:38092534). In a TMB-14 / TIL-rich / MSS TNBC the ICI rationale is strong, but a B2M-deficient subclone would predict primary ICI failure even with the favorable TIL and TMB signals, and is detectable on the same FFPE block used for PD-L1 and TIL re-scoring. docs.title: 3+ stromal TIL infiltration
docs.text:
PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences essentialPD-L1 IHC (22C3 pharmDx CPS for pembrolizumab; SP142 IC for atezolizumab if relevant)co-mutationIHC1 FFPE block or 4-6 unstained slides5-7 business daysPembrolizumab + chemotherapy (KEYNOTE-355) in 1L metastatic TNBC; CPS ≥10 anchors the indication.In metastatic TNBC the pembrolizumab + chemotherapy label (KEYNOTE-355) requires PD-L1 CPS ≥10 by the 22C3 pharmDx companion diagnostic; in early-stage TNBC the KEYNOTE-522 indication is PD-L1-agnostic. The case is de novo M1, so PD-L1 CPS is the rate-limiting biomarker for the 1L ICI + chemo decision, and PD-L1 expression in TNBC is discordant between primary breast and liver metastasis in roughly 20-30% of paired samples (pmid:34626408, pmid:31166680). Skipping it means defaulting to PD-L1-agnostic backbones and missing the chance to anchor a CPS ≥10 case onto the pembrolizumab + chemo regimen.Labcorp Oncology · PD-L1 IHC 22C3 pharmDx (Dako/Agilent) preferredtest info · 358 South Main Street, Burlington, NC 27215 · 1-800-345-4363FDA-approved companion diagnostic for pembrolizumab in metastatic TNBC; widely available with national next-day turnaround. The most defensible single assay for the KEYNOTE-355 CPS ≥10 cutoff.Mayo Clinic Laboratories · PD-L1 22C3 pharmDx UStest info · 3050 Superior Drive NW, Rochester, MN 55901 · 1-800-533-1710NeoGenomics Laboratories · PD-L1 22C3 pharmDx UStest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 1-866-776-5907CAP-accredited; fastest commercial turnaround in our experience.Quest Diagnostics · PD-L1 22C3 pharmDx UStest info · 500 Plaza Drive, Secaucus, NJ 07094 · 1-866-697-8378PMID 34626408PMID 31166680fda-label-pembrolizumab-tnbc-2020 mediumInternational TILs Working Group (ITWG) stromal-TIL re-scoring on H&E by a dedicated breast pathologist (Salgado 2014 methodology; 0-100% scale on a single tumor-bearing section)confirmatoryIHC1 representative H&E slide; archival acceptable1-2 weeksICI-combination rationale strength (KEYNOTE-522, IMpassion-style); reinforces but does not gate enrollment.The '3+ stromal TILs (high)' label sits cleanly with the ITWG methodology only if it was scored as a continuous 0-100% percentage on a single H&E section by a pathologist trained on the Salgado 2014 guideline; ad-hoc '1+/2+/3+' grading is a known pitfall and inflates inter-observer variability (pmid:32195312, pmid:25214542). The re-score does not gate ICI eligibility (TIL-rich status is informative, not labeled), but it is the reference standard the ImPACT/KEYNOTE-522 literature uses and it makes the TIL signal defensible at tumor board. docs.title: Research question
docs.text: In newly diagnosed metastatic high-grade uterine leiomyosarcoma, systemic-therapy naive with bilateral pulmonary metastases and doxorubicin + trabectedin (LMS-04) planned and imminent, what interventions could target the histology, the entirely unmeasured molecular landscape (HRR/HRD, RB1, B7-H3, FAP, NTRK, TMB/MSI) and the pulmonary disease pattern, gated on the pre-induction workup and on HRR/HRD confirmation for the PARP branch?

docs.title: Patient profile (scrubbed)
docs.text:
• Female, age band 30-39.
  • High-grade uterine leiomyosarcoma, spindle-cell morphology, confirmed on both the pulmonary biopsy and the re-reviewed uterine specimen by a reference pathology laboratory (August 2026).
  • Stage IV: bilateral pulmonary metastases, read by the consulting sarcoma oncologist as unusually infiltrative and possibly inflammatory. Lifetime never-smoker.
  • The 6.0 cm myometrial primary was resected September 2024 during hysterectomy for a presumed benign leiomyoma and signed out benign; the diagnosis was corrected in July 2026 and confirmed in August 2026, an interval of roughly 23 months. Whether the specimen was morcellated is unknown; the operative report has not been retrieved.
  • Systemic-therapy naive. Planned first line: doxorubicin + trabectedin with trabectedin maintenance (the LMS-04 regimen), not yet started.
  • ER <1% and PR <1% by IHC, recorded as a decision-relevant negative. The specimen provenance of that stain (2024 primary vs 2026 lung core) is unverified.
  • Everything else is untested: no TP53, RB1, ATRX, MED12, HRR/BRCA2, NTRK, TMB, MSI/MMR or PD-L1 result exists. No laboratory values of any kind were supplied at intake. No LVEF, no PFTs, no CBC.
  • ECOG 1 is an intake ASSUMPTION, never documented by a clinician. She is symptomatic with cough and dyspnea yet travelled for specialist consultation, which fits either ECOG 1 or 2.
  • Resides at roughly 8,500 ft (~2,600 m). Chronic altitude adaptation shifts her baseline haemoglobin, oximetry and dyspnea thresholds, which bears on every anaemia, pneumonitis and pulmonary-reserve call to come.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text:
• None were stated. Every value in preferences.json is an assumed intake default with no user statement behind it: the 0.7 efficacy weight, the empty toxicity-veto list, the empty modality constraints, and prefers_trials: true.
  • Goals of care were not discussed at intake. A 39-year-old accepting an aggressive planned induction plausibly implies maximal-disease-control intent, but the profile itself labels that as inference.
  • The advocate named four questions that must be asked before any of these defaults hardens into her chart: whether she accepts 80% grade 3-4 neutropenia and 28% febrile neutropenia for a PFS hazard ratio of 0.41; whether she wants trials at all, and how far she will travel from a home at 8,500 ft; what ovarian function and the hormonal aftermath of chemotherapy mean to her at 39 (hysterectomy does not settle this, and no one has raised it); and how much off-label authorization fighting she will absorb, since her first-line regimen already needs some.
  • Nothing on this page treats an intake default as her wish.

docs.title: Target validation paths
docs.text: Two test sets carry the weight of this case. An echocardiogram with LVEF and a clinician-documented ECOG decide whether the planned doxorubicin + trabectedin induction (the LMS-04 regimen, NCT02997358) can be given at all, and a tumor HRR/HRD panel decides whether olaparib + temozolomide (NCI protocol 10250, NCT03880019) exists as an option at progression. Neither result is on file. If the cardiac or pulmonary screen fails, the first-line fitness conversation changes and belongs to the treating team, not to Libby; if the HRR panel returns proficient, the olaparib + temozolomide branch closes for practical purposes. Nearly everything else below runs in parallel with induction and costs no treatment days.

docs.title: uLMS histology
docs.text: Three items are essential before cycle 1. A transthoracic echocardiogram with LVEF and strain (same day to 1 week), because the anthracycline cannot be dosed without a reference value. A clinician-documented ECOG, because the 1 on file is an intake assumption and her symptoms fit either 1 or 2, a difference that decides full-dose induction and most trial screens. And a hepatic-renal panel with creatine kinase, which sets the trabectedin starting dose and its dose-modification rules. The CBC with reticulocytes and ferritin needs an altitude-adjusted reference interval stated in the chart: at roughly 8,500 ft her baseline haemoglobin runs high, and a sea-level-normed count will under-read chemotherapy anaemia. Expert sarcoma pathology review of both specimens, with mitotic index, coagulative necrosis and FNCLCC grade, is the essential item that gates no drug: a 6.0 cm mass handled as a benign fibroid was very unlikely to be sampled at the one-block-per-centimetre standard, major revisions occur in about a quarter of sarcoma second opinions, and the deeper levels should be cut before the molecular orders exhaust the block.

docs.title: Bilateral pulmonary pattern
docs.text: PFTs with DLCO and oximetry recorded at residence altitude come before induction. Without them, an on-treatment desaturation cannot be split into progression, pneumonitis or altitude physiology, and the same numbers later price any lung-directed surgery or radiation. PD-L1 with CD3 and CD8 on the 2026 lung core answers whether the infiltrative, possibly inflammatory radiologic read reflects an immune infiltrate; it gates nothing on its own, and if the core runs scant, the MMR and B7-H3 stains take priority.

docs.title: Unmeasured molecular landscape
docs.text: One RNA-inclusive tumor NGS panel on the 2024 resection block does most of the work here. The HRR gene set with an LOH score gates olaparib + temozolomide via NCT03880019 (2-3 weeks, archival FFPE). RNA fusion calling must be specified on the requisition: NTRK breakpoints sit in large introns, a DNA-only panel returns a false negative that reads as a closed question, and a positive gates larotrectinib, entrectinib or repotrectinib under the tumor-agnostic approval. TMB from a validated comprehensive panel and the four-stain MMR IHC close the pembrolizumab doors (TMB >=10 mut/Mb, or dMMR); both are rare in this histology and cheap to settle. B7-H3 IHC carries the best odds of a positive of any surface target (97% of soft-tissue sarcomas stained positive, 69% at high level) and gates screening for the B7-H3 ADC programs. The germline panel (BRCA1/2, PALB2, RAD51C/D, ATM, TP53 and the Lynch genes) goes out with the somatic order, after the consent conversation it actually is; ERN GENTURIS puts germline TP53 testing before genotoxic chemotherapy. HLA class I typing at allele-level resolution is one blood draw, with PRAME and MAGE-A4 IHC held as reflex stains until a restricting allele returns; that prices the TCR-T and ImmTAC class (IMA203, brenetafusp, the SURPASS programme) without spending tissue speculatively. TP53, RB1, ATRX and MED12 ride along free on the panel, and paired ATRX IHC on both blocks answers whether the 2024 primary represents the 2026 disease for the price of two stains. One assay cannot be ordered at all: the RAD51 foci test, the functional readout that separated 11.2 from 5.4 months of PFS in the olaparib + temozolomide trial, has no CLIA provider anywhere. Do not hold the somatic panel for it; ask any PARP-inhibitor trial site whether they run it at screening.

docs.title: ER/PR <1%
docs.text: The <1% ER and PR result genuinely forecloses aromatase inhibition, since durable benefit with letrozole occurred only in tumours staining above 90%, but only if the stain was run on current disease with working controls. So the first step is a records one: which specimen was stained, which clone, and whether the internal control worked. A failed stain on the 2024 block reads identically to a true negative. If the result came off the 2024 primary, repeat ER and PR on the 2026 lung core with percentage and intensity reported; if it was already run on the lung core, skip the restain and leave the door closed.

docs.title: The 2024-2026 interval
docs.text: Two records requests, one letter to the 2024 institution. The September 2024 operative report and gross description settle whether the specimen was morcellated; morcellation of an unrecognised leiomyosarcoma disperses tumour through the peritoneum, so a yes means pelvic and peritoneal disease must be actively excluded rather than assumed absent. And the pre-treatment CT with named RECIST target lesions has to happen before cycle 1, because the clean baseline window closes the day induction starts. Any interval imaging on disc bounds the growth rate of the lung disease, the closest available measure of tempo in a therapy-naive patient.

docs.title: Biomarkers measured, but not to decision resolution
docs.text: This case has almost nothing in the category, and that is itself the finding. The biomarker survey handed eight questions across (HRR/HRD, NTRK fusion, MSI/MMR, TMB, HLA class I, B7-H3, PRAME and MAGE-A4), and every one arrived never measured or not assessable rather than measured at insufficient resolution; each has its closing assay in the sections above. The one result on file whose resolution is in question is the ER/PR <1% itself: the assay is decision-grade, the specimen provenance is not, and the records step above is what closes that gap.
