docs.title: What this page is
docs.text:
This is the patient and caregiver version of a longer, more technical report Libby wrote about treatment options for your cancer. Libby is a research tool, not a doctor. It read the records you shared, went through the published studies and open clinical trials for treatments aimed at your cancer's specific features, and ranked what it found. This page walks through that list in plain language: what each option is, what the studies actually showed, the main risks, and where the evidence is thin. It covers the experimental and feature-targeted side of the picture; the standard approved treatments for this disease are tracked separately and belong to the conversation you have with your own oncology team.

One thing before anything else: nothing on this page asks you to wait. The tests described below run alongside your first chemotherapy cycle, not in front of it.

docs.title: What we know about your cancer
docs.text:
You already know the hardest part of this story, so I will say it once, plainly, rather than treat it as a footnote. The tumour removed from your uterus in 2024 was read as benign. It was not, and the error was found only this summer, when the spots in your lungs were biopsied and the original tissue was re-examined. It cost you 23 months. Nothing about that was your fault, and several of the practical steps below exist specifically to put that 2024 surgery's records and stored tissue to work for you now.

The diagnosis is high-grade uterine leiomyosarcoma, a rare cancer arising from the muscle wall of the uterus, and it has spread to both lungs. On scans the lung disease has an unusual, diffuse appearance, which matters later when we talk about measuring response and about ever treating the lungs directly. You have never smoked. You live at roughly 8,500 feet, which shifts what "normal" looks like on blood counts and oxygen readings, so every lab result in this treatment should be read against altitude-adjusted ranges rather than sea-level ones.

Two more facts shape the list. First, you have had no chemotherapy or any other body-wide treatment yet, so every first-line option is still fully open. And for what small comfort it offers, the fact that the lung disease took roughly two years to declare itself, rather than weeks, says something about its pace. Second, almost nothing about the tumour's molecular makeup has been measured. The one result that exists is hormone receptors: the tumour tested negative for both estrogen and progesterone receptors (under 1% of cells stained), which closes the door on hormone-blocking treatment, an approach that only helps when those receptors are strongly present. One caveat worth chasing: that stain seems to have been run on the 2024 tissue, and a stain that failed technically looks identical to a true negative. It is worth confirming the test's controls worked, and if there is any doubt, repeating it on the 2026 lung biopsy. Everything else, including the DNA-repair status that decides one of the options below, is unmeasured. Measuring it is itself the first step.

docs.title: What you told us matters most
docs.text:
Here I have to be honest about a gap: nobody has asked you. The preferences behind this report are entirely assumptions, made at intake so the analysis could run. They assume you would weight effectiveness heavily against side effects, that you have no hard lines on toxicity, and that you would consider clinical trials. None of that came from you. A 39-year-old preparing for aggressive chemotherapy plausibly wants maximum control of this disease, but that is an inference, and it should not harden into your chart without you saying it.

Four questions in particular are yours to answer, and they come back at the bottom of this page: whether the trade the planned chemotherapy offers, its real benefit against its real toxicity, is one you accept; whether you want clinical trials at all, and how far from home you would travel for one; what the hormonal aftermath of treatment means to you at 39, since a hysterectomy does not settle that question and no one has raised it; and how much insurance fighting you are willing to absorb, because your first treatment already involves some.

docs.title: The first step: tests that run alongside treatment, not before it
docs.text:
The top item on Libby's list is not a drug. It is a package of tests, and putting it first does not mean delay. Nearly all of it runs in parallel with your first chemotherapy cycle, none of it is toxic (blood draws, a heart ultrasound, a CT scan, stains on tissue already sitting in a pathology lab, and two records requests), and most results come back within one to three weeks while treatment is already under way.

A few items genuinely cannot be done later, and these are the only ones that touch the treatment calendar:

  • A heart ultrasound (echocardiogram) before the first dose of doxorubicin. Doxorubicin can strain the heart, the trial your regimen comes from required this scan before starting, and once the first dose is given the clean "before" picture is gone forever.
  • A CT scan that measures the lung tumours before treatment starts, so that every later scan has something honest to compare against.
  • A blood test for an inherited change in a gene called TP53, which guidelines say should happen before this kind of chemotherapy. This one is a decision, not a formality. If it finds an inherited change, that information touches your relatives, who may want testing of their own, and it could reshape how much doxorubicin your team is willing to give you over a lifetime. Whether you want that knowledge at all is your call, and the consent conversation should come before the needle.

The rest runs in the background while chemotherapy proceeds:

  • A single testing package on the stored 2024 tumour tissue: DNA and RNA sequencing plus a set of stains. This is what opens or closes almost everything below. It answers the DNA-repair question that gates Option 2, checks the proteins behind Options 3 and 5, and looks for a few rare any-cancer-type markers that, if positive, would open approved treatments through your regular care team. One practical note your team should handle in a single conversation: the 2024 tissue block is finite, so all the orders should be planned together before any one test uses it up.
  • The operative report from your 2024 surgery. The load-bearing question is whether the tumour was removed whole or broken up inside the abdomen (called morcellation). If it was broken up, the chance that cells seeded the abdomen is meaningfully higher (about 44 in 100 versus about 13 in 100 in one comparison), and your team would want to check the abdomen carefully before ever planning treatment aimed at the lungs.
  • Baseline blood counts, lung function, and oxygen readings, all recorded with your altitude noted, so that later changes on chemotherapy are read against your real baseline.
  • The hormone-receptor provenance check described above.

docs.title: The options
docs.text: These are in Libby's rank order. The ranking reflects the strength of the evidence, the risks, and the practical path to each option. It is not a verdict, and your oncologist may reasonably weigh things differently.

docs.title: Option 1 — Doxorubicin plus trabectedin, then trabectedin maintenance
docs.text:
This is the treatment your sarcoma oncologist has already planned, and it is also the best-evidenced treatment in this disease. Those two things do not always coincide. Here they do.

In the one large randomized trial, 150 people with newly diagnosed metastatic leiomyosarcoma received either doxorubicin alone, the long-time standard, or doxorubicin plus trabectedin followed by trabectedin maintenance. On the combination, half the patients went about 12 months before the cancer grew, versus about 6 months on doxorubicin alone. Longer term, half the people on the combination were still alive at about 33 months, versus about 24 months on the single drug. About two-thirds of the trial's patients had uterine primaries like yours; the trial was not sized to give that group its own precise number, but nothing suggests the benefit skipped them.

The price is heavy, and you should hear it in full. About 8 in 10 people on the combination had a severe drop in infection-fighting white cells, nearly half had a severe drop in platelets, and about 3 in 10 developed a fever while their white cells were low, which means hospital admission. That number has direct consequences for how cycle 1 gets written. Preventive white-cell booster injections should be in the orders for the very first cycle, not added after trouble arrives. And you need a written when-to-call plan for fevers before you leave the clinic. Doxorubicin can also injure the heart in a way that adds up over a lifetime of exposure, which matters more at 39 than at 70, so the running dose plan and a protective drug called dexrazoxane belong in the conversation before cycle 1. One altitude-specific trap: because your blood counts run naturally high at 8,500 feet, chemotherapy anemia can hide inside a number that looks normal by sea-level standards. The altitude-adjusted baselines from the workup are what make it visible.

Two more things to know. First, insurance. Trabectedin's official approval is for use after another chemotherapy has been tried, and you have not had one, so this first-line use is "off-label." That is a paperwork status, not a scientific one; the trial behind the regimen was itself first-line. But it makes an initial denial predictable, so the request should be filed as off-label from day one with the trial publications attached. A denial discovered late, at the pharmacy stage, is the one thing on this page that could actually delay your treatment. Second, the maintenance phase, likely the part you will be on longest, is the least-tested part of the plan. No study has compared continuing trabectedin against stopping once the cancer is controlled, and the maintenance side-effect details were never fully published, so monitoring borrows from trabectedin's record as a single drug: liver enzymes and a muscle enzyme called CK on a regular schedule. That gap is a reason to revisit, every few cycles, whether staying on maintenance is still earning its keep. It does not undermine the decision to start.

Whether you accept this regimen's trade of benefit against toxicity has not been asked. It should be, before the first bag hangs.

docs.title: Option 2 — Olaparib plus temozolomide, queued for the day the first regimen stops working
docs.text:
This option is only available if the DNA-repair test comes back positive. A minority of leiomyosarcomas lose part of their machinery for repairing damaged DNA; doctors call this homologous recombination deficiency, or HRD, and the BRCA genes are the best-known members of that machinery. The tumour testing in the first step looks for exactly this, which is why it goes out now: so the answer is already in your chart on the day it matters. If the test comes back showing normal repair, this option comes off the table. The other options on this page do not depend on it and still stand, and standard next-line treatments for this disease exist as well; those sit outside what this page ranks and belong to a separate conversation with your oncologist.

What the evidence shows: in a small study, 22 women with previously treated uterine leiomyosarcoma took olaparib, a pill that blocks a backup DNA-repair route (a PARP inhibitor), together with temozolomide, an oral chemotherapy. Tumours shrank in about 1 in 4 of them, and half the women went about 7 months before the cancer grew, a good result in a setting where single drugs often manage far less. A deeper analysis hinted that women whose tumours carried the repair defect did clearly better than those whose tumours did not, roughly 11 months versus 5 before growth. That hint came from 18 evaluable patients and used a specialized research assay that no clinical laboratory currently offers, so the panel your team can actually order is a reasonable stand-in rather than the same test. A positive result improves the odds without promising the 11-month figure. And keep the size of the whole thing in view: 22 women, everyone got the drug, no comparison group.

The costs. This combination is hard on bone marrow, and yours would just have absorbed the induction above, so documented count recovery comes before any prescription. The study reported its severe white-cell drops two different ways in its own publications, 75% in one place and 59% in another; that is a reporting problem worth knowing about, and the honest summary is "a majority." About a third of patients had severe platelet or red-cell drops. Finally, the dedicated trials are closed to new patients, so getting this combination today means another off-label insurance case, one that only holds together if a positive repair-test result is sitting in your chart. Which is, again, why the test goes out now.

docs.title: Option 3 — B7-H3 antibody-drug conjugate (a trial door, opened or closed by one stain)
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here is the tradeoff to weigh.

An antibody-drug conjugate is a targeted way of delivering chemotherapy: an antibody finds a particular protein on the cancer cell's surface and drags a potent drug payload to it. The protein here is called B7-H3, and the case for it in your disease is that it is very likely present. In a survey of 153 soft-tissue sarcomas, 97 in 100 carried B7-H3, and about 69 in 100 carried it at high levels. A single stain on your stored 2024 tissue, costing about two slides, answers whether yours does.

The caveats are substantial. A protein being present is not the same as the cancer depending on it, and related research suggests these drugs do little when the target sits at low levels, so a strongly positive stain is what would matter, not a barely positive one. No B7-H3 drug has any reported results in leiomyosarcoma, so there is no response rate to quote you, only the logic of the target. The open study is an early dose-finding trial: everyone gets the drug, there is no comparison group, and early participants can receive doses later shown to be too low. And an earlier drug in this same class was halted after safety findings in a prostate-cancer trial; whether that problem belonged to that one drug or travels with the class is not yet answered.

What Libby actually recommends here is modest. Run the stain now, while it is nearly free. Book nothing until your blood counts have recovered from induction and until someone has asked you directly whether you want a trial and how far you would travel for one. If the stain comes back strongly positive, this is probably the most reachable experimental door for a second or third line.

docs.title: Option 4 — FAP-targeted radioligand (a trial door, opened or closed by one scan)
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here is the tradeoff to weigh.

A radioligand is a small radioactive drug that circulates until it finds its target protein, then irradiates the cells immediately around it. The target here is FAP, a protein sarcomas are unusually rich in; in this disease the cancer cells themselves often carry it, at meaningful levels in roughly half of sarcomas. What makes this branch easy to explore is that the eligibility question is answered by a special PET scan rather than by tissue. The scan either lights up, meaning the target is there, or it does not, and a negative closes this door cleanly at no cost to you.

The concern is specific and worth taking seriously. FAP also sits on support cells inside bone marrow. In mouse experiments, an earlier FAP-directed treatment, an engineered cell therapy and so a different technology, caused severe marrow damage. A short-lived radioactive drug that clears through the kidneys is a genuinely different exposure than an engineered cell that persists in the body, but no human data yet says how different, and the trial that would generate that data has not reported. Add the obvious: your marrow will just have taken the heaviest chemotherapy in this disease, and no baseline blood count even exists yet. There is also no human efficacy data for this drug in sarcoma; it too is an early dose-finding study.

The recommendation is again screen-first. If and when the first regimen stops working, get the PET scan; it can piggyback on the restaging scan you would have anyway. Any actual treatment decision waits on the trial's own safety data and on your recovered blood counts.

docs.title: Option 5 — REC-617, a CDK7 inhibitor, after RB1 testing
docs.text:
This option carries caveats. Here is the tradeoff to weigh.

REC-617 blocks a protein called CDK7 that fast-dividing cancer cells lean on. The trial taking leiomyosarcoma patients requires a tumour stain showing loss of a gene called RB1, and there is an oddity in how that gate works in your disease: RB1 loss is nearly universal in leiomyosarcoma. So the stain almost always comes back "eligible," and what it routes you into is an early-phase trial arm with no leiomyosarcoma results at all. The scientific idea behind the drug was worked out with a different compound in a different cancer, small-cell lung cancer, and nothing yet shows it transfers. Then the practical load: it is a dose-finding study at one single hospital, a long trip from a home at 8,500 feet, and it requires a fresh biopsy and precisely measurable disease, both uncertain given the diffuse way your lung disease looks on scans.

What survives all that is cheap and worth doing: the RB1 stain joins the bundled tissue work at essentially no cost, and it keeps this door real rather than theoretical for a second line, if, and only if, you decide trial travel is something you want.

docs.title: Option 6 — Abemaciclib plus gemcitabine, in a first-line trial
docs.text:
This option was considered but not recommended. It is on the page because Libby surfaces what was weighed and rejected, not just what was kept. Here is what the concern was.

This trial pairs gemcitabine, a chemotherapy with a track record in this disease, with abemaciclib, a pill that pauses the cell-division cycle. It was the only recruiting first-line trial open to leiomyosarcoma patients who have never had chemotherapy, which is the only reason it was ever on the list. The problem is the schedule. Laboratory work suggests that a cell-cycle-pausing drug given at the same time as chemotherapy can actually shield some cancer cells from that chemotherapy. The version of this idea that worked in leiomyosarcoma lab models gave the drugs in sequence, one after the other, and this trial gives them together. On top of that, joining a first-line trial would spend something you only have once: your never-treated status is exactly what qualifies you for the proven regimen at Option 1, with its roughly 33-month survival result. Trading that for an untested combination whose own schedule argues against its rationale is a poor exchange.

One thing from this option deserves to outlive it: it existed partly to force the question of whether you want trials at all. That question still has not been asked, and it should be, whatever happens to this particular study.

docs.title: Treating the lung spots directly: a maybe-later, not a plan
docs.text: You may wonder why nothing above involves operating on or irradiating the lung tumours themselves, since your consulting oncologist has explicitly kept that on the table. The answer is that two gates sit in front of it, and neither has been passed. First, chemotherapy has to work. The surgical and radiation studies that report good local results were done in people with a small number of well-defined lung nodules, and your current pattern, spread through both lungs with a diffuse appearance, is what those studies screened out. If induction shrinks and sharpens the picture, the question gets asked again for real. Second, the 2024 operative report has to answer the morcellation question, because if tumour was broken up during that surgery, the abdomen needs a careful look before anyone plans lung-directed treatment. So: kept open, and meant seriously, but a question for later rather than a plan for now.

docs.title: Other ideas Libby logged and set aside
docs.text: Behind the six options above sit sixteen more possibilities the search turned up, kept on the record so nothing disappears silently. None is a live door today. Two are alternate versions of Options 3 and 4 run by other sponsors; one is the discontinued predecessor drug described under Option 3; several are early-stage ideas with no results in this disease to weigh; and the rest have no way in, because the trial is closed, restricted to a different sarcoma type, running only overseas, or built for an anatomy you do not currently have. Two are worth watching from a distance rather than joining: a trial abroad asking the exact continue-or-stop maintenance question Option 1 leaves open, and a closed trial of a similar first-line combination whose eventual results will either back up Option 1's evidence or complicate it.

docs.title: Questions to ask your oncologist
docs.text:
1. Is my echocardiogram scheduled before the first doxorubicin dose, and are the baseline CT and blood work ordered so that none of these tests delays cycle 1?
  2. Will preventive white-cell booster injections be in my first cycle's orders, and exactly when, and whom, do I call if I get a fever at home?
  3. Has the insurance authorization for this regimen been filed as off-label with the trial publications attached, and what is plan B if it is denied on the first pass?
  4. Before the germline TP53 blood draw: what would a positive result mean for me, for my doxorubicin planning, and for my family, and can I decide after that conversation whether I want the test at all?
  5. Has the DNA-repair (HRD) panel been sent from my 2024 tissue, and when will it be back? If it shows normal repair, what does my second-line plan look like instead?
  6. Was my hormone-receptor stain run on the 2024 tissue or the 2026 lung biopsy, did its controls work, and should it be repeated on the newer sample?
  7. Has the operative report from my 2024 surgery been requested, and was the tumour morcellated? If it was, what changes about my scans and about ever treating the lungs directly?
  8. Given that my blood counts and oxygen readings run differently at 8,500 feet, will my labs be read against altitude-adjusted ranges, and how will we decide, cycle by cycle, whether staying on trabectedin maintenance is still worth it?

And four questions to expect, or to raise yourself, because the answers are yours alone: whether Option 1's trade of benefit against toxicity is acceptable to you; whether you want clinical trials, and how far you would travel for one; what the hormonal aftermath of treatment means to you at 39; and how much insurance fighting you are willing to take on.

Reading the columns

These are candidate ideas that are earlier than clinical development, or not yet developed at all. Stage is how far the candidate has progressed (conceptual through IND-enabling). Evidence strength is the qualitative weight of the preclinical support. Counter-productive MoA is the mechanism-level risk that the candidate's own pathway could blunt its therapeutic goal. None of these options is enrollable today; they are a horizon scan, not the ranked clinical recommendations on the Recommendations table.

docs.title: Shared first step

Reading the columns

Toxicity burden is patient-level G3+ AE severity (Low / Moderate / High) summarized from trial publications. Counter-productive MoA is the mechanism-level risk that the intervention's own pathway could blunt the therapeutic goal — distinct from patient AEs. The board's endorse / dissent / veto state appears as pills under each intervention; full per-persona rationale lives on the board page.

docs.title: Standard of care options — ulms-highgrade-pulm-mets-er-pr-neg-qqvt
docs.text: The treatment strategies that are standard for this patient's situation, meaning a regulator approved them for a population that includes this patient or a major academic or clinical-society guideline carries them. This report runs alongside the targetable-feature ranking rather than in place of it, and it does not narrow what that ranking surfaces.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
• Standard of care options (offline HTML) — the same standard-of-care assessment, self-contained HTML that opens offline
  • Standard of care options (PDF) — print-friendly, grouped by next step

17 standard options assessed: 8 to consider now, 2 behind an open gate, 0 already received.

Seventeen standard-of-care options were assessed for this systemic-therapy-naive metastatic uterine leiomyosarcoma; eight are actionable now. The guideline-preferred systemic choice at this decision point is single-agent doxorubicin, graded I,A by BSG 2025 and on the US label for metastatic soft tissue sarcoma. The planned doxorubicin plus trabectedin combination outperformed it in LMS-04 but is off-label first line and ranked on the Experimental table, so both regimens, plus gemcitabine and docetaxel as the fallback if cardiac or pulmonary screening fails, are competing for one chemotherapy-naive slot. The other consider-now rows are the supportive scaffolding an anthracycline demands and this record lacks: baseline echocardiogram with cumulative-dose planning, primary G-CSF prophylaxis against a 28% febrile neutropenia rate, fertility and ovarian-function counselling whose window closes at cycle 1, early palliative care, and tumour NGS with germline TP53 testing.

Nothing standard has been spent yet. The 2024 hysterectomy was surgery for a presumed fibroid, not therapy, so every systemic line remains available; the sequencing risk runs the other way, since trabectedin maintenance would spend the on-label second-line trabectedin slot, and dacarbazine would close a PARP-trial door.

Two rows sit behind gates: the pembrolizumab and TRK-inhibitor tumour-agnostic approvals, untested rather than negative, both closed or opened by the NGS panel already ordered. Lung-directed consolidation waits on the 2024 operative report and on whether induction converts the anatomy. Later lines are honestly thin: eribulin's LMS subgroup is null and pazopanib's uterine evidence is a 44-patient retrospective pooling.

This report adds the standard options alongside the case's targeted ranking; it does not narrow or reorder the options ranked elsewhere on this page.

docs.title: Assessed and set aside
docs.text:
1 option(s) screened against this patient and set aside

Screened against this patient and found not to apply. Listed for the audit trail.

  • Aromatase inhibition (letrozole): Listed so its absence is explained rather than wondered about: endocrine therapy in uLMS belongs to receptor-expressing tumours, and hers stained under 1% for both ER and PR, which closes this door. The one residual thread is provenance: if the stain came off the 2024 block rather than current disease, the restain in the rank-1 workup could in principle reopen the question, though a true conversion is unlikely.

docs.title: How these sit alongside the targeted options
docs.text:
The ranked recommendations stay scoped to this case's targetable features, and nothing on this page changes that ranking. What this section adds is the sequencing: where a standard option and a targeted option compete for the same line, and where taking one would close the door on the other.

Competes for the same line of therapy

  • Doxorubicin, single agent: The guideline-preferred single agent and the planned off-label LMS-04 combination spend the same chemotherapy-naive first-line slot, and the same echocardiogram gates both. This row names the trade the treating team is already weighing; it does not resolve it. (interacts with: doxorubicin-trabectedin-lms04)
  • Gemcitabine + docetaxel: Holds the fallback slot for the same first-line window the ranked LMS-04 regimen occupies: a failed echocardiogram or pulmonary screen moves the first-line conversation here without touching the rest of the ranking. (interacts with: doxorubicin-trabectedin-lms04)
  • Pazopanib: At first progression this approved anchor and the ranked experimental doors ask for the same treatment slot; an on-label option a payer recognises exists at that line whichever way the team goes. Its wound-healing liability would also matter if metastasectomy ever became real. (interacts with: olaparib-temozolomide, b7h3-adc, fap-radioligand, rec-617-cdk7)
  • Doxorubicin + ifosfamide: A third occupant of the single chemotherapy-naive first-line slot the ranked LMS-04 regimen is planned to spend; listing it does not reopen the choice, it maps the slot. (interacts with: doxorubicin-trabectedin-lms04)
  • Eribulin: By third line the approved shelf in LMS is thin, which is the backdrop against which the ranked phase 1 doors were surfaced; this row shares that slot without arguing against them. (interacts with: b7h3-adc, fap-radioligand, rec-617-cdk7)

May foreclose a targeted option

  • Gemcitabine + dacarbazine (or dacarbazine alone): The randomized successor trial behind the ranked PARP branch excludes prior temozolomide or dacarbazine, so giving this regimen first would close that trial door while the HRR/HRD result that would make the PARP branch live is still unmeasured. The order in which this row is reached matters more than usual. (interacts with: olaparib-temozolomide)

May be foreclosed by a targeted option

  • Trabectedin monotherapy: Progression on LMS-04 maintenance is progression on trabectedin, which closes the on-label second-line use of the same drug; single-agent doxorubicin first line would leave it open. The upstream regimen choice decides whether this row survives, and that is a sequencing fact rather than advice. (interacts with: doxorubicin-trabectedin-lms04)

Comes before the targeted options

  • Fertility and ovarian-function counselling before gonadotoxic chemotherapy: Any oocyte retrieval or suppression decision has to land before the ranked induction begins. This names the timing pressure; it is not an argument to delay treatment, and the window is days rather than weeks. (interacts with: doxorubicin-trabectedin-lms04)

Can run alongside the targeted options

  • Baseline echocardiogram, cardiac surveillance and cumulative anthracycline planning: The echocardiogram in this row is the same one the Experimental table's rank-1 workup names as a true gate on cycle 1 of the ranked induction regimen; a failed screen moves the first-line conversation to this table's gemcitabine plus docetaxel row. (interacts with: gating-workup-baselines-molecular, doxorubicin-trabectedin-lms04)
  • Primary G-CSF prophylaxis through induction chemotherapy: Belongs in the cycle 1 orders of the ranked induction regimen. If single-agent doxorubicin is chosen instead, its 9% febrile neutropenia rate sits below the ASCO threshold, so the G-CSF call follows the regimen choice. (interacts with: doxorubicin-trabectedin-lms04)
  • Tumour NGS with germline TP53 testing before genotoxic chemotherapy: This is the same panel, consent conversation and block-allocation question the Experimental table carries at rank 1, and it is what opens or closes the pembrolizumab and TRK rows below. One requisition set serves both tables. (interacts with: gating-workup-baselines-molecular)
  • Early specialist palliative care alongside active treatment: Runs alongside induction and every later branch; it neither delays nor competes with any ranked option. (interacts with: doxorubicin-trabectedin-lms04)
  • Pembrolizumab (tumour-agnostic: MSI-H/dMMR or TMB-H): The gate closes on the same one-pass NGS panel the Experimental rank-1 workup orders; nothing extra is spent. A positive would move this row to on-label care at progression. (interacts with: gating-workup-baselines-molecular)
  • TRK inhibitor (larotrectinib or entrectinib), tumour-agnostic if NTRK fusion-positive: Priced by the same rank-1 requisition; the workup already specifies RNA-inclusive fusion calling because a DNA-only panel could return a false negative that reads as a closed question. (interacts with: gating-workup-baselines-molecular)

Comes after the targeted options

  • Pulmonary metastasectomy: Only becomes assessable if the ranked induction converts bilateral infiltrative disease into a resectable pattern, and after the rank-1 workup retrieves the 2024 operative report; the morcellation answer decides whether peritoneal restaging comes first. (interacts with: doxorubicin-trabectedin-lms04, gating-workup-baselines-molecular)
  • Stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) to pulmonary metastases: Like the surgical row, this is a consolidation question that only opens if the ranked induction converts the anatomy; the same operative-report and staging gates apply. (interacts with: doxorubicin-trabectedin-lms04, gating-workup-baselines-molecular)

Reading this report

An option earns a row here only if a regulator approved it for a population that includes this patient, or a major society's guideline carries it. What makes it standard names the endorsing body and, next to it, whether that endorsement was written for this patient's situation or for a different population. Fit to this patient is judged against the case profile alone, so an option the patient has already had and progressed on is marked rather than re-offered. This page is additive: it runs alongside the ranked recommendations and does not narrow, rerank, or filter the targeted options that ranking surfaces.

Back to case · Recommendations · Target validation · Biomarker survey · Trials · Evidence · Access guide · Board

Decision support, not medical advice

Libby is experimental. Standard of care is set by a treating team using the full clinical record, not by this page. Guideline versions and approvals move, eligibility here is inferred from a scrubbed profile rather than an examination, and nothing on this page is a recommendation to start, stop, or sequence a treatment. See PHI policy.

The letrozole trial selected on ER and/or PR positivity and found the longest PFS in strongly and diffusely positive tumors (PMID 24222211), so the question worth answering is not positive versus negative but whether any meaningful expression exists on current disease. docs.title: Unmeasured molecular landscape (the actionable gap)
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences essentialTumor NGS covering BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, RAD51C, RAD51D, ATM and the wider HRR gene set, with a reported genomic-instability / LOH scoreconfirmatoryNGS_panelarchival FFPE acceptable; the 2024 resection block is preferred for tumor content and volume, with the 2026 lung core held in reserve2-3 weeksOlaparib plus temozolomide (NCI protocol 10250, NCT03880019) and PARP-inhibitor trial entry at progression.Of everything untested here, homologous-recombination status is the entry this histology most earns: olaparib plus temozolomide produced a 27% objective response rate and a median PFS of 6.9 months in pretreated advanced uterine leiomyosarcoma, and 31% of the enrolled patients carried an HRR gene mutation (PMID 37467452). Uterine leiomyosarcoma has a recognised HR-deficient subset including BRCA2 deletion and mutation (PMID 37143137). Skipping it leaves the one non-cytotoxic branch in this case unopened at the point where first-line chemotherapy fails.Caris Life Sciences · MI Profile (whole exome plus whole transcriptome) preferredtest info · 4610 South 44th Place, Phoenix, AZ 85040 · 1-888-979-8669Exome-plus-transcriptome design returns the HRR gene set, genomic LOH, TMB, MSI and RNA fusions off one archival order, which is the bundling this case needs. Preferred over a DNA-only panel because it also closes the NTRK question in the same run.Foundation Medicine · FoundationOne CDx UStest info · 150 Second Street, Cambridge, MA 02141 · 1-888-988-3639Reports HRR genes and a genomic LOH score, but is DNA-only; a separate RNA fusion assay would still be needed.Myriad Genetics · MyChoice CDx UStest info · 320 Wakara Way, Salt Lake City, UT 84108 · 1-800-469-7423The genomic-instability score with the best analytical validation, but its threshold of at least 42 was set and validated in ovarian carcinoma, not sarcoma; treat the score as descriptive here rather than as a companion-diagnostic call.Tempus AI · xT plus xR UStest info · 600 West Chicago Avenue, Suite 510, Chicago, IL 60654 · 1-800-739-4137PMID 37467452PMID 37143137NCT03880019 essentialMismatch-repair protein IHC (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6), with reflex MLH1 promoter methylation and BRAF V600E if MLH1 is lostconfirmatoryIHCarchival FFPE; 4-5 unstained slides from either block, bundled with the other IHC in one cut3-5 daysPembrolizumab or dostarlimab under the tumor-agnostic MSI-H / dMMR indication, and Lynch syndrome referral.Four stains on a block that is already being cut close a tumor-agnostic PD-1 indication that would otherwise sit open as a question at progression. Uterine leiomyosarcoma is nearly always mismatch-repair proficient, so a negative is the expected result and the value is in settling it cheaply and early. Loss of any one protein in a woman in her thirties also carries Lynch syndrome implications for her and for first-degree relatives, which is a second reason not to leave it unmeasured.NeoGenomics Laboratories · MMR IHC panel preferredtest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 1-866-776-5907Runs the four-stain MMR panel and the other IHC in this case (PD-L1, HER2, B7-H3) as a single accession, which keeps the archival block cut to one pass.ARUP Laboratories UStest info · 500 Chipeta Way, Salt Lake City, UT 84108 · 1-800-522-2787Labcorp Oncology UStest info · 358 South Main Street, Burlington, NC 27215 · 1-800-845-6167Mayo Clinic Laboratories · MMR IHC with reflex MLH1 methylation UStest info · 3050 Superior Drive NW, Rochester, MN 55901 · 1-800-533-1710Quest Diagnostics UStest info · 500 Plaza Drive, Secaucus, NJ 07094 · 1-866-697-8378NCT02628067NCT02715284 essentialRNA-based fusion NGS panel covering NTRK1, NTRK2, NTRK3 (and RET, ALK, ROS1 in the same run)confirmatoryRNA_seqarchival FFPE acceptable; runs on the same 2024 resection block as the DNA panel, no separate procedure2-3 weeksLarotrectinib, entrectinib or repotrectinib under the tumor-agnostic NTRK fusion indication.This must be an RNA-based assay: NTRK breakpoints sit in large introns and a DNA-only panel misses them, so ordering comprehensive profiling without confirming RNA fusion calling would produce a false negative that reads as a closed question. Prevalence in uterine leiomyosarcoma is very low, but spindle-cell morphology is exactly the setting in which an NTRK-rearranged mesenchymal neoplasm is misclassified, and this tumor was already signed out as a benign leiomyoma once. A positive converts a chemotherapy-only plan into an oral TRK inhibitor with durable response rates.Caris Life Sciences · Whole transcriptome sequencing (MI Profile) preferredtest info · 4610 South 44th Place, Phoenix, AZ 85040 · 1-888-979-8669Whole-transcriptome sequencing calls fusions without a fixed breakpoint list and is bundled with the DNA panel already recommended, so no second block cut is needed.Foundation Medicine · FoundationOne Heme UStest info · 150 Second Street, Cambridge, MA 02141 · 1-888-988-3639Includes RNA sequencing for fusions; FoundationOne CDx does not, so the assay must be specified by name when ordering.NeoGenomics Laboratories · NeoTYPE Fusion Profile (RNA) UStest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 1-866-776-5907Tempus AI · xR RNA sequencing UStest info · 600 West Chicago Avenue, Suite 510, Chicago, IL 60654 · 1-800-739-4137NCT02576431NCT02568267NCT03093116 essentialValidated comprehensive genomic profiling panel reporting TMB in mutations per megabase (with MSI and the BRAF codon 600 call in the same report)confirmatoryNGS_panelarchival FFPE acceptable; same 2024 resection block and same accession as the HRR panel2-3 weeksPembrolizumab under the tumor-agnostic TMB-H indication (KEYNOTE-158, NCT02628067).TMB here is unknown rather than low, because no sequencing of any kind has been performed. Leiomyosarcoma is copy-number driven and usually low-TMB, so a value at or above 10 mut/Mb would be unusual, but the same order returns MSI, BRAF V600E, the HRR genes and the TP53/RB1/ATRX/MED12 backbone, which makes TMB close to free once the panel is placed. Specify a validated comprehensive assay: a TMB figure from a small hotspot panel does not satisfy the tumor-agnostic indication and is not portable between platforms.Foundation Medicine · FoundationOne CDx preferredtest info · 150 Second Street, Cambridge, MA 02141 · 1-888-988-3639The TMB reporting used to define eligibility in the KEYNOTE-158 tumor-agnostic cohort, so a borderline value from this assay is the one least likely to be challenged at trial or payer review.Caris Life Sciences · MI Profile TMB UStest info · 4610 South 44th Place, Phoenix, AZ 85040 · 1-888-979-8669NeoGenomics Laboratories UStest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 1-866-776-5907Tempus AI · xT UStest info · 600 West Chicago Avenue, Suite 510, Chicago, IL 60654 · 1-800-739-4137NCT02628067 highB7-H3 (CD276) IHC on tumor tissueconfirmatoryIHCarchival FFPE; 2-3 unstained slides, bundled into the same block cut as the MMR, PD-L1 and HER2 stains1 weekScreening access to B7-H3-directed ADC, bispecific and CAR-T programs; trial-only, with no approved agent in this class.B7-H3 carries the best odds of a positive result of any surface target in this histology: 97% of soft tissue sarcomas stained positive and about 69% were high in a 153-patient series across 15 subtypes (PMID 39478506). Nothing is approved against it, so a positive buys trial access rather than a prescription, but the ADC and bispecific programs generally require documented expression at screening and a later referral should not stall while tissue is hunted down. Expression is spatially heterogeneous, which argues for reading the larger resection rather than the core alone.NeoGenomics Laboratories · Custom IHC / pharma services preferredtest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 1-866-776-5907Offers B7-H3 as a custom or laboratory-developed stain alongside the routine IHC in this case; scoring is not standardised between sponsors, so treat the result as a screening signal rather than a portable score.Discovery Life Sciences UStest info · 601 Genome Way, Huntsville, AL 35806Runs B7-H3 IHC as a research-use assay; useful when a trial specifies its own antibody clone.MD Anderson Cancer Center, Department of Pathology UStest info · 1515 Holcombe Boulevard, Houston, TX 77030 · 1-877-632-6789Academic sarcoma pathology laboratories will often run the stain on request when a specific trial referral is in play.PMID 39478506 highHLA class I genotyping at 4-digit (allele-level) resolutiongermlineother5-10 mL whole blood (ACD or EDTA) or a buccal swab; no tumor tissue consumed1-2 weeksPRAME, MAGE-A4 and NY-ESO-1 directed TCR-T and ImmTAC programs, all of which are allele-restricted.Every HLA-restricted agent that could reach this patient names its restricting allele, most often HLA-A*02:01, so without a genotype the PRAME and MAGE-A4 rows sit as unassessable rather than negative. It is a blood draw that spends no tumor tissue and costs little, and the result either opens the TCR-T and ImmTAC class for later consideration or closes it cleanly. Ordering it now avoids a two-step delay if she progresses through first-line chemotherapy while a trial slot is open.Histogenetics · Allele-level HLA class I typing preferredtest info · 300 Executive Boulevard, Ossining, NY 10562 · 1-914-762-0400High-volume dedicated HLA laboratory with routine allele-level class I typing and a short turnaround, which is what the cell-therapy programs ask for; the general reference labs will do it but often at lower resolution unless specified.ARUP Laboratories · HLA class I typing, high resolution UStest info · 500 Chipeta Way, Salt Lake City, UT 84108 · 1-800-522-2787Labcorp Oncology UStest info · 358 South Main Street, Burlington, NC 27215 · 1-800-845-6167Versiti Diagnostic Laboratories · HLA typing, high resolution UStest info · 638 North 18th Street, Milwaukee, WI 53233 · 1-800-245-3117— highTP53, RB1, ATRX and MED12 status from the comprehensive tumor NGS panelco-mutationNGS_panelno additional tissue; reported from the same 2024 resection accession as the HRR and TMB panel2-3 weeksPrognostic framing and biological classification; informs trial matching but gates no current agent.These four genes are the mutational backbone of uterine leiomyosarcoma on exome sequencing (PMID 26891131) and they ride along free on the panel already being ordered for HRR, TMB and MSI. ATRX loss in particular tracks with the alternative lengthening of telomeres phenotype, aggressive histology and shorter survival in leiomyosarcoma (PMID 25229770), so it feeds the prognostic conversation and the urgency of the treatment plan. None of the four is directly druggable today, which is why this is a high rather than an essential row.Caris Life Sciences · MI Profile preferredtest info · 4610 South 44th Place, Phoenix, AZ 85040 · 1-888-979-8669Same accession as the HRR and fusion work; no separate order or specimen is required.Foundation Medicine · FoundationOne CDx UStest info · 150 Second Street, Cambridge, MA 02141 · 1-888-988-3639Tempus AI · xT UStest info · 600 West Chicago Avenue, Suite 510, Chicago, IL 60654 · 1-800-739-4137PMID 26891131PMID 25229770 highGermline multigene hereditary cancer panel including BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, RAD51C, RAD51D, ATM, TP53 and the Lynch genesgermlinegermline_panel5-10 mL whole blood (EDTA); drawn on the same visit as HLA typing2-4 weeksCascade testing for relatives, Li-Fraumeni surveillance if TP53 is positive, and germline confirmation of any somatic HRR finding for PARP-inhibitor trial screening.A germline result matters twice over here: it settles whether any somatic HRR finding is inherited, and at 39 with a high-grade sarcoma it carries direct implications for her siblings, children and any future pregnancy decisions. Uterine leiomyosarcoma is part of the Li-Fraumeni tumor spectrum, so TP53 belongs on the panel rather than being inferred from a somatic result. Somatic-only testing leaves this open, which is why the blood panel should go out alongside the tumor panel rather than as a reflex after it.Myriad Genetics · MyRisk Hereditary Cancer Test preferredtest info · 320 Wakara Way, Salt Lake City, UT 84108 · 1-800-469-7423Broad hereditary cancer panel with established insurance pathways and integrated genetic counselling, which matters for a patient who will need cascade testing arranged for relatives.Ambry Genetics · CancerNext-Expanded UStest info · 1 Enterprise, Aliso Viejo, CA 92656 · 1-866-262-7943GeneDx UStest info · 207 Perry Parkway, Gaithersburg, MD 20877 · 1-888-729-1206Labcorp Oncology · Labcorp hereditary cancer panel UStest info · 358 South Main Street, Burlington, NC 27215 · 1-800-845-6167PMID 37143137PMID 37467452 mediumMAGE-A4 IHC on archival tissue, ordered only if HLA class I typing returns a restricting alleleconfirmatoryIHCarchival FFPE; 2 unstained slides from the same cut as the PRAME stain1-2 weeks after the HLA resultMAGE-A4-directed TCR-T trials (SURPASS programme); trial-only for this histology, and conditional on HLA type.MAGE-A4 stays unknown until the HLA type is back, since the whole class is allele-restricted. Even a positive stain would not make her eligible for afamitresgene autoleucel, which was studied and licensed in synovial sarcoma and myxoid round cell liposarcoma rather than in sarcoma generally (PMID 38554725), so the realistic destination is a MAGE-A4 solid-tumor TCR-T trial of the kind run across histologies in HLA-A*02-positive patients (PMID 36624315). Stain it in the same antigen set as PRAME rather than as a separate order.NeoGenomics Laboratories · MAGE-A4 IHC preferredtest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 1-866-776-5907Same accession and same block cut as the PRAME stain, which is the only sensible way to order a two-antigen reflex.Discovery Life Sciences UStest info · 601 Genome Way, Huntsville, AL 35806Mayo Clinic Laboratories UStest info · 3050 Superior Drive NW, Rochester, MN 55901 · 1-800-533-1710PMID 38554725PMID 36624315 mediumPRAME IHC on archival tissue, ordered only if HLA class I typing returns a restricting alleleconfirmatoryIHCarchival FFPE; 2 unstained slides, ideally from the 2024 resection to preserve the lung core1-2 weeks after the HLA resultPRAME-directed ImmTAC and TCR-T programs (brenetafusp, IMA203); trial-only, and conditional on HLA type.PRAME cannot be called in either direction right now, because neither the antigen nor the restricting HLA allele has been tested. Sequence the two: if HLA typing returns A*02:01, PRAME IHC gates entry to the ImmTAC and TCR-T programs, and if it does not, this row closes with no tissue spent. Reported PRAME expression in leiomyosarcoma runs below the levels seen in synovial sarcoma, so a negative stain would not be surprising.NeoGenomics Laboratories · PRAME IHC preferredtest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 1-866-776-5907Carries PRAME on its routine IHC menu and can hold the order pending the HLA result.Discovery Life Sciences UStest info · 601 Genome Way, Huntsville, AL 35806Labcorp Oncology UStest info · 358 South Main Street, Burlington, NC 27215 · 1-800-845-6167Mayo Clinic Laboratories UStest info · 3050 Superior Drive NW, Rochester, MN 55901 · 1-800-533-1710— mediumRAD51 foci immunofluorescence assay for functional homologous-recombination deficiencyfunctional assayfunctional_assayarchival FFPE; feasibility should be confirmed with the receiving laboratory before slides are cut4-6 weeks; availability dependentRefines the olaparib plus temozolomide decision beyond HRR mutation status; supplements rather than replaces the somatic panel.In NCI protocol 10250 the RAD51 functional assay, not the mutation list, was what separated outcomes: median PFS was 11.2 months in homologous-recombination-deficient tumors versus 5.4 months in proficient ones (PMID 37467452). That makes it the most direct read on whether this tumor would benefit from olaparib plus temozolomide, and it can be positive in tumors with no HRR gene mutation. Clinical availability is the problem: it is largely an academic and research assay with no widely offered CLIA version, which is why this ranks medium rather than essential.Discovery Life Sciences preferredtest info · 601 Genome Way, Huntsville, AL 35806Research-services route for the assay. I could not identify a major US reference laboratory offering a CLIA-validated RAD51 foci assay as a catalogue test, so treat access as trial-linked or academic collaboration rather than orderable.MD Anderson Cancer Center, Department of Pathology UStest info · 1515 Holcombe Boulevard, Houston, TX 77030 · 1-877-632-6789Academic sarcoma programs running PARP-inhibitor studies are the realistic access point; ask whichever centre holds the trial slot.PMID 37467452PMID 37143137 mediumATRX IHC on both the September 2024 primary and the 2026 pulmonary metastasisheterogeneityIHCarchival FFPE; 1-2 unstained slides from each block, bundled with the other IHC1 weekWhether the 2024 primary is representative of the 2026 metastatic disease; prognostic rather than treatment-selecting.Paired sequencing of both blocks was floated and is not worth the cost here: no systemic therapy was given in the 23-month interval, so there is no treatment-driven selection pressure to have produced genomic divergence, and the 2024 resection has the tumor content the panel needs. Paired ATRX IHC is the cheap version of the same question, and ATRX loss with the ALT phenotype tracks with aggressive histology and shorter survival in leiomyosarcoma (PMID 25229770). Two stains on blocks already being cut will show whether the primary is representative of the metastatic disease.NeoGenomics Laboratories · ATRX IHC preferredtest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 1-866-776-5907Runs ATRX as part of its routine sarcoma and glioma IHC menu, and can take both blocks on one accession.ARUP Laboratories UStest info · 500 Chipeta Way, Salt Lake City, UT 84108 · 1-800-522-2787Labcorp Oncology UStest info · 358 South Main Street, Burlington, NC 27215 · 1-800-845-6167Mayo Clinic Laboratories UStest info · 3050 Superior Drive NW, Rochester, MN 55901 · 1-800-533-1710PMID 25229770PMID 26891131

docs.title: Bilateral pulmonary metastases with an infiltrative, possibly inflammatory radiologic pattern
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences essentialBaseline pulmonary function tests with DLCO, plus resting and ambulatory pulse oximetry recorded at residence altitudefunctional assayotherno tissue; spirometry with DLCO and oximetry1 weekFitness for LMS-04 induction with extensive bilateral lung disease, and the reserve calculation for later metastasectomy or SBRT.Bilateral infiltrative pulmonary disease in a never-smoker at 8,500 ft needs a measured baseline before induction, because a resting saturation that looks abnormal at sea-level norms may be her physiological steady state, and a saturation that looks acceptable may hide real loss of reserve. The same numbers later decide whether metastasectomy or SBRT is survivable once systemic control is achieved, which the consulting sarcoma oncologist explicitly kept on the table. Without a pre-treatment measurement, any on-treatment desaturation cannot be separated into progression, pneumonitis, or altitude physiology.—PMID 35835135 mediumPD-L1 IHC with the clone and scoring system matched to the intended agent, plus CD3 and CD8 T-cell infiltrate density, on the 2026 pulmonary metastasis coremicroenvironmentIHCarchival FFPE; 3-4 unstained slides from the 2026 lung core, bundled with the MMR and B7-H3 stains1 weekSupporting information for checkpoint-blockade discussion and for interpreting the infiltrative radiologic appearance; gates nothing on its own.PD-L1 gates no approval in soft tissue sarcoma, so this informs rather than decides, and the results that would actually open checkpoint blockade for her are MSI and TMB. It earns a row because the pulmonary lesions were read as infiltrative and possibly inflammatory, and someone will ask whether that appearance reflects an immune infiltrate or tumor growth pattern; a CD3 and CD8 read on the lung core answers that directly. Run it on the 2026 metastasis rather than the 2024 primary, since current immune phenotype is the point.NeoGenomics Laboratories · PD-L1 IHC (22C3, 28-8, SP142, SP263) with CD3 / CD8 preferredtest info · 9490 NeoGenomics Way, Fort Myers, FL 33912 · 1-866-776-5907Offers the licensed PD-L1 clones and the T-cell markers on one accession, which keeps a small core specimen from being cut twice.Labcorp Oncology UStest info · 358 South Main Street, Burlington, NC 27215 · 1-800-845-6167Mayo Clinic Laboratories UStest info · 3050 Superior Drive NW, Rochester, MN 55901 · 1-800-533-1710Quest Diagnostics UStest info · 500 Plaza Drive, Secaucus, NJ 07094 · 1-866-697-8378PMID 39478506

docs.title: ~23-month interval between resection of the primary (September 2024, signed out benign) and correct diagnosis (July-August 2026)
docs.text: PriorityTestTypeModalityTissueTurnaroundDecision gatedRationaleProvidersReferences highPre-treatment CT chest, abdomen and pelvis with measurable RECIST target lesions, read against any imaging from the September 2024 to July 2026 intervalfunctional assayimagingno tissue; contrast-enhanced CT, with prior outside imaging requested on disc1 weekRECIST baseline for LMS-04 response assessment and for any subsequent trial screening; also bounds disease tempo.Induction has not started, so there is still a clean window to fix a pre-treatment baseline with named target lesions; once cycle 1 is given, that window is gone and response assessment becomes an argument about which prior scan counts. Any imaging from the 23-month interval would bound the growth rate of the pulmonary disease, which is the closest thing available to a measure of tempo in a systemic-therapy-naive patient. The infiltrative, possibly inflammatory appearance also needs to be documented before treatment, because it will complicate the reading of every subsequent scan.—PMID 35835135 highRetrieval of the September 2024 operative report and gross pathology description: route of hysterectomy, whether power or manual morcellation was used, specimen integrity and margin statusconfirmatory—no tissue; operative note and gross description from the September 2024 hysterectomydays; records requestWhether peritoneal and pelvic disease must be actively excluded, and how the staging imaging field is drawn.A 6.0 cm myometrial mass removed as a presumed benign fibroid in 2024 may have been morcellated, and morcellation of an unrecognised leiomyosarcoma disperses tumor through the peritoneum and has been linked to worse outcomes (PMID 28209496; PMID 26646120). The current staging picture is pulmonary only; if the specimen was disrupted, peritoneal and pelvic disease has to be actively excluded rather than assumed absent. The answer sits in an operative note that nobody has yet had reason to re-read.—PMID 28209496PMID 26646120

docs.title: Research question
docs.text: In systemic-therapy-naive metastatic high-grade uterine leiomyosarcoma with bilateral pulmonary metastases and LMS-04 planned but not started, what non-standard-of-care interventions could target the hypothesised SMARCB1/INI1 deficiency, the confirmed HLA-A*02:01 restriction allele, or the unmeasured homologous-recombination and cell-cycle landscape, gated on a tissue workup that has not yet been ordered?

docs.title: Patient profile (scrubbed)
docs.text:
• Woman, age band 30-39. ECOG 1 is an intake assumption, never scored by a clinician, and the schema forced an integer where the honest value is unknown.
  • High-grade uterine leiomyosarcoma, spindle-cell morphology, confirmed by a reference pathology laboratory on both the pulmonary biopsy and the re-reviewed uterine specimen.
  • Stage IV: bilateral pulmonary metastases. The consulting sarcoma oncologist read the lesions as unusually infiltrative and possibly inflammatory.
  • Primary resected in September 2024 for a presumed benign 6.0 cm myometrial fibroid and signed out benign; the case was amended after re-review in July 2026, roughly a 23-month interval.
  • No systemic therapy has ever been given. Doxorubicin + trabectedin with trabectedin maintenance (LMS-04) is planned and not started.
  • ER <1% and PR <1% by IHC — confirmed, and a decision-relevant negative that closes the endocrine door.
  • SMARCB1 G344Afs*13 — plasma ctDNA only, IHC pending. Truncating, heterozygous, tumour fraction not supplied. No tissue confirmation.
  • TP53 Q52* — plasma ctDNA only, NGS pending, with an explicit clonal-haematopoiesis caveat and no paired white-cell sequencing.
  • HLA-A*02:01 — confirmed present (allele-level typing; also A*03:01, B*39:01, B*44:02, C*05:01, C*12:03).
  • MAGE-A4 / PRAME / NY-ESO-1 expression — not tested. Type first, stain second; the stain has not happened.
  • RB1, ATRX, MED12, HRD/BRCA, NTRK fusion, TMB — all NGS-pending on tissue. Plasma non-detection at unstated tumour fraction settles none of them.
  • MSI and mismatch repair — untested. PD-L1 — untested.
  • Four ctDNA variants of uncertain significance at 0.09-1.1% VAF recorded and explicitly not pursued; ERBB3 G914E at 0.9% is not a HER-family rationale.
  • Organ function: no laboratory values were supplied at intake or at this re-run. No LVEF, no pulmonary function tests, no oximetry, no baseline haemoglobin.
  • Resides at roughly 8,500 ft (~2,600 m). Lifetime never-smoker.
  • Geography band: US.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text:
• Efficacy/toxicity weight: 0.7 — an intake default, not her number.
  • Toxicity vetoes: none listed — because nobody asked, not because nothing is off the table.
  • Modality constraints: none listed — same caveat.
  • Trial preference: prefers trials — yes, another intake default.
  • Free text: the file says outright that no preferences were stated by the user and that every value in it is an assumption. Goals of care were never discussed at intake. A woman in her thirties with an aggressive induction planned plausibly implies curative or maximal-disease-control intent, but that is inference. prefers_trials is newly load-bearing at this re-run because both hypothesis branches the new molecular data opened are trial or off-label pathways.

docs.title: Target validation paths
docs.text: One block-release request decides most of what this case can become. Nearly every open question runs on two archival specimens, the September 2024 uterine resection and the 2026 pulmonary core, and the orders should go out together on a single request naming both. The INI1/SMARCB1 stain and the tissue SMARCB1 sequencing decide whether tazemetostat exists as an off-label route or the whole SWI/SNF branch closes; the HRR/HRD panel decides whether olaparib plus temozolomide (the NCI protocol 10250 regimen, NCT03880019) is winnable as an off-label authorisation at progression; the mismatch-repair and TMB reads decide whether tumor-agnostic pembrolizumab or dostarlimab is reachable; the RNA fusion panel decides whether a TRK inhibitor is even conceivable; and the antigen stains behind her confirmed HLA-A*02:01 decide whether IMA203 (NCT03686124) and its neighbours are worth a screening call. The clinic half, an echocardiogram, baseline labs and a scored ECOG, gates the planned doxorubicin plus trabectedin induction itself. Stains return in 3 to 5 days once a block is in the laboratory and tissue sequencing in 2 to 3 weeks; the slow step is administrative, because the 2024 block sits at an outside institution and nobody clinical currently owns the release request. A fully negative panel would still be a productive result: closed branches, a fitness baseline the planned chemotherapy needs anyway, and a clean record of what was looked for. The conversation about standard care from there belongs to the treating team, not Libby.

docs.title: SMARCB1
docs.text: The plasma G344Afs*13 frameshift is a hypothesis, not a finding, and the prior against it is steep: 170 of 170 uterine smooth-muscle tumours retained SMARCB1 in the one consecutive IHC series in this histology (PMID 34271067). The decision-grade read is INI1/SMARCB1 IHC (BAF47/SNF5 antibody, clone 25 or MRQ-27) showing complete loss of nuclear staining in tumour cells against an intact internal control; that is the result the tazemetostat basket accepted, with biallelic molecular loss as the alternative where the stain is equivocal (NCT02601950). Order the stain and the tissue SMARCB1 sequencing with copy-number and deletion calling at the same time rather than in sequence, because an equivocal stain with no molecular backup is a two-to-three-week delay this first-line window cannot absorb. Stain both specimens separately: the shedding compartment is the lung, and a metastasis-acquired event would be invisible on the 2024 block. Expectations should stay modest either way, since even a confirmed loss buys a 9 percent response rate in the INI1-negative non-epithelioid basket cohort (PMID 41882006). Germline SMARCB1 sequencing is a reflex, ordered only if tumour loss is confirmed; a reported schwannomatosis-associated uterine leiomyosarcoma (PMID 26001331) makes the question real but not urgent enough to front-load the counselling burden.

docs.title: HLA-A*02:01 and the cancer/testis antigens
docs.text: The typing is done and it is the expensive half of the gate: allele-level HLA class I typing confirms A*02:01. What is missing is every antigen result that would pair with it. PRAME is the most plausible positive of the three and both programs behind it, IMA203 (NCT03686124) and brenetafusp (NCT04262466), enrol on the same two-part gate she is halfway through; the operative caution is that IMA203 screens on the sponsor's IMADetect RT-qPCR, not IHC, so a local stain (clone EPR20330) is a one-slide screen whose negative closes the axis cheaply but whose positive still has to be reproduced on the assay that decides entry. MAGE-A4 is scored to a protocol threshold, at least 1+ staining in at least 10 percent of cells in SPEARHEAD-1 (NCT04044768), and the approved product is licensed in synovial sarcoma, not this histology; smooth-muscle sarcomas expressed MAGE-A4 in only a minority in the one multi-subtype series carried here (PMID 40152485). NY-ESO-1 earns one slide on the same block cut and no more, since expression runs low across sarcoma subtypes and the enrolling master protocol (NCT03967223) is currently histology-restricted away from her disease. The resistance check rides along free: ask the sequencing laboratory to report allele-specific HLA copy number, because somatic loss of A*02:01 would undercut the entire class at once, however strong the antigen stain.

docs.title: Unmeasured molecular landscape
docs.text: Plasma non-detection at unstated tumour fraction settles nothing, and that sentence covers most of this case. One validated comprehensive tissue panel is the single order that answers several questions at once: an MSI call, a TMB in mutations per megabase, the HRR gene set with a genomic-instability score, RNA fusion calling, and whether TP53 Q52* is in the tumour at all. Four mismatch-repair stains (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6) on the block already being cut are the fast orthogonal read, and either route closes or opens the tumor-agnostic PD-1 indications (NCT02628067, NCT02715284). The NTRK question needs RNA rather than DNA, because plasma capture misses breakpoints in the large NTRK introns, and a spindle-cell tumour once signed out as benign is exactly where an NTRK-rearranged mesenchymal neoplasm hides. The HRR/HRD result is the one that opens a branch rather than closing one: uterine leiomyosarcoma has a recognised HR-deficient subset including BRCA2 events (PMID 37143137), and olaparib plus temozolomide produced a 27 percent response rate with median PFS 6.9 months in pretreated disease (PMID 37467452), so this is the panel result an off-label authorisation would lean on. TP53 attribution deserves its own order: paired buffy-coat sequencing or tissue interrogation of the Q52* position separates tumour DNA from clonal haematopoiesis, which contributed features to 53.2 percent of cfDNA mutations in matched sequencing (PMID 31768066), and the answer calibrates how much weight the rest of the plasma report, the SMARCB1 call included, can carry. The RB1/ATRX/MED12 backbone with its IHC surrogate panel (sequencing concordance kappa 0.941, PMID 36788080) corroborates a diagnosis whose primary was once called benign and supplies the co-alteration context trial screens ask about; the Rb read in that panel is also what the abemaciclib study (NCT06498648, Rb-intact required) and the REC-617 study (NCT07633756, Rb-loss required) will each want to see before screening. A germline multigene hereditary panel runs on the same draw as any other blood work; the slow parts are counselling and insurance, not the assay.

docs.title: uLMS histology and fitness
docs.text: Three orders are essential before cycle 1 and none involves tumour tissue. A transthoracic echocardiogram with LVEF and strain, because the LMS-04 schedule carries doxorubicin into the cardiotoxicity surveillance band and no cardiac reference value exists (PMID 35835135; PMID 27918725; PMID 36017568). A metabolic panel with bilirubin, transaminases and creatine kinase plus a CBC, because trabectedin's dose-limiting hepatotoxicity needs a baseline to be read against, and her count needs an altitude-adjusted haemoglobin reference: at roughly 8,500 feet a sea-level-normed CBC will make real chemotherapy-induced anaemia look normal. And a clinician-scored ECOG with Karnofsky equivalent, because the 1 on file is an intake assumption, and nearly every protocol in scope, from the PRAME TCR-T program (NCT03686124) to olaparib plus temozolomide (NCT03880019), sets a 0-to-1 ceiling at screening. The FNCLCC grading parameters behind the phrase high-grade are a report request rather than a new assay; the reference-laboratory diagnosis itself is settled and needs no second opinion.

docs.title: Bilateral pulmonary pattern
docs.text: Nobody has measured the pulmonary reserve of a lifetime never-smoker living at 8,500 feet with infiltrative bilateral metastases. Baseline pulmonary function tests with DLCO, plus resting and ambulatory oximetry recorded at her own altitude and labelled as such, are the only reference against which on-treatment dyspnea can be attributed to progression, adaptation or treatment; several cell-therapy protocols in scope set saturation floors of 90 percent room air, one at 92, written for sea level. A pre-treatment CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis does double duty: it establishes whether the infiltrative pattern yields RECIST v1.1 measurable target lesions at all, better discovered before a screening slot than during one, and read against anything shot in the 2024-to-2026 interval it bounds the growth kinetics of disease that went untreated for roughly 23 months. PD-L1 with matched clone and scoring, plus CD3 and CD8 infiltrate density on the lung core, informs rather than decides: it is the one way to learn whether the inflammatory radiologic impression corresponds to anything in the tissue.

docs.title: ER/PR <1%
docs.text: The result is confirmed and it forecloses the endocrine branch, but the report on file does not say which specimen produced it. This is a records question first: if the under-1-percent call came from the 2026 lung core, nothing more is needed; if it came from the 2024 primary, a repeat stain on the metastasis costs two slides and makes sure the door is genuinely shut, since hormone-receptor expression can differ between a uterine primary and a distant metastasis.

docs.title: The 2024-2026 interval
docs.text: A 6.0 cm myometrial mass removed as a presumed benign fibroid may have been morcellated, and morcellation of an unrecognised leiomyosarcoma disperses tumour through the peritoneum and worsens outcomes (PMID 28209496; PMID 26646120). The staging picture is currently pulmonary only, and whether peritoneal disease must be actively excluded rather than assumed absent turns on an operative note nobody has yet had reason to re-read. Retrieving the September 2024 operative report and gross description is free, and it decides how wide the staging imaging field needs to be drawn.

docs.title: Biomarkers measured, but not to decision resolution
docs.text: Two results on file are real measurements that cannot carry a decision as they stand, and both are plasma non-detections. The NTRK call is a DNA assay's silence at unstated tumour fraction, which the survey behind this report declined to read as a negative; the assay that closes it is an RNA-based fusion panel on tissue, agnostic to where in the intron a breakpoint sits. The homologous-recombination call is the same problem one step worse: the plasma panel reported no BRCA1/2 alteration but cannot produce a genomic-instability score at all, so HR status is open rather than proficient, and closing it takes tissue NGS across the HRR genes with an HRD score plus a germline panel on blood. The distinction matters: nobody doubts these targets were looked for, the looking was just done with an instrument that cannot rule them out. Six further handoffs, mismatch repair, TMB, MAGE-A4, PRAME, NY-ESO-1 and B7-H3, were forwarded because they were never measured on any assay, not because an existing number fell short; each has a matching workup order above, and no handoff was dropped. Reading either group as negative would be the mistake; the record supports pending, nothing stronger.
